lessons.title: How the planet works
lessons.summary: Seasons, time zones, coordinates and the ocean's central heating.

cards.title: Why we have seasons
cards.text:
It isn't about distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of our winter.

Seasons come from Earth's tilt of about 23.4°. In June the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so sunlight hits it more directly and days are longer. In December it leans away.

deep.x: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4° relative to its path around the Sun, and it keeps pointing the same way in space all year (towards the Pole Star). So for half the year the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun, and for the other half it leans away.
Two effects that add up

x: **Angle**: when the Sun is high, a beam of light falls on a small patch of ground and heats it strongly. When it's low, the same beam spreads over a bigger area.
**Day length**: in summer the Sun is above the horizon longer, so the ground collects heat for more hours than it loses at night.

deep.x: Distance hardly matters. Earth's orbit is almost a circle: we are about 147 million km from the Sun in early January and about 152 million km in early July, a difference of only about 3%.
Opposite hemispheres

Because of the tilt, the hemispheres take turns. When Lisbon has summer, Rio de Janeiro and Maputo have winter, and Australians eat Christmas lunch on the beach. Near the equator the Sun is high all year, so there are wet and dry seasons rather than hot and cold ones.

deep.w: Summer happens when Earth is closest to the Sun
deep.r: Earth is closest in January; seasons come from the tilt

deep.x: Seasons are about the angle of sunlight and the length of the day, not distance from the Sun.

cards.title: Try it: time zones
cards.text: Earth turns 360° a day, so each hour of time difference is about 15° of longitude. Countries round that off to suit their borders, and a few, like India, use half hours. Move Lisbon's clock (winter time) and watch the world follow.

deep.x: The Sun is highest in the sky at noon, but "noon" happens at a different moment for every line of longitude. Before railways, each town kept its own **solar time**: Porto's clocks ran about 2 minutes ahead of Lisbon's. Fast trains and telegraphs made that chaotic, so in 1884 an international conference chose Greenwich in London as the zero line, and standard time zones followed.
360° ÷ 24 h = 15° per hour

x: Tokyo is near 140° E
Japan uses UTC+9

deep.x: Clocks follow politics, not just the Sun

Zones bend around borders. China spans about four zones' worth of longitude but uses one time (UTC+8), so in western China the Sun can rise after 9 a.m. by the clock. India uses UTC+5:30, and Nepal even UTC+5:45.
Portugal's odd neighbour

Spain lies mostly west of Greenwich, like Portugal, but it has used Central European Time since 1940. That is why Spanish clocks are an hour ahead of Portuguese ones and Spaniards eat dinner so "late" by the clock. Portugal itself tried Central European Time from 1992 to 1996 and went back, partly because winter mornings stayed dark until after 8:30.
France has more time zones than any other country, about twelve, thanks to overseas territories from the Pacific to the Caribbean.
A time zone is a deal between the Sun and politics: roughly 15° per hour, adjusted to suit countries.

cards.title: Latitude and longitude
cards.text:
Every place on Earth has two coordinates. Latitude says how far north or south of the equator you are, from 0° to 90°. Longitude says how far east or west of the Greenwich meridian in London, from 0° to 180°.

Viana do Castelo sits at about 41.7° N, 8.8° W.

deep.x: Coordinates turn the round Earth into a grid. **Latitude** lines (parallels) run east–west and measure the angle north or south of the equator. **Longitude** lines (meridians) run from pole to pole and measure the angle east or west of Greenwich.
How big is a degree?

One degree of latitude is always about 111 km. A degree of longitude is 111 km at the equator but shrinks towards the poles, because the meridians converge. At Viana do Castelo's latitude it is only about 83 km.

x: 1° of latitude ≈ 111 km
that's one nautical mile

deep.x: Why latitude was easy and longitude hard

Sailors could find latitude from the height of the Sun at noon or of the Pole Star at night, which Portuguese navigators did with astrolabes and quadrants in the 1400s. Longitude needs an accurate clock: you compare local noon with the time at home. Only in the 1760s did John Harrison's marine chronometer solve the problem at sea.
Your phone's GPS gives coordinates to about 5 decimal places of a degree, which pins you down to roughly a metre.
Latitude tells you how far from the equator you are; longitude tells you how far round the world from Greenwich.

cards.title: The ocean's central heating
cards.text:
Porto and New York sit at almost the same latitude, yet Porto's winters are far milder. Part of the reason is the Gulf Stream and its extension, which carry warm tropical water north-east across the Atlantic.

Westerly winds blowing off that warm ocean bring the heat ashore. Cold water returns south, completing a vast loop.

deep.x: Porto (41° N) has January days around 14 °C; New York (41° N) averages around 0 °C and often sees snow. Both sit beside the same ocean, so why the difference? Two things work together: warm water and the direction of the wind.
The warm conveyor

The **Gulf Stream** carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico up the American coast and out across the Atlantic. Its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, brings that warmth towards Ireland, Britain and Norway. As the water cools and becomes salty and dense near Greenland, it sinks and flows back south at depth.
Wind matters even more

At these latitudes the winds mostly blow from the west. Europe's west coast receives air that has crossed thousands of kilometres of relatively warm ocean. New York gets air from the frozen interior of North America. Scientists think this wind pattern explains much of the contrast, with the ocean current adding to it.

deep.w: The Gulf Stream alone keeps Europe warm
deep.r: Westerly winds off the ocean do much of the work too

deep.x: Scientists are watching whether this Atlantic circulation is slowing as the Arctic warms; a big slowdown could bring colder winters to north-western Europe even in a warmer world.
Western Europe is mild because westerly winds blow in off a warm ocean.

cards.title: Day and night

steps: Sun appears to rise in the east

cards.text: Earth spins once on its axis about every 24 hours, from west to east. That's why the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, and why Japan sees sunrise hours before Portugal.

deep.x: Earth turns on its axis from west to east, so the Sun, Moon and stars appear to move from east to west. One full turn relative to the Sun takes 24 hours: that's a **solar day**. Relative to the distant stars, a turn takes about 23 h 56 min, because Earth also moves along its orbit and must turn a little extra to face the Sun again.
Why you don't feel it
We spin at over 1,000 km/h, but smoothly and steadily, and the air turns with us. You only feel changes in speed, not speed itself, just as you can sleep on a smooth flight.
Sunrise travels west

Japan is about 9 hours ahead of Portugal, so its sunrise happens while Portugal is still in the night before. The line between day and night, the **terminator**, sweeps westward across the globe at the speed of the spin.

steps: Sun seems to rise in east

deep.x: Earth's spin is slowly getting slower, mainly because of the Moon's tides. About 400 million years ago a day lasted only around 22 hours.

deep.w: The Sun moves across the sky
deep.r: The Sun stays put; Earth turns beneath it

deep.x: Sunrise is not the Sun rising; it is your part of Earth turning to face it.

cards.title: The International Date Line
cards.text: Somewhere the calendar must change day. The date line runs roughly along 180° longitude through the Pacific; crossing it westward you jump a day ahead.

deep.x: Imagine flying west around the world, setting your watch back an hour in each zone. After 24 zones you'd have lost a whole day. Somewhere the calendar has to jump to keep the count honest, and that place is the **International Date Line**, roughly along 180° longitude, opposite Greenwich.
Why it zigzags

The line runs through the Pacific because few people live there, but it bends around island nations so that each one keeps a single date. In 2011 Samoa switched sides to share business days with Australia and New Zealand; it skipped Friday 30 December entirely.
A famous puzzle

When the survivors of Magellan's expedition reached Cape Verde in 1522 after sailing west around the world, their careful log said Wednesday, but the Portuguese on the islands said Thursday. They had not miscounted: sailing west, they had turned one fewer time relative to the Sun.
For a few hours each day there are three different dates on Earth at once, because some islands use UTC+14 and others UTC−12.
The date line is where the world agrees to restart the calendar day, bent to keep nations in one piece.

cards.title: Equinoxes and solstices
cards.text: Around 21 June, the northern hemisphere has its longest day (summer solstice); around 21 December its shortest. At the equinoxes in March and September, day and night are nearly equal everywhere.

deep.x: As Earth orbits, its tilt makes the Sun's highest point drift north and south over the year. The four turning points are named moments. A **solstice** ("Sun stands still") is when the Sun's noon height stops climbing or falling and turns back. An **equinox** ("equal night") is when the Sun is directly above the equator.
What happens at each

x: June solstice: Sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer (23.4° N); longest day in the north
December solstice: Sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn (23.4° S); longest day in the south
Equinoxes: Sun overhead at the equator; around 12 hours of day almost everywhere

deep.x: The tropics and polar circles are defined by these extremes. The Arctic Circle (about 66.6° N) marks where the Sun doesn't set on the June solstice.

deep.w: Equinox means exactly 12 hours of day
deep.r: Light bending in the air makes day a few minutes longer

deep.x: Portugal's São João and Santo António festivals in June grew out of much older midsummer celebrations around the solstice.
Solstices are the turning points of the Sun's yearly swing; equinoxes are the moments it crosses the equator.

cards.title: Daylight in Portugal
cards.text: In Lisbon, the longest day has about 14 h 50 min of daylight and the shortest about 9 h 30 min. Near the poles, summer brings the midnight sun.

deep.x: Day length depends on latitude and season. At the equator it stays near 12 hours all year. The further you go from the equator, the bigger the swing between summer and winter. Portugal, around 37–42° N, sits in the middle: a strong seasonal change, but nothing like Scandinavia's.

x: Lisbon, June: ~14 h 50 min
Lisbon, December: ~9 h 30 min
difference ≈ 5 h 20 min

deep.x: Midnight sun and polar night

North of the Arctic Circle the Sun doesn't set for some days around midsummer. At Tromsø, in northern Norway, it stays up from about late May to late July, and in midwinter it doesn't rise for about seven weeks. At the poles there is one six-month day and one six-month night.
Why summer evenings feel so long

In summer Portugal also moves its clocks forward an hour (UTC+1). Lisbon's sunset in late June comes after 21:00, so evenings stay light for outdoor dinners. Because of where Portugal sits in its time zone, winter sunrises come around 7:50.
The further from the equator, the bigger the gap between summer and winter days.

cards.title: Earth's layers
cards.text: Beneath the thin crust lies the hot mantle, then a liquid outer core and a solid inner core about as hot as the Sun's surface.

deep.x: Earth is about 12,740 km across, but nobody has drilled through more than about 12 km of it. Everything we know about the interior comes mostly from **seismic waves**: earthquake vibrations change speed and bend as they pass through different materials, and some kinds can't cross liquids at all.
Layer by layer

x: **Crust**: thin and rocky, about 5–10 km under oceans and 30–70 km under continents. Like the skin of an apple.
**Mantle**: solid rock, but so hot that over millions of years it flows slowly, like very stiff toffee. This movement drives plate tectonics.
**Outer core**: liquid iron and nickel. Its swirling creates Earth's magnetic field, which shields us from the solar wind and makes compasses work.
**Inner core**: solid despite the heat, because the pressure is enormous.

deep.x: The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia reached about 12.2 km in 1989. That's less than 0.2% of the way to the centre.

deep.w: The mantle is a sea of lava
deep.r: It's mostly solid rock that creeps very slowly

deep.x: We know Earth's deep interior mostly by listening to earthquakes echo through it.

cards.title: Plate tectonics
cards.text: Earth's crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Where they meet, we get earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

deep.x: The crust and the top of the mantle form a rigid shell, the **lithosphere**, broken into about 15 major plates and many smaller ones. They float on softer mantle below and drift a few centimetres a year, pushed and pulled by the slow churn of the mantle and by old, heavy plate edges sinking.
What happens at the edges

Where plates pull apart, as along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, magma rises and makes new sea floor. Where they collide, one may dive under the other, making deep trenches and volcanoes, or both crumple up into mountains. Where they slide past, stress builds and releases in earthquakes, as on California's San Andreas Fault.
Portugal's place

Portugal sits near the boundary between the Eurasian and African plates, which runs west through the Azores and the Gulf of Cádiz. Movement there caused the great **Lisbon earthquake of 1755**, which, with the tsunami and fires that followed, destroyed much of the city and killed tens of thousands of people.
The idea of drifting continents was proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912 and widely mocked; it was only accepted in the 1960s, once sea-floor maps showed spreading ridges.
Earth's surface is a slow-moving jigsaw, and the edges of the pieces are where the action is.

quiz.explain: The 23.4° tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere through the year.

quiz.q: Two places are 45° of longitude apart. Roughly how many hours apart are their clocks?

quiz.explain: Rotation makes the Sun appear to move.

quiz.explain: Roughly as fast as fingernails grow.

cards.title: If the world were 100 people
cards.text:
About 8 billion people live on Earth; the UN marked the milestone in November 2022. Shrink that to 100 people and roughly 59 live in Asia, 18 in Africa, 9 in Europe, 8 in Latin America, 5 in North America and 1 in Oceania.

India and China alone hold more than a third of humanity. Africa is the fastest-growing region.

deep.x: Big numbers are hard to picture. Shrinking 8 billion people to a village of 100 makes the patterns easier to see. Each person in the village stands for about 80 million real people, roughly the population of Germany.
Two giants

India and China each have about 1.4 billion people, so between them they make up about 35 of the 100 villagers. The next most populous country, the USA, would be about 4 villagers. Portugal, with about 10.6 million people, would be a little over one tenth of one person.

x: Portugal ≈ 10.6 million
8 billion ÷ 100 = 80 million per villager
10.6 ÷ 80 ≈ 0.13 of a person

deep.x: The village is changing

Africa's share is growing fastest, because its population is young and families are larger. Europe's share is shrinking: in 1950 it held around a fifth of humanity; today it holds under a tenth. By 2050, the UN expects about one person in four to be African.
More than half the world's people live inside a circle in Asia, centred on Myanmar, that covers only a small part of the globe.
Asia is the world's centre of population, and Africa is its centre of growth.

cards.title: The most spoken languages
cards.text:
Count everyone who speaks a language, natives and learners together, and English comes first, with Mandarin Chinese second. Count only native speakers and Mandarin leads by a long way.

Portuguese has around 260 million speakers worldwide, most of them in Brazil, which makes it the most spoken language in the southern hemisphere.

deep.x: How many people speak a language depends on what you count. **Native speakers** grew up with it. **Second-language speakers** learned it later, often for school, work or the internet. English is the giant of the second category: perhaps 1.5 billion people speak it, but only about 380 million as a first language.
Native speakers

By native speakers, Mandarin leads with over 900 million, then Spanish with around 480 million, then English. Estimates vary widely because censuses ask different questions and many people are bilingual, so treat all these figures as rough.
Portuguese on the map

Brazil has about 210 million speakers, more than 20 times as many as Portugal. Portuguese is the most spoken language south of the equator, ahead of Spanish, because Brazil, Angola and Mozambique are all mostly in the southern hemisphere.

deep.w: English is the most spoken mother tongue
deep.r: It leads only when learners are included

deep.x: There are two rankings of languages: by who was born into them, and by who uses them.

cards.title: Why cities sit on rivers and coasts
cards.text:
Before railways and roads, water was the motorway. Rivers and sheltered harbours offered drinking water, fertile soil, fish and, above all, cheap transport for trade.

That's why so many great cities stand at a river mouth or a natural harbour: Lisbon on the Tagus, Porto on the Douro, London on the Thames, Shanghai at the mouth of the Yangtze.

deep.x: For most of history, moving heavy goods by land was slow and expensive. A horse-drawn cart might carry a tonne; a river barge could carry dozens of tonnes with the same effort. Water was the cheapest motorway, so towns grew where water routes met.
The best spots

The most valuable places combined a sheltered harbour for sea ships with a river reaching inland. Lisbon sits on the wide Tagus estuary, one of Europe's finest natural harbours. Porto grew where the Douro could be crossed and where boats could bring wine down from the valley. London grew at the first point where the Thames could be bridged.
Still on the water

Railways and roads changed the rules, but the old cities stayed where they were, and trade still follows water. About 80% of world trade by volume still travels by sea. The world's busiest ports, like Shanghai, Singapore and Rotterdam, sit on coasts or river mouths.
Roughly 40% of humanity lives within about 100 km of a coast, which makes coastal cities especially exposed to sea-level rise.
Cities grew where water offered food, safety and above all cheap transport.

cards.title: How many countries are there?
cards.text:
The usual answer is 195: the 193 members of the United Nations plus two observer states, the Vatican City and Palestine. Some places, like Taiwan and Kosovo, govern themselves but aren't UN members, so counts differ.

The largest is Russia, at about 17 million km². The smallest, Vatican City, is under half a square kilometre.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"></g><text class="a" x="80" y="92" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:48px">193</text><text class="" x="158" y="92" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:38px">+ 2</text><text class="r" x="240" y="92" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:46px">= 195</text><text class="" x="80" y="124" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">UN members</text><text class="" x="158" y="124" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">observers</text><text class="" x="240" y="124" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">countries</text><text class="" x="160" y="164" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">observers: Vatican City and Palestine</text></svg>

deep.x: "How many countries?" sounds like a simple question, but it depends on who recognises whom. The most common answer, 195, counts the 193 UN member states plus the two observer states. Other lists give anything from about 190 to over 200.
The grey zones

x: **Taiwan** runs its own affairs, army and currency, but China claims it, and most countries don't formally recognise it.
**Kosovo** declared independence from Serbia in 2008; about half of UN members recognise it, including Portugal.
Places like Northern Cyprus or Somaliland function on their own but are recognised by almost no one.

deep.x: The biggest and the smallest

Russia covers about 17 million km², nearly a ninth of the world's land and almost 190 times the size of Portugal. Vatican City is 0.44 km², smaller than many city parks. Most countries are in between: Portugal is around the 110th largest.
South Sudan, which became independent in 2011, is the world's newest widely recognised country.
A country exists partly because others agree that it does, which is why counts differ.

cards.title: Population growth
cards.text: World population took until about 1800 to reach 1 billion, then grew rapidly with better medicine and food: 2 billion in 1927, 4 billion in 1974, 8 billion in 2022.

deep.x: For most of history, human numbers grew very slowly because many babies and children died. Then, from the 1800s, cleaner water, vaccines, better farming and modern medicine cut death rates sharply. Births stayed high for a while, so population shot up.
The demographic transition

Demographers describe a pattern seen in country after country. First deaths fall, then, a generation or two later, births fall too, as children survive, women gain education and work, and cities grow. Portugal went through this in the 20th century; many African countries are in the middle of it now.
Slowing down

Growth peaked at about 2% a year in the late 1960s and is now under 1%. The UN expects the world to peak at around 10.3 billion in the 2080s and then slowly decline. The speed at which billions were added shows the change: the jump from 7 to 8 billion took about 12 years.

x: 1 → 2 billion: ~123 years
3 → 4 billion: ~14 years
7 → 8 billion: ~12 years

deep.w: Population will keep exploding forever
deep.r: Growth is already slowing and should peak this century

deep.x: Population boomed when death rates fell before birth rates did.

cards.title: The most populous countries
cards.text: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023, each with about 1.4 billion people. Then come the USA, Indonesia and Pakistan.

deep.x: For centuries China was the world's most populous country. In 2023, according to UN estimates, India overtook it. China's population is now shrinking, while India's is still growing, so the gap will widen.
Why China stopped growing

China's one-child policy (1980–2015) and rapid urbanisation pushed birth rates very low. Today Chinese women have on average around one child each, well below the 2.1 needed to keep a population stable without migration. India's rate has also fallen, to about 2.
Who's coming up

Nigeria, already over 220 million, is growing fast and may pass the USA later this century. Pakistan, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are also climbing the table. Europe's largest country, Russia, is around ninth, and Germany is around 19th.
India alone has more people than the EU, the USA and Russia put together.
India is now number one, and the next big climbers are in Africa.

cards.title: Ageing populations
cards.text: Many rich countries, including Portugal, Italy and Japan, have low birth rates and long lives, so populations are ageing. Portugal has one of the oldest populations in Europe.

deep.x: A population ages when fewer babies are born and people live longer. Both are signs of success, better health and more choice for women, but they change the shape of society. The key number is the **fertility rate**: about 2.1 children per woman keeps a population stable.
Portugal's case

Portugal's fertility rate has been below replacement since the early 1980s. About a quarter of residents are 65 or older, one of the highest shares in the EU. Many young people have also emigrated, which speeds up ageing in the regions they leave.
What it means

x: Fewer workers per pensioner, putting pressure on pensions and health care
Schools closing in villages while care homes fill up
More demand for nurses, carers and accessible housing
Immigration becomes important to fill jobs

deep.x: Japan sells more adult nappies than baby nappies, a vivid sign of an ageing society.
Ageing is the price of long lives and small families, and it reshapes everything from pensions to schools.

cards.title: Life expectancy
cards.text: Global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900, from about 32 years to over 70. Portugal's is around 81 years.

deep.x: **Life expectancy at birth** is the average number of years a newborn would live if today's death rates stayed the same. It was low in 1900 mainly because so many children died young, not because adults rarely reached old age. Someone who survived childhood could often live to 60 or more.
What drove the rise

x: Clean water and sewers stopped cholera and typhoid
Vaccines against smallpox, measles and polio
Antibiotics from the 1940s
Better food and fewer famines
More recently, treatment of heart disease and cancer

deep.x: Big gaps remain

Japan and Switzerland reach around 84 years; some countries in Africa remain in the low 60s. Portugal is around 81–82, with women living about five to six years longer than men. Its infant mortality fell from among Western Europe's highest in the 1960s to among the lowest today.

deep.w: People in the past died at 30
deep.r: Average was low because so many children died

deep.x: Life expectancy soared mainly because far fewer children die.

cards.title: Migration
cards.text: About 280 million people live outside the country where they were born, around 3.5% of humanity. Portugal has been a country of emigration and, more recently, of immigration too.

deep.x: People move for work, safety, study, family or love. The UN counts about 280 million **international migrants**, people living outside their country of birth. That's a small share of humanity, but they matter hugely to economies through work and the money they send home.
Portugal: from leaving to arriving

For centuries Portugal sent people abroad, to Brazil, then in the 1960s to France, Germany and Luxembourg, often escaping poverty and the dictatorship's colonial wars. Over a million left in that decade. Since the 2010s, and especially the 2020s, Portugal has received many immigrants, notably from Brazil, India, Nepal, Cape Verde and Angola, plus retirees and remote workers from across Europe.
Money sent home
**Remittances**, money migrants send home, add up to more than all foreign aid combined. For some countries, like Cape Verde, they are a major part of the economy.
Around 1.5–2 million people born in Portugal live abroad, one of the largest diasporas in Europe relative to population.
Migration is small as a share of humanity but huge in its effect on the countries people leave and join.

cards.title: Portuguese around the world

items: Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe

cards.text: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries on four continents, from Brazil to Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde and Timor-Leste. Millions more Portuguese descendants live in France, the USA, Canada, Brazil and Switzerland.

deep.x: Portuguese spread with sailors, traders and colonists from the 1400s onwards. Today it's spoken by around 260 million people and is official in nine countries, linked through the **CPLP**, the Community of Portuguese Language Countries, founded in 1996.
The nine

Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe, Equatorial Guinea and Timor-Leste. It's also co-official in Macau, China. Each has its own accent and vocabulary: Brazilian and European Portuguese differ in pronunciation, spelling details and everyday words.
The diaspora

France has one of the largest Portuguese communities, perhaps over a million people of Portuguese origin, many from the 1960s emigration. Others live in Switzerland, Luxembourg (where they are about 15% of residents), the USA (especially Massachusetts and California), Canada and Venezuela. The Portuguese summer still fills with emigrants returning for August festivals.
Equatorial Guinea added Portuguese as an official language in 2010, mainly to join the CPLP, though few people there speak it.
Portuguese is a world language mainly thanks to Brazil, but its family stretches across four continents.

quiz.explain: Roughly 59 out of every 100 people live in Asia.

quiz.explain: Mandarin leads on native speakers; English leads when learners are included.
