lessons.title: Continents and oceans
lessons.summary: The big pieces of the world map.

cards.title: Seven continents
cards.text: The usual list is Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia/Oceania. Some countries count the Americas as one continent, or Europe and Asia as Eurasia.

deep.x: A continent is a big landmass, but there's no strict scientific rule for where one ends and another begins. The list we learn is partly geology and partly tradition, which is why different countries teach different numbers.
Not everyone counts seven

x: In Portugal, Spain and much of Latin America, schools often teach the Americas as one continent.
Some geographers merge Europe and Asia into **Eurasia**, since no sea separates them.
The Olympic rings stand for five inhabited continents: Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania.

deep.x: Size and people don't match

Antarctica (about 14 million km²) is bigger than Europe or Australia, yet has no permanent population. Australia is the smallest continent at about 8.6 million km². Asia is both the largest and the most populous, with about 60% of humanity on 30% of the land.
Geologists have identified a mostly sunken continent called Zealandia around New Zealand; about 94% of it lies under the sea.

deep.w: There is one official list of continents
deep.r: How many you count depends on convention

deep.x: Continents are partly nature and partly agreement, so the number depends on who you ask.

cards.title: Five oceans
cards.text: The Pacific is the biggest, larger than all the land combined. Then come the Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.

deep.x: All the oceans are connected into one World Ocean, but we divide it into five basins. The **Southern Ocean**, around Antarctica, was the last to gain wide recognition: the International Hydrographic Organization proposed it in 2000, and National Geographic added it to its maps in 2021.
The giant Pacific

The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all the continents together (about 149 million km²). It is also the deepest ocean, with an average depth of about 4 km, and is ringed by volcanoes and earthquake zones, the "Ring of Fire".
Portugal's ocean

The Atlantic is the youngest of the big oceans, opening about 180 million years ago as Pangaea split. It is still widening by a few centimetres a year. Portugal's sea zone, including the waters of the Azores and Madeira, is one of the largest in the EU, about 1.7 million km², around 18 times the country's land area.
Magellan named the Pacific ("peaceful") because his crossing in 1520–21 met calm weather, despite its fierce storms elsewhere.
The five oceans are really one connected World Ocean, with the Pacific alone bigger than all the land.

cards.title: Mostly water
cards.text: About 71% of Earth's surface is ocean. Most fresh water is locked in ice; less than 1% of all water is fresh and easy to reach.

deep.x: From space Earth is blue, because about 71% of its surface is ocean. Yet water is a thin film: all of it together would form a ball only about 1,400 km across, smaller than the Moon.
Where the fresh water is

Only about 3% of Earth's water is fresh. Most of that is frozen in the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland. Much of the rest is groundwater, some of it too deep to pump. The lakes, rivers and soil moisture we can easily use are a tiny fraction.

x: All water = 100%
Fresh water ≈ 3%
Easily reached (lakes, rivers) ≈ well under 1%

deep.x: Why water is renewable, but not unlimited

The water cycle constantly purifies water: the Sun evaporates sea water, leaving the salt behind, and it falls again as rain. The problem isn't running out of water globally but having enough in the right place at the right time. Southern Portugal and Spain face more frequent droughts, and the Algarve is turning to desalination to supplement supply.

deep.w: Earth has plenty of drinkable water
deep.r: Most is salty or frozen; usable fresh water is scarce

deep.x: The blue planet is mostly salty: usable fresh water is a tiny, precious sliver.

cards.title: The deepest point
cards.text: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, in the Pacific, is about 11 km deep, deeper than Everest is high.

deep.x: The Mariana Trench is a curved gash in the western Pacific, about 2,500 km long, near Guam. It forms where the old, heavy Pacific Plate dives beneath the smaller Mariana Plate. Its deepest known spot, the **Challenger Deep**, lies about 10,900–11,000 m below the surface.
Crushing pressure

Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere of pressure. At the bottom it's over 1,000 times the pressure at the surface, roughly the weight of an elephant pressing on every postage stamp of surface. It's also pitch dark and close to freezing. Yet animals live there, including tiny shrimp-like amphipods.

x: 10 m of water ≈ 1 atmosphere
10,900 m ÷ 10 ≈ 1,090 atmospheres
about 1,100 times surface pressure

deep.x: Who's been there
More people have walked on the Moon (12) than had reached the Challenger Deep before 2019 (3).
The ocean's deepest point is deeper than the tallest mountain is high, by about 2 km.

cards.title: Pangaea
cards.text: About 300 million years ago, the continents were joined in a supercontinent called Pangaea. It broke apart slowly; South America and Africa still fit together like puzzle pieces.

deep.x: Look at a map and the bulge of Brazil seems to slot into the Gulf of Guinea. That's no coincidence. About 300 million years ago almost all land was joined in one supercontinent, **Pangaea** ("all land"), surrounded by a single ocean, Panthalassa.
The evidence
Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, argued in 1912 that the continents had drifted apart. His clues still hold:

x: Coastlines that fit together, especially at the edge of the continental shelf
The same fossils, like the reptile *Mesosaurus*, in Brazil and southern Africa
Matching rock layers and old mountain belts across oceans
Traces of ancient glaciers in today's tropical lands

deep.x: Supercontinents come and go

Pangaea wasn't the first. Earth seems to assemble and break up supercontinents every few hundred million years. Geologists predict another in perhaps 200–250 million years; one model, "Pangaea Proxima", closes the Atlantic, which would push Portugal against America again.

deep.w: Continents have always been where they are
deep.r: They drift a few cm a year and have moved thousands of km

deep.x: The world map is a snapshot of a slow dance; 300 million years ago the continents were one.

cards.title: Where does Europe end?
cards.text: Europe and Asia share one landmass. By convention the boundary follows the Ural Mountains, the Ural River, the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, which means Russia and Turkey span both.

deep.x: Physically, Europe is a western peninsula of the huge Eurasian landmass. Its eastern border is a cultural agreement, not a coastline. The line most geographers use was drawn in the 1700s by the Swedish officer Philip Johan von Strahlenberg and later adjusted.
Countries on both sides

x: **Russia**: about 75% of its land is in Asia, but about 75% of its people live in the European part.
**Turkey**: Istanbul straddles the Bosporus; most of the country, Anatolia, is in Asia.
**Kazakhstan**: a small part lies west of the Ural River.
Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan sit on the disputed Caucasus border.

deep.x: Culture versus maps

Membership of European clubs adds to the blur. Cyprus is geographically in Asia but is an EU member. Israel, Azerbaijan and Australia compete in the Eurovision Song Contest. Football's UEFA includes Kazakhstan and Israel.
Istanbul is the largest city in Europe if you count its whole population, with more than 15 million people, ahead of Moscow and London.
Europe's eastern edge is a line people agreed on, not one nature drew.

cards.title: Islands
cards.text: Greenland is the world's largest island. Portugal's Atlantic islands, Madeira and the Azores, are volcanic; the Azores sit where three tectonic plates meet.

deep.x: An island is land surrounded by water and smaller than a continent. Australia is counted as a continent, which makes **Greenland**, at about 2.2 million km², the world's largest island. It's about 24 times the size of Portugal, but most of it is under an ice sheet up to 3 km thick, and only about 57,000 people live there.
How islands form

items: Hills cut off by sea rise

deep.x: Portugal's volcanic islands

Madeira rose from a volcanic **hotspot**, a plume of hot mantle rock beneath the African Plate. The Azores are more unusual: they sit at the **triple junction** where the North American, Eurasian and African (Nubian) plates meet, astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The islands are still active: Capelinhos on Faial erupted in 1957–58 and added new land, and earthquakes are frequent.
Flores and Corvo, the westernmost Azores islands, sit on the North American Plate, while the others lie on the Eurasian and African side: two continents' plates in one Portuguese region.
Portugal's Atlantic islands are volcanoes, the Azores sitting right where three plates meet.

cards.title: Ocean currents
cards.text: Ocean currents act like conveyor belts, carrying heat around the planet. The Gulf Stream warms western Europe; the cold Canary Current runs down Portugal's coast, keeping summer seas cool.

deep.x: Surface currents are driven mostly by steady winds, steered by Earth's rotation and the shape of the continents. In each big ocean they form giant loops called **gyres**: clockwise in the northern hemisphere, anticlockwise in the southern.
Warm and cold currents

Currents flowing away from the equator, like the Gulf Stream, carry warm water to cooler places. Those flowing towards the equator, like the **Canary Current** off Portugal, bring cool water south. That's why the sea at Viana do Castelo is often only around 17–19 °C in August, while the Mediterranean at the same latitude can reach 25 °C.
Upwelling: good for fish

In summer, northerly winds along Portugal's coast push surface water offshore, and cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below. This **upwelling** feeds plankton and makes Portuguese waters rich in sardines, one reason the sardine is the star of the Santo António festivals.
In 1992, a container of rubber ducks fell into the Pacific; the toys drifted for years and helped scientists track currents around the world.
Currents move heat around the planet: warm ones soften winters, cold ones cool summer seas.

cards.title: Seas and straits
cards.text: Narrow straits are vital shipping lanes: Gibraltar (Atlantic–Mediterranean), Suez Canal (Mediterranean–Red Sea), Hormuz (Persian Gulf), Malacca (Indian Ocean–Pacific), Panama Canal.

deep.x: A **strait** is a narrow channel between two bodies of water; a **canal** is one built by people. These chokepoints concentrate the world's shipping, so a blockage or conflict at one can raise prices worldwide within days.
Why they matter

x: About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Strait of Malacca carries roughly a quarter of world trade by sea, between China, India and the Middle East.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, saves ships about 7,000 km between Europe and Asia.
Ships too big for canals must go around the Cape of Good Hope, as the Portuguese first did in 1488.

deep.x: A lesson from 2021

In March 2021 the container ship Ever Given got stuck across the Suez Canal for six days. The canal normally carries around 12% of world trade, and hundreds of ships queued at each end. Attacks on Red Sea shipping from late 2023 again sent many ships the long way around Africa.
A few narrow channels carry a huge share of world trade, so trouble there is felt everywhere.

cards.title: Antarctica
cards.text: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent, covered by ice up to 4.8 km thick. It holds about 70% of the world's fresh water. No country owns it; the 1959 Antarctic Treaty reserves it for science.

deep.x: Antarctica is about 14 million km², about one and a half times the size of the USA. Almost all of it lies under an ice sheet averaging about 2 km thick, up to about 4.8 km. If all that ice melted, sea levels would rise by around 58 m.

items.l: sea rise if all ice melted

deep.x: Cold, dry, windy

The interior gets so little snow that it counts as a desert. Cold, dense air pours down the slopes towards the coast as **katabatic winds**, which can exceed 200 km/h. No humans lived there until scientific bases arrived; today a few thousand researchers stay in summer, around a thousand in winter.
A continent for science

The **Antarctic Treaty**, signed in 1959 by 12 countries and now joined by over 50 (including Portugal), bans military activity and mining, freezes territorial claims and keeps the continent for peaceful research. Seven countries have claims, some overlapping, but these are on hold.

deep.w: The North and South Poles are alike
deep.r: The Arctic is frozen ocean; Antarctica is a continent under ice

deep.x: Antarctica is a frozen desert holding most of the world's fresh water, shared by treaty for science.

quiz.q: Which is the largest ocean?
What was Pangaea?
options: A supercontinent joining all the land
quiz.explain: It broke apart over millions of years.

quiz.q: What share of Earth's surface is ocean?
quiz.explain: Most of the planet is water.

lessons.title: Climates and biomes
lessons.summary: Why deserts, rainforests and tundra are where they are.

cards.title: Climate vs weather
cards.text: Weather is what happens today; climate is the average pattern over decades. "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get."

deep.x: **Weather** is the state of the atmosphere at a given moment: today's rain in Braga or a heatwave in Évora. **Climate** is the long-term pattern, usually averaged over 30 years: how warm, wet and windy a place tends to be, including how often extremes occur.
Why forecasts fade but climate can be predicted

Weather is chaotic: tiny differences grow, so detailed forecasts lose skill after about a week to ten days. Climate is about averages, which are governed by bigger things like sunlight, oceans and greenhouse gases. You can't say whether 15 August 2040 will be sunny in Lisbon, but you can say August will very likely be hot and dry.
One cold day proves nothing

A snowy week doesn't disprove global warming, just as one hot day doesn't prove it. Climate change shows up in the trend: Portugal's average temperature has risen by well over 1 °C in the last century, and very hot days are now more frequent.

deep.w: A cold winter means the climate isn't warming
deep.r: Climate is the long-term trend, not one season

deep.x: Weather is your mood today; climate is your personality.

cards.title: Latitude and sunlight
cards.text: Near the equator the Sun is high all year, so it's hot. Towards the poles, sunlight arrives at a low angle and is spread out, so it's cold.

deep.x: The single biggest control on climate is how much sunlight a place gets, and that depends on latitude. Near the equator the midday Sun is nearly overhead all year. Near the poles it skims the horizon and disappears for months.
Two extra penalties for the poles

x: **Spreading**: a beam hitting at a low angle covers a larger area, so each square metre gets less energy.
**More air**: slanted light passes through much more atmosphere, losing more energy along the way.
**Bright ice**: snow reflects up to 80–90% of sunlight back to space, keeping cold places cold.

deep.x: Heat on the move

If each latitude kept its own sunlight, the tropics would be even hotter and the poles even colder. Winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward, smoothing the difference, and they also create local exceptions, which is why Lisbon is milder than places further inland at the same latitude.
The equator gets roughly two and a half times as much yearly sunshine energy as the poles.
The lower the Sun, the more its heat is spread thin: that's why the poles are cold.

cards.title: Climate zones
cards.text: The Köppen system classifies climates by temperature and rainfall. Most of Portugal has a Mediterranean climate (Csa/Csb): hot or warm dry summers and mild wet winters.

deep.x: In 1884 the German-Russian scientist Wladimir **Köppen** devised a system that still underpins climate maps. He noticed that plants reflect climate, so he classified places by temperature and rainfall patterns using letter codes.
Reading the code

The fifth main group is **E – Polar**. Extra letters add detail: "s" means dry summer, "w" dry winter, "f" no dry season. Then "a" means hot summers and "b" warm ones. So Lisbon's **Csa** reads: temperate, dry summer, hot summer. Porto and Viana do Castelo are **Csb**: dry, warm (not hot) summer.

x: C = temperate
s = dry summer
a = hot summer → Csa (Lisbon, Seville, Athens)

deep.x: Mediterranean climates worldwide

This climate type is rare, covering only a few percent of land. It occurs on west coasts around 30–45° latitude: the Mediterranean basin, California, central Chile, the Cape in South Africa and parts of southern Australia. All are famous for wine, olives and wildfire risk.
Some parts of the far southeast of Portugal are now close to the boundary of a semi-arid (BSk) climate.
A Köppen code compresses a climate into letters: Portugal is mostly Csa and Csb.

cards.title: Deserts
cards.text: Deserts get less than about 250 mm of rain a year. Many lie around 30° latitude, where dry air sinks. The Sahara is the largest hot desert; Antarctica is technically the largest desert of all.

deep.x: A desert is defined by dryness, not heat: less than about 250 mm of precipitation a year, and often more evaporation than rain. For comparison, Lisbon gets around 700 mm and parts of the Minho over 1,500 mm.
Why deserts form where they do

x: **Sinking air** around 30° latitude: air that rose and rained over the equator descends, warms and dries out (Sahara, Arabian, Australian deserts).
**Rain shadows** behind mountains (the Gobi, Patagonia).
**Cold coastal currents** that chill the air so it can't rise and rain (the Atacama, the Namib).
**Distance from the sea** in continental interiors.

deep.x: Not just sand

Only about a fifth of the Sahara is sand dunes; much of it is rock and gravel. Deserts can freeze at night because dry air holds little heat. The Atacama in Chile is the driest non-polar place on Earth: some weather stations there have recorded almost no rain for decades.

deep.w: Deserts are always hot and sandy
deep.r: Antarctica is a desert, and most deserts are rock, not dunes

deep.x: A desert is any place that hardly gets rain, which makes icy Antarctica the biggest of all.

cards.title: Rainforests
cards.text: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator with heat and rain all year. They cover about 6% of the land but hold over half of all species. The Amazon is the largest.

deep.x: Tropical rainforests grow within about 10° of the equator, where it's warm (around 25–28 °C) and wet all year, with typically 2,000 mm of rain or more. Rising hot, moist air forms clouds and afternoon downpours almost daily.
Why so many species?

Steady warmth and water mean plants grow all year, and the forest's layers create many different homes. A single hectare of Amazon can hold more tree species than all of Europe. Rainforests probably host over half of all land species, many still undescribed.
Rich forest, poor soil

Surprisingly, rainforest soil is often thin and poor. Nutrients sit in the living plants and are recycled fast by fungi and insects. Once trees are cleared for cattle or soy, the soil is quickly exhausted. Deforestation of the Amazon peaked in the early 2000s, fell, rose again in the late 2010s and fell sharply from 2023.

deep.w: The Amazon is the lungs of the world, supplying our oxygen
deep.r: It uses about as much oxygen as it makes; its value is carbon, rain and species

deep.x: Rainforests are thin strips of the planet holding over half its land life.

cards.title: Biomes
cards.text: A biome is a large region with similar climate, plants and animals: tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, Mediterranean scrub, temperate forest, taiga, tundra, grassland.

deep.x: A **biome** is a big community of plants and animals shaped by a similar climate. Unrelated places can look alike: the Portuguese montado, California's chaparral and Chile's matorral all have tough, evergreen shrubs because they share hot, dry summers.
Temperature plus rain

Two numbers predict a biome surprisingly well: average temperature and yearly rainfall. Hot and wet gives rainforest; hot with a long dry season gives savanna; cold and dry gives tundra. Altitude repeats the pattern: climb a high mountain and you pass through forests, then alpine meadows, then bare rock and snow.
Portugal's biomes

Portugal sits where Atlantic temperate forest (oaks and chestnuts in the north) meets Mediterranean woodland and scrub (cork and holm oak, rockrose, rosemary in the south). The **montado**, a cork oak savanna grazed by pigs, sheep and cattle, is a human-shaped landscape that supports rich wildlife and about half the world's cork.
The Mediterranean basin is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, with around 25,000 plant species, about half found nowhere else.
Similar climates produce similar-looking landscapes, even on opposite sides of the world.

cards.title: Mountains change climate
cards.text: Temperature drops about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m of altitude. Serra da Estrela can be snowy while Lisbon is mild. Mountains also force air up, making one side wet and the other dry (rain shadow).

deep.x: As air rises it expands, because there's less air pressing down from above, and expanding air cools. On average temperature falls about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb. That's why the summit of Kilimanjaro, almost on the equator, has glaciers.

x: Lisbon (sea level): yearly average ~17 °C
Torre, Serra da Estrela: ~2,000 m up

deep.x: The rain shadow
When moist wind meets a mountain, it's forced up. It cools, its moisture condenses, and it rains on the windward side. Coming down the far side, the now-dry air warms and gives little rain.
Examples close to home

The Gerês and Peneda mountains catch Atlantic storms and are among the wettest places in Portugal, with over 3,000 mm in places. Just inland, behind them, parts of Trás-os-Montes and the Douro valley are far drier and hotter in summer, perfect for port wine grapes.
Funchal and the high peaks of Madeira are only about 15 km apart, but the peaks can be frosty while the capital stays above 15 °C.
Climb 1,000 m and you lose about 6.5 °C; cross a mountain and you may lose the rain too.

cards.title: Monsoons
cards.text: In South Asia, summer winds reverse and blow in from the warm ocean, bringing months of heavy rain. Over a billion people depend on the monsoon for farming.

deep.x: "Monsoon" comes from the Arabic *mawsim*, meaning season. It describes winds that reverse with the seasons, bringing a wet season and a dry season. Portuguese sailors learned to ride these winds: they sailed to India in summer and returned in winter.
How it works

Land heats up faster than sea. In summer the Indian subcontinent becomes very hot, air rises over it, and moist air is drawn in from the Indian Ocean. Rising over land and the Himalaya, it pours down as rain. In winter the pattern reverses.
Life and death

India gets about three-quarters of its yearly rain in the June–September monsoon. A late or weak monsoon can mean poor harvests; an extreme one brings floods. Cherrapunji and Mawsynram in north-east India are among the wettest places on Earth, with over 11,000 mm a year.
The monsoon's arrival on the Kerala coast, around 1 June, is so important that it is tracked by Indian news like a national event.
A monsoon is a seasonal wind reversal: land heats, sucks in ocean air, and it rains for months.

cards.title: Portugal's contrasts
cards.text: The northwest (Minho) is one of Europe's rainiest regions; the interior Alentejo is hot and dry, often over 40 °C in summer. The Atlantic coast is mild; the interior has bigger temperature swings.

deep.x: Portugal is small, but its climate changes sharply over short distances. Two factors drive it: distance from the Atlantic, and mountains that catch rain in the north-west.
The Atlantic north-west

The Minho faces the westerly storm track, and the land rises quickly inland, squeezing rain out of the clouds. Winters are mild and wet, summers warm and fresh. That's why the landscape is green and why vinho verde grapes are grown high on pergolas.
The continental interior

Far from the sea, the Alentejo and the Beira Interior heat up and cool down quickly. Summer afternoons regularly pass 40 °C. Portugal's record, 47.3 °C, was set at Amareleja (Alentejo) in 2003. Winter nights in Trás-os-Montes or Guarda can drop below −5 °C.
Some years, Portugal sees snowfall in the north on the same day sunbathers are on the Algarve's beaches.
Portugal's climate runs from Atlantic green in the north-west to near-desert heat in the south-east.

cards.title: Microclimates
cards.text: Cities are warmer than the countryside (urban heat islands); valleys collect cold air at night; coasts are milder. Vineyards and gardens exploit these small differences.

deep.x: A **microclimate** is a small area whose climate differs from its surroundings: a city centre, a valley floor, a south-facing wall. Differences of a few degrees can decide whether lemons survive winter or vines ripen.
Urban heat islands

Asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight by day and release it at night, while buildings block cooling winds and there are few trees to give shade and evaporate water. City centres can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside on summer nights. Trees, parks and lighter-coloured roofs help cool them.
Cold air drains downhill

On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat and the air above it cools. Cold air is dense, so it slides downhill and pools in valleys. That's why frost often forms on valley floors while the slopes stay milder, and why farmers plant sensitive crops on hillsides.
Terraces and walls
The Douro's terraced vineyards exploit sun-baked schist slopes. Old walled gardens and south-facing walls store warmth, letting gardeners in cooler places grow figs and citrus.
In the Douro, vineyard plots are officially graded from A to F, partly on altitude, slope and how much sun they face.
Small differences in surface, slope and shelter create their own little climates.

quiz.q: Most of Portugal has which climate?
quiz.explain: Hot dry summers, mild wet winters.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does temperature drop per 1,000 m of altitude?
What causes a rain shadow?
options: Mountains forcing air up so rain falls on one side

lessons.title: Rivers and mountains
lessons.summary: The world's great rivers and ranges.

cards.title: The longest rivers
cards.text: The Nile and the Amazon compete for the title of longest river, each around 6,400–7,000 km depending on how it's measured. The Amazon carries by far the most water.

deep.x: Measuring a river sounds simple, but it isn't. Where exactly is the source: the farthest trickle, or the main spring? Where does it end in a wide, braided delta or estuary? And do you follow every bend? Different choices change the answer by hundreds of kilometres.
Nile or Amazon?

Most reference books give the title to the Nile, at about 6,650 km. But some Brazilian and Peruvian studies trace the Amazon from a more distant source in the Peruvian Andes and measure it at about 7,000 km, which would make it the longest. The debate is still open.
Length versus size

The Nile crosses the Sahara with little rain to feed it and loses water to evaporation and irrigation, so it carries surprisingly little. The Amazon is fed by rain over a basin almost as big as Australia.
The Yangtze in China is the longest river that flows entirely within one country.
Length depends on how you measure; the Amazon wins easily on the amount of water.

cards.title: The Amazon's flow
cards.text: The Amazon discharges about 20% of all river water entering the oceans, more than the next seven largest rivers combined.

deep.x: A river's **discharge** is the volume of water passing a point each second. The Amazon's averages around 200,000 cubic metres per second, enough to fill an Olympic swimming pool in about 1/80 of a second.
Why so much?

x: Its basin covers about 7 million km², about 40% of South America.
It drains the rainiest large region on Earth, with 2,000–3,000 mm of rain a year in places.
Hundreds of tributaries, a dozen of them longer than 1,500 km, feed it from both hemispheres, so some are always in flood.

deep.x: A river you can drink at sea

items.l: of all river water to oceans

deep.x: The Amazon pushes so much fresh water into the Atlantic that the sea stays noticeably less salty far from the coast. In 1500 the Spanish captain Vicente Yáñez Pinzón found fresh water far out at sea before he even saw land, and named it the "Mar Dulce", the sweet sea.
No bridge crosses the main Amazon anywhere along its length; the river is wide, floods seasonally and flows through few roads.
The Amazon carries about a fifth of all river water reaching the oceans.

cards.title: Rivers and civilisation
cards.text: The first civilisations grew along rivers: the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus and the Yellow River, with water, fertile soil and transport.

deep.x: The first cities, writing systems and states appeared in river valleys between about 3500 and 2000 BCE. Rivers offered reliable water in dry lands, yearly floods that left fertile silt, and a highway for boats.
From floods to states

Controlling water was hard work. Canals, dykes and storage needed many people to cooperate, calendars to predict floods and records to share out land and harvests. Some historians see this as one root of government, mathematics and writing.
Rivers still shape power

Egypt depends on the Nile for about 90% of its fresh water, which is why Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam upstream, completed in 2025, has caused tension. Iberia has similar, if calmer, arrangements: the 1998 **Albufeira Convention** sets how much water Spain must let flow into Portugal down the Tagus, Douro, Guadiana, Minho and Lima.
Ancient Egyptians measured the Nile's rise with "nilometers", stone staircases or wells marked with levels, and used the readings to set taxes.
Civilisation began where rivers made dry land fertile and forced people to organise.

cards.title: Portugal's rivers
cards.text: The Tejo (Tagus) is the longest river in Iberia, rising in Spain and reaching the sea at Lisbon. The Douro, Guadiana and Minho also start in Spain; the Mondego is the longest entirely Portuguese river.

deep.x: Most of Portugal's big rivers are Iberian rivers: they rise on the Spanish plateau (the Meseta) and flow west to the Atlantic, because the peninsula tilts gently towards the ocean. Portugal is downstream, so water management has to be shared with Spain.
The big four

x: **Tejo**: rises in Spain's Montes Universales, passes Toledo, reaches Lisbon in a broad estuary called the Mar da Palha.
**Douro**: cuts a deep valley through schist, home of the Douro wine region and port wine.
**Guadiana**: forms part of the border in the south and feeds the Alqueva reservoir.
**Minho**: marks the northern border with Galicia, past Valença and Caminha.

deep.x: Truly Portuguese

The **Mondego**, about 234 km, rises in the Serra da Estrela and flows past Coimbra to Figueira da Foz. Other wholly Portuguese rivers include the Vouga, the Sado and the Zêzere, a major tributary of the Tagus. The **Lima**, which reaches the sea at Viana do Castelo, rises just across the border in Galicia.
The Romans believed the Lima was the mythical river Lethe, which made you forget your past; soldiers reportedly refused to cross until their commander did.
Most of Portugal's great rivers begin in Spain, so the country lives downstream.

cards.title: The highest mountains
cards.text: All fourteen peaks over 8,000 m are in the Himalaya and Karakoram in Asia. Everest, at 8,849 m, is the highest above sea level.

deep.x: The 14 peaks above 8,000 m, the "eight-thousanders", are all in the Himalaya and the neighbouring Karakoram, on the borders of Nepal, China, India and Pakistan. They are there because the Indian plate is still pushing into Asia, lifting the land.
Measuring Everest

Everest's official height, 8,848.86 m, was agreed by Nepal and China in 2020 after new surveys with GPS and satellite data. It is called Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet. It was first climbed in 1953 by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay.
Highest depends on the question
Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo, only about 6,263 m high, is about 2 km farther from the planet's centre than Everest's.
The summit of Everest is made of marine limestone containing fossils of sea creatures, lifted from an ancient sea floor.
All the world's 8,000 m peaks rise where India is still ramming into Asia.

cards.title: Highest in Portugal
cards.text: Portugal's highest point is Mount Pico in the Azores, a volcano of 2,351 m. On the mainland, the highest is Torre in the Serra da Estrela, at 1,993 m.

deep.x: Portugal's highest summit is not on the mainland at all. **Mount Pico** on Pico island in the Azores rises 2,351 m straight from the Atlantic, a near-perfect volcanic cone. Its last eruptions on the island were in the 1700s, and it is considered dormant, not extinct.
Serra da Estrela

On the mainland, the **Torre** in the Serra da Estrela reaches 1,993 m. A stone tower was built on top in the 1800s, reportedly so the summit would reach a round 2,000 m. The range was shaped by glaciers in the last Ice Age: look for U-shaped valleys and glacial lakes like the Lagoa Comprida. It's the only place in Portugal with a ski resort.
From the coast you can see the difference
Climbing Pico takes about 3–4 hours up from the mountain house at 1,200 m. Numbers are limited and climbers must register, because fog can roll in fast.
On Pico's summit sits a small, younger cone called Piquinho, where warm volcanic gases still seep from the rock.
Portugal's roof is a volcano in the Atlantic; the mainland's is a glaciated granite range.

cards.title: How mountains form
cards.text: Most great ranges form where tectonic plates collide and crumple: the Himalaya (India hitting Asia), the Alps (Africa pushing into Europe). Others are volcanic, like the Andes' peaks.

deep.x: Mountains are made in a few main ways, almost all linked to plate tectonics. Rock can be pushed up, folded, piled up as lava, or left standing as everything around it wears away.
Collision ranges

When two continents collide, neither sinks easily, so the crust crumples and thickens. The **Himalaya** began rising when India hit Asia about 50 million years ago; they still rise a few millimetres a year. The **Alps** come from Africa's slow push into Europe. The **Andes** are different: the ocean plate dives under South America, and melting rock feeds a chain of volcanoes.
Old and young mountains

Young ranges like the Himalaya and Alps are tall and jagged. Old ranges have been worn down by hundreds of millions of years of rain, ice and frost. Northern Portugal's granites and schists are roots of a range formed when Pangaea assembled, about 300 million years ago, long since eroded to rounded hills.

deep.w: Mountains are permanent
deep.r: They rise for millions of years and are slowly worn away

deep.x: Most great mountains are the crumple zones of colliding plates, then sculpted by erosion.

cards.title: Glaciers
cards.text: Glaciers are rivers of ice that carve U-shaped valleys and fjords. They store fresh water but are shrinking almost everywhere as the climate warms.

deep.x: A glacier forms where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer. Over years the snow compacts into dense ice, which becomes so heavy that it flows downhill under its own weight, usually a few centimetres to a few metres a day.
Sculptors of landscape

Ice armed with rocks grinds the land like sandpaper. Glaciers turn V-shaped river valleys into broad **U-shaped valleys**, leave long ridges of rubble called moraines, and carve deep troughs. When the sea flooded those troughs after the Ice Age, Norway's **fjords** were born.
Retreating everywhere

Alpine glaciers have lost roughly 40% of their volume since 2000, and Switzerland alone lost about 10% in just 2022–2023. Scientists expect many small glaciers, including in the Pyrenees, to disappear this century. Melting land ice also raises sea levels.
About 20,000 years ago, the sea was so low that you could have walked from France to Britain, and Portugal's coast lay many kilometres west of today's.
Glaciers are slow rivers of ice that carve valleys, and almost all of them are shrinking.

cards.title: Lakes
cards.text: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake by area; Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest and oldest, holding about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.

deep.x: A lake is a body of water surrounded by land. They form in hollows left by glaciers, in rift valleys where the crust pulls apart, in volcanic craters, or behind dams built by people or by landslides.
The Caspian: lake or sea?

The **Caspian** covers about 370,000 km², about four times Portugal. It's slightly salty, a leftover of an ancient ocean. Whether it counts as a sea or a lake mattered for oil and gas rights; the five countries around it signed a special convention in 2018.
Baikal, the record-breaker

Lake **Baikal** in Siberia fills a rift where the crust is splitting apart. It is about 25 million years old and 1,640 m deep, holding about 23,000 km³ of water, more than all five North American Great Lakes together. Around 80% of its animal species, including the Baikal seal, live nowhere else.
The Azores' Sete Cidades lakes, one blue and one green, sit inside a volcanic crater about 5 km across.
The biggest lake is salty Caspian; the deepest and oldest is Baikal, a fifth of the world's surface fresh water.

cards.title: Waterfalls
cards.text: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall (979 m). Victoria Falls and Iguaçu are among the widest and most spectacular.

deep.x: Waterfalls form where a river meets a sudden drop: hard rock over softer rock, a fault, a cliff carved by glaciers, or a plateau edge. Water erodes the soft layer, undercutting the hard one, so many falls slowly retreat upstream.
Tallest and widest

**Angel Falls** (Kerepakupai Merú) in Venezuela tumbles 979 m from the flat top of a tepui, a table mountain. The water often turns to mist before reaching the bottom. **Victoria Falls**, between Zambia and Zimbabwe, is about 1.7 km wide, forming one of the largest sheets of falling water. Locals call it *Mosi-oa-Tunya*, "the smoke that thunders".
Iguaçu
On the border of Brazil and Argentina, **Iguaçu** is a chain of about 275 falls along almost 3 km. The Devil's Throat, a U-shaped chasm, takes about half the flow.
Angel Falls is named after Jimmie Angel, an American pilot who landed his plane on top of the tepui in 1937; it got stuck in the bog.
The tallest waterfall is a thin ribbon in Venezuela; the mightiest are wide curtains in Africa and South America.

quiz.q: Which river carries the most water?
quiz.explain: About a fifth of world river discharge.

quiz.q: What is Portugal's highest point?
How did the Himalaya form?
options: The Indian plate colliding with Asia

lessons.title: Europe
lessons.summary: A small continent with many countries and languages.

cards.title: Many countries in little space
cards.text: Europe has about 44–50 countries depending on how you count, with around 745 million people, on just 7% of the world's land.

deep.x: Europe is a small continent, about 10 million km², with a lot of countries. Its long, complicated coastline, mountains and peninsulas, plus centuries of kingdoms, wars and nationalism, broke it into many states. The count depends on whether you include Russia, Turkey, Kosovo and the Caucasus countries.
Dense and urban

Europe averages about 70 people per km², far denser than the Americas or Africa. Its core, from England through the Netherlands and Germany to northern Italy, is one of the most crowded regions in the world. Russia, including its Asian part, is huge but thinly populated.
Borders that moved

Europe's map has changed often. Since 1990 alone, the Soviet Union, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia have broken up, creating more than 20 states, while Germany reunified. Portugal is unusual: its land border with Spain has barely changed since the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, making it one of the oldest borders in Europe.
No point in Portugal is more than about 220 km from the sea, but in Europe's largest countries you can be over 1,000 km inland.
Europe packs dozens of countries and many languages into a small corner of the world.

cards.title: The European Union
cards.text: The EU has 27 member states that share a single market, free movement of people and many common laws. 21 of them use the euro; Bulgaria was the latest to join, in 2026.

deep.x: The EU began in 1951 with six countries pooling coal and steel to make another war between France and Germany impossible. It grew into a union of 27 states with about 450 million people, its own parliament, court and laws in many areas.
What membership means

x: **Single market**: goods, services, money and people move freely.
**Common rules** on product safety, competition, consumer rights and the environment.
**Funds** for poorer regions: Portugal has received large EU funds for motorways, schools and water systems.
A shared voice in trade deals with the rest of the world.

deep.x: The euro

The euro became a currency in 1999 and notes and coins arrived in 2002. Portugal was a founding member. Countries joined over time: Croatia in 2023, Bulgaria in January 2026, bringing the eurozone to 21. Others, like Denmark, Sweden, Poland and Hungary, keep their own currencies.

deep.w: The EU and Europe are the same thing
deep.r: Norway, Switzerland and the UK are European but outside the EU

deep.x: The EU is a club of 27 democracies sharing a market, many laws and, for most, a currency.

cards.title: Schengen
cards.text: In the Schengen area, people cross borders without passport checks. It includes most EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

deep.x: The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 in the village of Schengen, in Luxembourg, where the borders of France, Germany and Luxembourg meet. Since 1995 its members have scrapped routine passport checks at their shared borders. Portugal was one of the first countries to apply it.
What it means in practice

You can drive from Valença into Galicia, or from Lisbon to Copenhagen, without showing a passport. In return, members check the external border more strictly, share a database of wanted people and stolen documents, and issue a common short-stay visa. Romania and Bulgaria became full members in 2025.
Not quite borderless

Countries can bring back temporary checks during emergencies, as many did during the 2015 migration crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. You should still carry ID, and airlines usually ask for it. From 2025 a new **Entry/Exit System** registers non-EU travellers' fingerprints and photos at the outer borders.
About 3.5 million people in the Schengen area cross an internal border every day, many to work in a neighbouring country.
Schengen turned many European borders into lines on a map that you cross without stopping.

cards.title: Languages
cards.text: The EU has 24 official languages. Most European languages belong to the Indo-European family: Romance (Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian), Germanic (English, German, Dutch) and Slavic (Polish, Czech).

deep.x: Most European languages descend from one ancestor, **Proto-Indo-European**, spoken perhaps 6,000 years ago somewhere around the steppes north of the Black Sea. Its descendants spread across Europe and into Iran and India, which is why Portuguese "mãe", German "Mutter" and Sanskrit "mātṛ" all sound alike.
Outside the big family

x: **Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian** are Uralic languages, related to each other but not to their neighbours.
**Maltese** is Semitic, a relative of Arabic, written in Latin letters.
**Basque** has no known relatives at all.

deep.x: Portuguese in the Romance family

Portuguese grew from the Latin spoken in the north-west of Iberia, shared a medieval ancestor with Galician (Galician-Portuguese), and absorbed words from Arabic, such as "azeite", "almofada" and "alface". Spanish and Portuguese share most of their vocabulary, though pronunciation differs a lot.

items.b: PT noite, ES noche, FR nuit
PT leite, ES leche, IT latte

deep.x: The EU translates and interprets between all 24 official languages, which makes over 550 possible language pairs.
Most European languages are cousins from one ancient family, with a few fascinating exceptions.

cards.title: Basque: a mystery
cards.text: Basque (Euskara), spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France, is unrelated to any other known language, probably older than the Indo-European languages around it.

deep.x: Basque, or **Euskara**, is a **language isolate**: no linguist has proven it related to any other language, living or dead. It's spoken by about 750,000 people in the Basque Country and Navarre in Spain and the French Basque Country, and understood by many more.
A survivor

Most scholars think Basque, or its ancestor, was already spoken before Indo-European languages arrived in western Europe, some 4,000–5,000 years ago. Place names suggest it once covered a wider area across the Pyrenees. It survived Roman, Visigothic and Arab rule, but also faced bans under Franco's dictatorship (1939–1975).
Revival
Since the 1980s, schooling in Basque, television and media have boosted it. Today most young people in the Spanish Basque Country can speak it, a rare case of a minority language growing.
Some Basque words may have passed into Spanish and Portuguese: "esquerdo/izquierdo" (left) is often traced to Basque "ezker".

deep.w: Basque is a kind of Spanish dialect
deep.r: It is unrelated to Spanish or any other known language

deep.x: Basque is Europe's linguistic survivor, older than the languages that surround it.

cards.title: Big economies
cards.text: Germany is Europe's largest economy, followed by the UK and France. Portugal's economy is mid-sized, with tourism, services, exports and manufacturing.

deep.x: Economists compare economies by **GDP** (gross domestic product), the total value of goods and services produced in a year. Germany's is around €4.3 trillion; Portugal's about €280 billion, roughly 1.5% of the EU's total.
Size versus wealth per person

Total GDP shows size; **GDP per person** shows how rich people are on average. Luxembourg, Ireland and Switzerland top that list. Portugal is about four-fifths of the EU average when adjusted for local prices, behind Spain and now also behind Czechia and Lithuania.

x: Portugal GDP ≈ €280 billion
population ≈ 10.6 million
≈ €26,000 per person

deep.x: Portugal's economy

Since the debt crisis of 2010–2014, when Portugal needed an EU–IMF bailout, it has cut its public debt sharply and run budget surpluses in recent years. Tourism has boomed, and the country makes over half its electricity from renewables in most years.

deep.w: A big GDP means people are rich
deep.r: Wealth per person depends on dividing GDP by population

deep.x: Germany is Europe's biggest economy; Portugal is mid-sized and catching up.

cards.title: Microstates
cards.text: Europe has tiny countries: Vatican City (0.44 km²), Monaco, San Marino, Liechtenstein and Andorra, which borders Spain and France high in the Pyrenees.

deep.x: Europe has five microstates, counting the Vatican. They survived as relics of medieval and feudal times, often under the protection of larger neighbours, and many thrive on tourism, banking or low taxes.
Quick profiles

x: **Vatican City**: about 0.44 km², headquarters of the Catholic Church, ruled by the Pope since 1929.
**Monaco**: about 2 km² on the Riviera, the most densely populated country, famous for its Grand Prix.
**San Marino**: claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, founded by tradition in 301.
**Liechtenstein**: between Switzerland and Austria; a leading maker of false teeth.
**Andorra**: in the Pyrenees, with two co-princes: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell.

deep.x: Malta is small but not micro
Malta, at 316 km², is the smallest EU member. All five microstates are outside the EU, though several use the euro by agreement.
Andorra has no airport and no railway; most visitors arrive by road from Spain or France.
Europe's microstates are medieval survivors that found modern niches.

cards.title: Rivers and mountains of Europe
cards.text: The Volga is Europe's longest river; the Danube flows through ten countries. The Alps are the highest range, with Mont Blanc at 4,806 m.

deep.x: Europe's great rivers were its first highways and remain freight routes today. Its mountains formed in different eras: the Alps are young, the Urals and Scandinavian mountains much older and lower.
The Volga and the Danube

The **Volga** flows entirely within Russia into the Caspian Sea. The **Danube** rises in Germany's Black Forest and reaches the Black Sea, passing through or along ten countries (more than any other river) and four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
The Alps

The Alps arc about 1,200 km across eight countries. **Mont Blanc**, on the French–Italian border, is about 4,806 m, though its icy summit changes height by a metre or two from year to year. Some count Mount Elbrus (5,642 m) in the Caucasus as Europe's highest, depending on where you draw the border.
The Rhine–Main–Danube Canal, completed in 1992, lets barges travel from the North Sea to the Black Sea.
The Danube links ten countries, and the young Alps form Europe's rooftop.

cards.title: Iberia

items.l: Strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest

cards.text: Portugal and Spain share the Iberian Peninsula, with Andorra and Gibraltar (British). The peninsula is separated from Africa by the 14 km Strait of Gibraltar.

deep.x: The **Iberian Peninsula** covers about 580,000 km² and is shared by Spain (about 85%), Portugal (about 15%), Andorra and the British territory of Gibraltar. A small corner also belongs to France. The name comes from the ancient Iberians, and perhaps from the river Ebro (Iberus).
A high, walled land

The heart of Iberia is the **Meseta**, a plateau about 600–800 m high, ringed by mountains. The Pyrenees form a wall with France, which is why Iberia developed its own history and climate. Its rivers mostly flow west into the Atlantic, through Portugal.
Gibraltar and Africa

Gibraltar is a limestone rock of about 6.8 km², British since 1713 and still claimed by Spain. Across the strait, about 14 km at its narrowest, lies Morocco, where Spain holds the cities of Ceuta and Melilla. The strait is the gateway between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
On a clear day you can see the mountains of Morocco from southern Spain, and Gibraltar's Barbary macaques are the only wild monkeys in Europe.
Iberia is a high plateau walled off by mountains and almost touching Africa.

cards.title: The north–south and east–west divides
cards.text: Europe's regions differ in climate, economy and history: Nordic welfare states, the industrial centre, the Mediterranean south, and former communist countries in the east.

deep.x: Generalisations about European regions are rough, but they capture real patterns in climate, wealth, religion and history. Many of these lines run back centuries.
North and south

Northern Europe is mostly Protestant, with cooler climates and, today, higher incomes. The south is mostly Catholic or Orthodox, sunnier and more dependent on tourism and farming. The euro crisis of 2010–2014 hit Greece, Portugal, Spain and Italy hardest, deepening talk of a north–south split.
East and west

After 1945, the Iron Curtain divided capitalist west from communist east. Since 1989, countries like Poland, Czechia and the Baltic states have grown fast; several have now caught up with or passed Portugal in income per person adjusted for prices.

deep.w: Eastern Europe is still much poorer than the south
deep.r: Several eastern states now match or pass southern ones

deep.x: Europe's regions differ, but the old lines between rich and poor are shifting fast.

lessons.title: Portugal's geography
lessons.summary: Districts, regions, rivers and islands.

cards.title: Shape and size
cards.text: Mainland Portugal is a rectangle about 560 km long and 220 km wide. With the Azores and Madeira, the country covers about 92,000 km² and has around 10.6 million people.

deep.x: Mainland Portugal is a tall rectangle on the western edge of Iberia, from Melgaço in the north to Cabo de São Vicente in the south-west. Its Atlantic coast runs for over 900 km, and its land border with Spain, about 1,200 km, is one of the oldest unchanged frontiers in Europe.
How big is that?

Portugal is about a sixth of Spain's size, a little larger than Hungary and a little smaller than Austria. Driving from Valença to Faro takes about 6 hours by motorway. Of the total area, the mainland accounts for about 89,000 km², the Azores about 2,300 km² and Madeira about 800 km².
The edge of Europe

**Cabo da Roca**, near Sintra, is the westernmost point of mainland Europe, at about 9.5° W. The Azores island of Flores reaches even further west, about 31° W, making Portugal one of Europe's westernmost countries.

x: Population ≈ 10.6 million
Area ≈ 92,000 km²
Density ≈ 115 people per km²

deep.x: The poet Luís de Camões described Cabo da Roca as the place "where the land ends and the sea begins", words now carved on a monument there.
Portugal is a narrow strip of Atlantic coast plus two archipelagos far out at sea.

cards.title: Mainland and islands
cards.text: Portugal includes two autonomous regions in the Atlantic: the Azores (nine islands) and Madeira (Madeira, Porto Santo and uninhabited islets).

deep.x: The Azores and Madeira are **autonomous regions**: each has its own elected government and regional parliament, which handle matters like health, education, transport and tourism. Defence, foreign policy and justice stay with Lisbon. Autonomy came with the 1976 Constitution, after the 1974 revolution.
Nine Azorean islands

x: **Eastern group**: São Miguel (the largest, with Ponta Delgada) and Santa Maria
**Central group**: Terceira, Graciosa, São Jorge, Pico and Faial
**Western group**: Flores and Corvo

deep.x: The regional government sits in Ponta Delgada, the parliament in Horta and some departments in Angra do Heroísmo, a balance between the old rival islands.
Madeira's archipelago

Madeira island holds almost all the people. Porto Santo, 40 km away, has a long golden beach. The Desertas and the Selvagens are uninhabited nature reserves; the Selvagens lie closer to the Canary Islands than to Madeira.
Corvo, the smallest Azorean island, has only about 400 inhabitants, the least populous municipality in Portugal.
Portugal stretches into the Atlantic through two self-governing island regions.

cards.title: North and south
cards.text: The north is greener, more mountainous and densely populated near the coast; the south is flatter and drier, with the Alentejo's plains and the Algarve's beaches. The Tejo roughly divides them.

deep.x: The Tejo is a rough natural dividing line. North of it, the land is higher, wetter and rockier, mostly granite and schist. South of it, it's flatter, lower and drier, with rolling plains, cork oaks and wide wheat fields.
Land and history

The pattern runs deep. In the north, land was divided again and again among heirs, creating tiny plots called **minifúndios** and a dense scatter of villages and parishes. In the Alentejo, land reconquered from the Moors was granted in huge estates, the **latifúndios**, worked by landless labourers. After 1974 these estates were the scene of land occupations and agrarian reform.
Food follows the land

The north eats caldo verde, cabbage, chestnuts and vinho verde; the south bread soups (açordas), olive oil, pork from acorn-fed black pigs, and robust Alentejo reds. The Algarve's flatter coastal strip grows citrus and almonds and draws most of the tourists.
Over half of mainland Portugal's area lies south of the Tejo, but only about a third of its people live there.
North of the Tejo is green, hilly and crowded; south is flat, dry and spacious.

cards.title: Coast and interior
cards.text: Most people live near the coast between Viana do Castelo and Setúbal. The interior has been losing population for decades, a challenge for services and fire prevention.

deep.x: Portugal's population is pulled towards the sea. The coastal strip from Viana do Castelo to Setúbal, with the Lisbon and Porto metropolitan areas, holds the great majority of the people, the industry and the jobs. Inland districts like Bragança, Guarda, Castelo Branco and Portalegre have far fewer people than a century ago.
Why the interior emptied
From the 1960s, people left the interior for Lisbon, Porto and abroad. Today many inland parishes have more deaths than births and more than a third of residents aged 65 or over.
Fire and abandoned land

When fields are abandoned, scrub and fast-growing trees like eucalyptus and pine take over, and fewer people are around to clear them. This makes summer wildfires larger. The fires of June and October 2017 killed over 100 people and pushed fire prevention and rural policy to the top of the national agenda.

deep.w: Portugal's population is spread evenly
deep.r: Most people live within about 50 km of the coast

deep.x: Portugal leans towards the sea: busy coast, emptying interior.

cards.title: Regions of the mainland
cards.text: Common regions (NUTS II): Norte, Centro, Área Metropolitana de Lisboa, Alentejo and Algarve. Older provinces like Minho, Trás-os-Montes and Beira are still used in everyday speech.

deep.x: Portugal has several overlapping maps. The 18 mainland **districts** date from 1835 and are still used for many purposes, such as car-free civil protection and football associations. The **NUTS II regions** are an EU statistical system, used to share out EU funds. And the old **provinces** live on in everyday speech and identity.

items: Alentejo (incl. Oeste e Vale do Tejo)

deep.x: The old provinces

People still say they're from the Minho, Trás-os-Montes, the Beira, the Ribatejo or the Alentejo. These traditional provinces were formally defined in 1936 and abolished as administrative units in 1976, but they still describe landscapes, accents, food and folklore better than any official map.
Municipalities and parishes

The units that run daily life are the **308 municípios** (councils) and their **freguesias** (parishes), around 3,000 of them. Portugal has no elected regional governments on the mainland; a 1998 referendum on creating them was rejected.
In 2024 the NUTS II map was redrawn: Lisbon split into Grande Lisboa and the Península de Setúbal, and Oeste and the Tejo valley moved into the Centro and Alentejo regions.
Districts, NUTS regions and provinces all coexist; the old provinces still define identity.

cards.title: The Minho

items: Ponte de Lima, Portugal's oldest town charter (1125)

cards.text: The Minho, in the far northwest, is green and rainy, known for vinho verde, granite villages, the Lima and Minho rivers, and towns like Viana do Castelo, Ponte de Lima and Braga.

deep.x: The Minho, Portugal's north-western corner, sits between the Minho and Douro rivers and faces straight into Atlantic storms. Its mild, wet climate makes it the greenest region in the country, a landscape of maize fields, vines on pergolas, granite walls and hillsides of oak and pine.
Vinho verde

"Green wine" refers to youth, not colour. It's light, fresh and often slightly sparkling, made from grapes like Alvarinho (especially around Monção and Melgaço) and Loureiro. Vines were traditionally trained high on trees and pergolas so that crops like maize and beans could grow below.
Culture and tradition

The Minho is known for **espigueiros** (granite granaries on stilts), the gold filigree and traditional costumes of Viana, and the Romaria d'Agonia in August. Ponte de Lima, with its medieval bridge, claims to be Portugal's oldest town, chartered in 1125.
Many espigueiros in Soajo and Lindoso, near Peneda-Gerês, are still used today and some are over 200 years old.
The Minho is Portugal's green, rainy, granite north-west, the land of vinho verde.

cards.title: Peneda-Gerês
cards.text: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects granite mountains, oak forests, wild Garrano horses, wolves and traditional villages along the Spanish border.

deep.x: The **Parque Nacional da Peneda-Gerês** covers about 700 km² in the far north, along the border with Galicia, where it joins Spain's Baixa Limia–Serra do Xurés park. It includes the Peneda, Soajo, Amarela and Gerês mountains, reaching 1,548 m.
Wild residents

The **Garrano** is a small, sturdy native horse that roams semi-wild in the hills. The park is a stronghold for the Iberian wolf, protected in Portugal since 1988, and for rare plants like the Gerês lily.
People in the park

Unlike many national parks, this one includes inhabited villages. Places like Soajo, Lindoso and Pitões das Júnias keep traditions such as communal grazing and the **brandas and inverneiras** system, where families moved between summer pastures up high and winter homes in the valleys. A Roman road, the Geira, crosses the park with many milestones still standing.
The ruined village of Vilarinho da Furna was flooded by a dam in 1972; in dry summers its stone walls reappear from the reservoir.
Portugal's only national park protects wild granite mountains and the villages that shaped them.

cards.title: Rivers and dams
cards.text: Portugal's big rivers have many dams for hydropower and water storage. The Alqueva reservoir on the Guadiana, completed in 2002, is one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes.

deep.x: Portugal has over 250 large dams. They store water from wet winters for dry summers, generate electricity and supply irrigation and drinking water. Some also help control floods. Most big hydroelectric dams are on the Douro, Cávado, Tejo and Zêzere.
Alqueva

The **Alqueva** dam on the Guadiana, closed in 2002, created a reservoir of about 250 km², one of the largest artificial lakes in Western Europe, with a shoreline over 1,000 km long. Its water irrigates over 120,000 hectares of the Alentejo, transforming dry farmland into olive groves, almond orchards and vineyards.
Costs and benefits

Dams flood valleys, villages and farmland, block fish migration and trap sediment that would otherwise feed beaches. The old village of Aldeia da Luz was rebuilt elsewhere for Alqueva. Hydropower is still a big part of Portugal's renewable electricity, varying from about 10% in dry years to 30% in wet ones, and some dams pump water back uphill to store wind and solar energy.
Dams let Portugal save winter rain for summer, at a cost to rivers and the coast.

cards.title: The Azores
cards.text: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Lisbon on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. They're volcanic, green and famous for crater lakes, hot springs, whales and tea plantations.

deep.x: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Lisbon, roughly a third of the way to North America. They grew from volcanoes along the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, at the meeting point of three tectonic plates, and they're still geologically active: earthquakes are common and some islands have hot springs and fumaroles.
Mild, wet and green

The climate is oceanic: mild all year (around 14–24 °C), humid and changeable, often with "four seasons in one day". The high pressure that forms in the region, the **Azores High**, shapes weather across Europe, bringing settled summers to Portugal.
Volcanic living

x: In Furnas, the **cozido das Furnas** stew is cooked for hours in pots buried in hot volcanic ground.
Pico's vineyards grow inside black lava walls, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape since 2004.
Gorreana on São Miguel is Europe's oldest tea plantation still working, since 1883.

deep.x: Former whaling lookouts (vigias) on Pico and Faial now guide whale-watching boats; about a third of the world's whale and dolphin species have been seen in Azorean waters.
The Azores are green volcanoes in mid-Atlantic, sitting where three plates meet.

cards.title: Madeira
cards.text: Madeira, about 1,000 km southwest of Lisbon, is a steep volcanic island with laurel forests (UNESCO), levadas (irrigation channels with walking paths) and its famous fortified wine.

deep.x: Madeira lies about 1,000 km south-west of Lisbon and about 600 km from Africa's coast. It's the top of a huge volcanic shield rising from the ocean floor, so steep that much of the island seems to stand on end. Its peaks reach 1,862 m at Pico Ruivo.
The laurel forest

The **Laurissilva** is a forest of laurel-type trees that once covered much of southern Europe millions of years ago. Madeira holds the largest surviving area, about 15,000 hectares, listed by UNESCO in 1999. It catches moisture from clouds and feeds the island's springs.
Levadas

Most rain falls on the wet north side, while farms and towns cluster on the sunnier south. From the 1500s, Madeirans cut **levadas**, narrow channels, into cliffs to carry water around the mountains. There are over 2,000 km of them, and the maintenance paths beside them are now famous walking trails.
Madeira wine

Madeira wine is fortified and then heated. Merchants found that casks carried through the tropics on ships improved, so producers began warming the wine on purpose. The result can last for well over a century.
Madeira's island records include Cristiano Ronaldo, born in Funchal in 1985, whose name is now on the island's airport.
Madeira is a steep volcanic garden, watered by ancient forest and hand-cut channels.

lessons.title: Africa
lessons.summary: A huge, young and diverse continent.

cards.title: Bigger than it looks
cards.text: Common world maps shrink Africa. It's bigger than the USA, China, India and most of Europe combined, at about 30 million km².

deep.x: Most world maps use the **Mercator projection**, invented in 1569 for sailors because it keeps compass directions straight. The cost is size: it stretches places more the further they are from the equator. Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but Africa is about 14 times larger.
Fitting the world inside Africa
Why projections distort

A sphere can't be flattened without stretching or tearing, just as you can't flatten an orange peel without splitting it. Every map chooses what to keep accurate: shape, area, distance or direction. Equal-area maps like the Equal Earth projection (2018) show Africa's true size.
Vast distances
From Tunisia to South Africa is about 8,000 km, and from Senegal to Somalia about 7,400 km. A flight from Lisbon to Johannesburg takes about 11 hours, longer than Lisbon to New York.

deep.w: Greenland is about as big as Africa
deep.r: Africa is about 14 times larger; Mercator maps exaggerate the north

deep.x: Africa is enormous; most maps simply shrink it.

cards.title: 54 countries
cards.text: Africa has 54 UN member states. Nigeria is the most populous (over 220 million), Algeria the largest by area.

deep.x: Africa has 54 internationally recognised countries, more than any other continent, about a quarter of the UN's members. Most current borders were drawn by European powers, particularly at the **Berlin Conference** of 1884–85, often with straight lines that ignored peoples, languages and geography.
Independence

Ethiopia and Liberia avoided long colonial rule. Most others gained independence from the 1950s to the 1970s. Portuguese colonies were among the last, after long liberation wars and the 1974 revolution in Lisbon. South Sudan, in 2011, is the newest.
The largest

**Algeria**, about 2.4 million km², is the largest by area, mostly Sahara. The DR Congo follows. The smallest mainland country is The Gambia, a thin strip along a river; the smallest overall is Seychelles, an island nation.
Western Sahara's status is disputed: Morocco controls most of it, but many countries and the African Union recognise the Sahrawi Republic.
Africa's 54 countries have borders mostly drawn by European powers in the 1880s.

cards.title: The youngest continent
cards.text: Africa's median age is about 19, compared with about 44 in Europe. By 2050, roughly a quarter of the world's people may live in Africa.

deep.x: The **median age** splits a population in half: half are older, half younger. In Africa it's about 19; in Niger and Uganda it's around 15–16. In Portugal it's about 47, one of the highest in the world. Roughly 40% of Africans are under 15.
Why so young?

Death rates, especially for children, have dropped sharply with vaccines, better nutrition and health care, while birth rates have fallen more slowly. In much of sub-Saharan Africa women have on average four or more children, though this is falling, especially in cities and where girls stay longer in school.
What it could mean

Economists talk of a possible **demographic dividend**: when many people are of working age and fewer are dependent children, economies can grow fast, as happened in East Asia. It depends on education, jobs and good government.
Every year roughly 10–12 million young Africans enter the job market, more than the entire population of Portugal.
Africa is young while Europe ages, and that will reshape the world this century.

cards.title: Languages
cards.text: Over 2,000 languages are spoken in Africa. Arabic, Swahili, Hausa, Amharic and Yoruba each have tens of millions of speakers. Portuguese is official in five countries.

deep.x: Africa is the world's most linguistically diverse continent after Asia, with perhaps a third of all the world's languages. Most fall into four large families, though some languages, like Hadza, are isolates.
Bridges between peoples

Because most countries have many languages, people use **lingua francas**: Swahili across East Africa, Hausa in West Africa, Arabic in the north. European languages left by colonisation, mainly English, French and Portuguese, are official in many states and used in government and schools.
Swahili

Swahili grew on the East African coast, mixing a Bantu base with many Arabic words from centuries of Indian Ocean trade. It even picked up some Portuguese words from the 1500s, such as *meza* (table, from "mesa") and *pesa* (money, possibly from "peso").
The clicks in Xhosa and Zulu came from contact with Khoisan languages; Xhosa has around 15 distinct click sounds.
Africa's thousands of languages are bridged by lingua francas like Swahili, Hausa and Arabic.

cards.title: Portuguese-speaking Africa
cards.text: Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau and São Tomé and Príncipe make up the PALOP. Luanda and Maputo are big, fast-growing cities.

deep.x: **PALOP** stands for Países Africanos de Língua Oficial Portuguesa. These five countries were Portuguese colonies until 1974–75, gaining independence after the Carnation Revolution ended the colonial wars. Equatorial Guinea later added Portuguese as an official language too.
Five different countries

x: **Angola**: rich in oil and diamonds; Luanda has around 9–10 million people.
**Mozambique**: long Indian Ocean coast, natural gas, Maputo as capital.
**Cape Verde**: ten volcanic islands, a stable democracy, many emigrants.
**Guinea-Bissau**: rice, cashews, the Bijagós archipelago.
**São Tomé and Príncipe**: tiny equatorial islands once famous for cocoa.

deep.x: Shared ties

Strong links remain: language, music like Cape Verde's morna (UNESCO heritage since 2019) and Angola's kizomba and semba, football, family ties and migration. Many people from Cape Verde, Angola and Guinea-Bissau live in Portugal.
Luanda and Maputo together have more Portuguese speakers than Lisbon and Porto combined.
The PALOP are five African nations bound to Portugal by language and a shared, often painful history.

cards.title: Natural wonders
cards.text: The Sahara desert, the Nile, Mount Kilimanjaro, Victoria Falls, the Serengeti's migrations and the Okavango Delta are among the world's great natural sights.

deep.x: Africa's landscapes are vast and varied: the world's largest hot desert, its longest river, great lakes in the Rift Valley, and wildlife spectacles found nowhere else.
The Great Migration

In the Serengeti (Tanzania) and Maasai Mara (Kenya), about 1.5 million wildebeest, with zebras and gazelles, move in a great loop following the rains and fresh grass. Crossing the Mara River, many fall to crocodiles.
The Rift Valley

The **East African Rift** is where Africa is slowly splitting apart. It created deep lakes like Tanganyika and Malawi, volcanoes like Kilimanjaro, and some of the oldest human fossil sites. In tens of millions of years, East Africa may become a separate landmass.
The Okavango
The Okavango river never reaches the sea. It spreads into a vast inland delta in Botswana's Kalahari, a green oasis teeming with elephants, hippos and birds. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Kilimanjaro, just south of the equator, has glaciers on its summit, though they have shrunk by over 80% in the last century.
Africa's wonders span desert, rift, river and the largest land migrations on Earth.

cards.title: Resources
cards.text: Africa holds large shares of the world's cobalt, platinum, diamonds, cocoa and many other resources. Turning them into broad prosperity remains a challenge.

deep.x: Africa holds a large share of the minerals the modern world needs. The DR Congo produces about 70% of the world's **cobalt**, vital for batteries in phones and electric cars. South Africa has most of the world's **platinum**. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grow over half the world's **cocoa**.
The resource curse

Being rich in resources doesn't guarantee prosperity. Economists talk of a **resource curse**: when wealth comes from a few mines or oil fields, it can feed corruption, conflict and dependence on volatile prices, while other industries struggle.
Breaking the pattern

Botswana is often cited as a success: diamond revenue, well managed since independence in 1966, helped it become an upper-middle-income country. Many governments now push to process minerals and cocoa locally, to keep more value at home.
Most of the world's chocolate is eaten in Europe and North America, while many cocoa farmers in West Africa earn only a few euros a day.

deep.w: Rich resources make a country rich
deep.r: Without strong institutions they can bring conflict and poverty

deep.x: Africa is resource-rich, but turning minerals into shared prosperity depends on how they're governed.

cards.title: Mobile money

steps: Pay and send money by SMS

cards.text: Africa leapt ahead with mobile money: Kenya's M-Pesa, launched in 2007, lets millions pay, save and send money by phone without a bank account.

deep.x: In 2007 the Kenyan mobile operator Safaricom, partly owned by Vodafone, launched **M-Pesa** ("pesa" means money in Swahili). Users deposit cash with a local agent, often a small shop, and can then send it by text message to anyone with a phone.
Why Africa led
Most people had no bank account and banks had few branches, but mobile phones spread quickly. Mobile money leapfrogged traditional banking, just as mobile phones leapfrogged landlines.
Effects

x: Workers in cities send money home to villages instantly and safely.
Small traders pay suppliers without carrying cash.
People can save, get small loans and buy insurance.
Studies in Kenya linked M-Pesa access to lower poverty, especially for women-headed households.

deep.x: Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for about two-thirds of the world's mobile money transactions by value; Portugal's MB Way, launched in 2015, is a smartphone cousin of the same idea.
Mobile money let Africa skip the bank branch and put finance on basic phones.

cards.title: The cradle of humankind
cards.text: Africa is where humans evolved. Fossils such as "Lucy" (3.2 million years old, Ethiopia) and the oldest Homo sapiens remains (about 300,000 years, Morocco) were found there.

deep.x: Africa is where our lineage split from that of chimpanzees, about 6–7 million years ago, and where our own species evolved. Humans spread to the rest of the world from Africa, mostly in the last 70,000 years or so.
Lucy

In 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, Donald Johanson's team found 40% of a skeleton of *Australopithecus afarensis*, about 3.2 million years old. She was about 1.1 m tall and walked upright but had a small brain. She was nicknamed after the Beatles song playing in the camp that night.
Jebel Irhoud

In 2017, fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco were dated to about 300,000 years old, pushing back the origin of *Homo sapiens* by about 100,000 years. They suggest our species evolved across Africa, not in one small "Eden".
Every person alive today, from Lisbon to Tokyo, carries DNA inherited from ancestors who lived in Africa.

deep.w: Humans evolved from chimpanzees
deep.r: Humans and chimps share a common ancestor; neither came from the other

deep.x: Every human family tree has its roots in Africa.

cards.title: Growth and challenges
cards.text: Many African economies are among the world's fastest growing, with booming tech hubs in Lagos, Nairobi and Kigali. Challenges include poverty, conflict in some regions and climate risks.

deep.x: Africa's story is often told as all crisis or all boom. The reality is both, and it varies hugely between 54 countries. In recent years several economies, such as Ethiopia, Rwanda, Côte d'Ivoire and Tanzania, have grown at 5–8% a year.
Tech hubs

**Lagos** has fintech companies valued in the billions. **Nairobi**'s "Silicon Savannah" grew around M-Pesa. **Kigali** in Rwanda has made itself a clean, well-run conference and tech centre. Africa's huge solar potential and its minerals could power its future.
Trade within Africa
The **African Continental Free Trade Area** (AfCFTA), launched in 2021, aims to cut tariffs between members and boost trade within the continent, which is currently low compared with Europe or Asia.
Climate
Africa produces under 4% of global greenhouse gases but faces severe climate impacts: droughts in the Horn of Africa, floods, and pressure on farming that employs most workers.
Africa combines fast growth and big challenges; its future depends on jobs for its young people.

lessons.title: Asia
lessons.summary: The largest continent, home to most of humanity.

cards.title: Scale
cards.text: Asia covers about 30% of Earth's land and holds nearly 60% of its people. It stretches from Turkey to Japan and from Siberia to Indonesia.

deep.x: Asia covers about 44 million km², roughly 4.5 times the size of Europe. It holds about 4.8 billion people, so nearly six in every ten humans live there. Russia alone spans 11 time zones, most of them east of the Urals.
Where does Asia end?

Europe and Asia sit on one landmass, **Eurasia**. The border is a convention, usually drawn along the Ural Mountains, the Ural River, the Caspian Sea, the Caucasus and the Bosporus strait. That is why Istanbul is a city on two continents.
A continent of extremes

x: The highest point on land: Everest, about 8,849 m
The lowest point on land: the shore of the Dead Sea, about 430 m below sea level
The deepest lake: Baikal in Siberia, about 1,640 m deep
Both the coldest inhabited towns (Siberia, below −60 °C) and some of the hottest deserts (Arabia)
