deep.w: Europe and Asia are separate continents
deep.r: They are one landmass; the dividing line is a historical convention

deep.x: Asia is so big that "Asian" covers more people and more ways of life than any other word for a continent.

cards.title: Regions

items: West and Central: Middle East, Kazakhstan

cards.text: Asia is usually split into East, South, Southeast, Central and West Asia (the Middle East), each with very different histories, religions and climates.

deep.x: Geographers usually split Asia into five regions, sometimes six if Siberia counts as North Asia. The lines follow history, religion and climate more than physical borders.
Different beliefs

x: East Asia: Buddhism blended with Confucian and Taoist ideas, and Shinto in Japan
South Asia: Hinduism in India, Islam in Pakistan and Bangladesh, Buddhism in Sri Lanka
Southeast Asia: Indonesia is the largest Muslim-majority country, the Philippines mostly Catholic, Thailand Buddhist
West Asia: overwhelmingly Muslim, with Israel majority Jewish

deep.x: Different climates

South and Southeast Asia live by the **monsoon**: winds that bring heavy summer rain from the ocean, then a dry season. Central Asia is dry steppe and desert, far from any sea. Siberia has long, bitter winters.
Kazakhstan, in Central Asia, is the world's largest landlocked country, about 30 times the size of Portugal.
Asia is not one culture but several worlds, each as different from the others as Europe is from Africa.

cards.title: China
cards.text: China has about 1.4 billion people, the world's second-largest economy and a history of continuous civilisation over 3,500 years. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers of any language.

deep.x: China has had a continuous written civilisation since at least the Shang dynasty, about 3,500 years ago, whose oracle-bone script is the ancestor of today's characters. It was first unified as an empire in 221 BCE under Qin Shi Huang.
From poverty to powerhouse

After 1978, Deng Xiaoping opened China to markets and foreign investment. Growth averaged close to 10% a year for three decades, and several hundred million people left extreme poverty. China is now the world's biggest manufacturer and exporter, and the second-largest economy at market prices.
Language

About 920 million people speak Mandarin as their first language. Written Chinese uses characters, not an alphabet; reading a newspaper needs roughly 3,000 of them. Many regional languages, like Cantonese, are spoken very differently but share the same writing.
A turning population
The one-child policy (1980–2015) slowed growth sharply. China's population began to fall in 2022, and India overtook it as the most populous country in 2023.

deep.w: The Great Wall is easily visible from space
deep.r: From orbit it is far too narrow to see with the naked eye

deep.x: China combines one of the world's oldest continuous civilisations with one of the fastest economic transformations in history.

cards.title: India
cards.text: India is the world's most populous country and largest democracy, with 22 scheduled languages and a booming technology sector. Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism were born on the subcontinent.

deep.x: In 2023 India overtook China as the most populous country, with about 1.44 billion people. It is also young: the median age is under 30, compared with about 47 in Portugal.
The largest democracy

India's 2024 general election had about 970 million registered voters, and around 640 million cast a ballot over six weeks. Voting is electronic, and by law no voter should have to travel more than about 2 km to a polling station.
Many languages

The constitution lists 22 "scheduled" languages. Hindi is the most widely spoken, but Bengali, Telugu, Marathi and Tamil each have tens of millions of speakers, and English works as a common language for business and law.
Birthplace of religions
A tech economy

Bengaluru and Hyderabad host huge software and IT-service industries that serve companies worldwide. India's UPI system handles more real-time digital payments than any other country, much like a giant MB Way.
Portugal's link is old: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, and Goa was Portuguese from 1510 until 1961.
India is a continent-sized democracy where many languages and faiths share one state.

cards.title: Japan
cards.text: Japan blends ancient traditions with advanced technology. Its population is shrinking and ageing fast; nearly 30% of people are over 65.

deep.x: Japan's population peaked at about 128 million around 2008 and is now about 124 million, falling by more than half a million a year. Women have on average only about 1.2 children, far below the 2.1 needed to keep numbers stable.
Why so old?

x: Very long lives: life expectancy is about 84, one of the highest anywhere
Few births: late marriage, high costs and long working hours
Little immigration until recently, though foreign residents now reach a record of over 3.5 million

deep.x: Consequences
Workers are scarce, so robots, care technology and older employees fill gaps. Millions of homes in the countryside stand empty, and some villages are kept alive by a handful of residents.
Old and new together

Japan modernised at astonishing speed after the **Meiji Restoration** of 1868, and launched the high-speed Shinkansen in 1964. Yet Shinto shrines, Buddhist temples, tea ceremony and seasonal festivals remain part of everyday life.
Some Japanese companies are among the oldest in the world: the temple builder Kongō Gumi was founded in 578 and ran independently for over 1,400 years.
Japan shows the future many rich countries, Portugal included, are heading towards: fewer, older people.

cards.title: Portuguese traces in Asia
cards.text: Portuguese traders left words and places across Asia: "pão" became "pan" in Japanese, tempura has Portuguese roots, Macau was Portuguese until 1999, and Kristang creole is still spoken in Malacca.

deep.x: In the 1500s Portugal built a chain of trading posts from East Africa to Japan. Its sailors were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543, bringing firearms, Christianity and new foods.
Words left behind
Living communities

x: **Macau** was handed to China on 20 December 1999; Portuguese is still an official language there
In Malacca, Malaysia, a small community still speaks **Kristang**, a Portuguese-based creole, though it is endangered
Sri Lanka and India have many families with surnames like Fernando, Perera and de Souza
East Timor chose Portuguese as an official language after independence

deep.w: Japanese "arigatō" comes from "obrigado"
deep.r: It is a native Japanese word, used long before the Portuguese arrived

deep.x: Portugal's empire in Asia was small in land but left words, foods, faiths and families across half a continent.

cards.title: The Middle East

items: About half of world oil reserves

cards.text: West Asia holds about half of the world's proven oil reserves and the holy sites of Judaism, Christianity and Islam in Jerusalem, Mecca and Medina.

deep.x: West Asia sits where Africa, Europe and Asia meet. That position made it a crossroads of trade and empires, and its rocks made it an energy giant.
Oil and gas

Most of the oil formed from tiny sea creatures buried in an ancient ocean basin. Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and the UAE hold the largest reserves, and Qatar and Iran share the world's biggest gas field. Oil revenue built cities like Dubai and Doha in a few decades.
Holy cities
About 2 million Muslims perform the Hajj in Mecca each year. Jerusalem is sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims, which is one reason it is so fiercely contested.
A cradle of civilisation

Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, saw some of the first cities and the first writing, cuneiform, around 3200 BCE. Farming of wheat and barley began nearby, in the "Fertile Crescent", about 11,000 years ago.

deep.w: The Middle East is all Arab
deep.r: Iranians, Turks, Kurds and Israelis are not Arabs and speak other languages

deep.x: The Middle East's oil and holy places give a small region an outsized role in world affairs.

cards.title: Economic tigers
cards.text: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong grew from poverty to wealth in a few decades through exports, education and technology. Today Taiwan makes most of the world's advanced chips.

deep.x: In 1960 South Korea was about as poor as many African countries, with an income per person of roughly $150 a year. Today its income per person is higher than Portugal's. Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong made similar leaps.
What they did

x: Exported to world markets instead of protecting home industry
Invested heavily in schools; South Korea now has one of the highest university rates on Earth
Governments steered credit to chosen industries, such as steel, ships, cars and electronics
Land reform and strong saving gave a broad base for growth

deep.x: Very different places

Singapore, independent since 1965, became a trading and finance hub with almost no natural resources. Hong Kong grew as a gateway to China. South Korea built giant family conglomerates, the **chaebol**, such as Samsung and Hyundai.
The chip island

TSMC, founded in Taiwan in 1987, makes roughly 90% of the world's most advanced processors, including chips for phones and AI systems. That makes Taiwan vital to the world economy and a geopolitical worry.
Singapore's port is one of the busiest container ports on the planet, handling about 40 million containers a year.
Exports, education and investment turned four poor places into rich ones within a single lifetime.

cards.title: Rivers and mountains
cards.text: Asia has the Himalaya, the Gobi desert, the Siberian taiga and great rivers like the Yangtze, Ganges, Mekong and Indus, which feed hundreds of millions of people.

deep.x: The **Himalaya** formed when India, drifting north, crashed into Asia about 50 million years ago. The collision continues, so the peaks still rise a few millimetres a year. All 14 mountains over 8,000 m are in the Himalaya and the nearby Karakoram.
The water tower of Asia

Glaciers and snow in the Himalaya and Tibet feed the Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Yangtze, Yellow River and Mekong. Well over a billion people depend on these rivers for drinking water, farming and fish.
Landscapes

x: The **Yangtze** is the third-longest river in the world; the Three Gorges Dam on it is the largest power station anywhere
The **Ganges** is sacred to Hindus, who bathe in it at Varanasi
The **Indus** valley held one of the first urban civilisations, around 2600–1900 BCE
The **Gobi** is a cold desert, famous for dinosaur fossils and eggs
The Siberian **taiga** is the largest forest on Earth

deep.w: Everest is the tallest mountain
deep.r: It has the highest summit; Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller from base to top

deep.x: Asia's mountains make its rivers, and its rivers feed a large share of humanity.

cards.title: Megacities
cards.text: Many of the world's largest cities are in Asia: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Mumbai, Beijing and others with populations over 20 million in their urban areas.

deep.x: Counting a city's population depends on where you draw its edge: the official city, the built-up area, or the whole commuter region. Tokyo's city wards hold about 10 million, but its urban area holds well over 30 million.
A new ranking

In 2025 the UN changed its method to use satellite maps of built-up land. On that basis Jakarta came out largest, at about 42 million, ahead of Dhaka and Tokyo. Rankings like these move a lot with definitions, so treat any "biggest city" claim with care.
Why they grow so fast
Different stories

x: **Tokyo** is rich, orderly and now shrinking slowly
**Delhi** and **Dhaka** grow by hundreds of thousands a year, many in informal housing
**Shanghai** was rebuilt in a generation; its Pudong skyline was mostly farmland in 1990

deep.x: Dhaka is one of the most crowded cities on Earth, with tens of thousands of people per km² in its core.
Asia's megacities are where most of the world's urban growth, and its urban problems, are happening.

quiz.q: Who were the first Europeans to reach Japan?
Until when was Macau administered by Portugal?
Roughly what share of humanity lives in Asia?

lessons.title: The Americas
lessons.summary: Two continents from the Arctic to Cape Horn.

cards.title: North, Central, South
cards.text: The Americas stretch about 14,000 km from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. North America includes Canada, the USA and Mexico; Central America links to South America at Panama.

deep.x: The Americas cover about 42 million km², nearly 30% of Earth's land, and are home to just over a billion people. They run from the Arctic islands of Canada to Cape Horn, about 56° south.
One continent or two?

In Portugal, Spain and Latin America, schools usually teach one continent, "América". In the English-speaking world it is normally two. Geologically, Central America and the Caribbean belong to North America; the join with South America is near the Panama–Colombia border.
A late land bridge

The **Isthmus of Panama** rose from the sea only about 3 million years ago. Animals crossed in both directions: armadillos and opossums went north, while cats, bears and deer went south. Closing the gap also redirected ocean currents and probably helped strengthen the Gulf Stream, which keeps western Europe mild.
"America" is named after the Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci, after a German map of 1507 used his name for the new lands.
The Americas are a single chain of land stitched together at Panama only in geologically recent times.

cards.title: First peoples
cards.text: People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago. Great civilisations followed: the Maya, the Aztecs with their capital Tenochtitlan, and the Inca empire in the Andes.

deep.x: During the last Ice Age, sea levels were so low that Siberia and Alaska were joined by a land bridge called **Beringia**. People crossed from Asia, then spread south along the coast and through ice-free corridors.
How long ago?
The site of Monte Verde in Chile shows people about 14,500 years ago. Footprints in White Sands, New Mexico, may be over 20,000 years old, though that date is still debated.
Great civilisations

x: **The Maya** built city-states in southern Mexico and Guatemala, with a full writing system, an accurate calendar and a symbol for zero. About 6 million people still speak Mayan languages.
**The Aztecs** built Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake, with causeways and floating gardens. It may have had 200,000 people, more than any Iberian city then. Mexico City stands on its ruins.
**The Inca** ran an empire of perhaps 10 million people along the Andes, linked by about 40,000 km of roads. They had no writing as we know it but kept records with knotted cords, the **quipu**.

deep.w: The Americas were a mostly empty wilderness in 1492
deep.r: Tens of millions lived there, in farms, towns and great cities

deep.x: The Americas had cities, empires and science long before any European ship arrived.

cards.title: European conquest
cards.text: After 1492, Spanish and Portuguese colonisation, followed by English, French and Dutch, transformed the Americas. Disease, war and forced labour killed a huge share of the native population.

deep.x: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean. In 1494 the **Treaty of Tordesillas** split the newly found lands between Spain and Portugal along a line in the Atlantic. That line is why Brazil, which Pedro Álvares Cabral reached in 1500, speaks Portuguese.
Why so few conquered so many

x: **Disease**: smallpox, measles and flu were new to the Americas, and people had no immunity
**Allies**: Cortés won with thousands of native allies who hated Aztec rule
**Weapons and horses**: steel, guns and cavalry gave an edge in battle

deep.x: The human cost

Estimates of the population in 1492 vary widely, but within about a century it may have fallen by as much as 90% in many regions. To replace native labour, Europeans shipped about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Portugal and Brazil were at the centre of this trade: Brazil alone received about 4.9 million people, around 40% of the total.

deep.w: Most native people died fighting Europeans
deep.r: Epidemic disease killed far more than war did

deep.x: The conquest of the Americas was one of the biggest demographic catastrophes in history, and Portugal played a large part in it.

cards.title: Brazil
cards.text: Brazil is the largest country in South America, with about 215 million people, the Amazon rainforest and the largest Portuguese-speaking population in the world.

deep.x: Brazil covers about 8.5 million km², nearly half of South America and about 90 times the area of Portugal. The 2022 census counted about 203 million people, now nearer 212 million. Its name comes from **pau-brasil**, a red dyewood the Portuguese exported.
A unique independence

When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1807, the royal family sailed to Rio de Janeiro, the only time a European empire was ruled from a colony. In 1822 Dom Pedro, the king's son, declared Brazil independent and became its emperor.
Farm of the world

Brazil is the world's largest exporter of soybeans, coffee, sugar, beef and orange juice, and a giant in iron ore. Most of its soy goes to China. Farming has pushed into the Cerrado savanna and the edge of the Amazon, which is why deforestation is a central political issue.
A mixed people

Brazilians descend from Indigenous peoples, Portuguese settlers, millions of enslaved Africans, and later Italian, German, Japanese and Arab immigrants. Brazil has the largest Japanese-descended community outside Japan, centred on São Paulo.
Brazil has more Portuguese speakers than all other Portuguese-speaking countries combined, about 20 for every one in Portugal.
Brazil is Portugal's biggest legacy: a continent-sized country that made Portuguese a global language.

cards.title: The USA
cards.text: The USA is the world's largest economy, with 50 states and about 340 million people. Its culture, technology and companies have global influence.

deep.x: The USA produces about a quarter of the world's output at market prices, around $29 trillion in 2024. It became independent in 1776, and its 1787 Constitution is the oldest written national constitution still in use.
Sources of strength

x: A huge single market of about 340 million consumers
Deep capital markets and venture funding for new firms
World-leading universities that attract talent from everywhere
The dollar: most international trade and reserves use it

deep.x: Global reach

Firms like Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Amazon are among the most valuable on Earth. Hollywood films, music, social media and fast food spread American culture far beyond its borders, a form of influence called **soft power**.
Growth by expansion
The country grew from 13 colonies on the Atlantic to 50 states by buying, conquering and settling land westward. Alaska and Hawaii became the last two states in 1959.
About 1.3 million Americans claim Portuguese ancestry, many of Azorean origin, concentrated in Massachusetts, California and Hawaii.
The USA's economic, technological and cultural weight is unmatched, though China's rise makes it less dominant than in 1990.

cards.title: Canada
cards.text: Canada is the world's second-largest country by area but has only about 40 million people, mostly living near the US border. English and French are official languages.

deep.x: Canada covers about 10 million km², second only to Russia. Yet it has only about 41 million people, fewer than Spain, because most of it is cold forest, tundra and Arctic islands.
Hugging the border

Most Canadians live in a narrow strip near the US border, where the climate is mildest and farmland best. Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver alone hold over a third of the population. The border with the USA, about 8,900 km, is the longest between two countries.
Two languages

French settlers founded Quebec in 1608, before Britain took over in 1763. Today about a fifth of Canadians speak French as a first language, mostly in Quebec, and federal services must be offered in both English and French.
A nation of immigrants
Canada admits a high share of immigrants for its size, and around a quarter of residents were born abroad. About half a million people of Portuguese descent live there, mostly around Toronto.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country, over 200,000 km, and more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
Canada is vast on the map but small in people, with almost everyone living in a thin band along its southern edge.

cards.title: Spanish and Portuguese America
cards.text: Spanish is spoken from Mexico to Argentina; Portuguese in Brazil. Spanish speakers in the Americas outnumber those in Spain by about ten to one.

deep.x: Spain and Portugal's colonies became today's **Latin America**. Spanish is the main language in 18 countries of the Americas; Portuguese in Brazil. Mexico, with about 130 million people, is the largest Spanish-speaking country on Earth.
Same language, different flavours
Like British and American English, the Iberian languages changed differently on each side of the Atlantic.
Why the spellings met

The 1990 Orthographic Agreement aimed to unify Portuguese spelling across Portugal, Brazil and the African countries. It was adopted gradually, in Portugal from 2009, and remains controversial with some writers.
Growing in the USA
About 40 million people in the USA speak Spanish at home, making it one of the largest Spanish-speaking populations anywhere.

deep.w: Portuguese spoken in Brazil is a different language
deep.r: It is the same language with differences in accent, vocabulary and grammar

deep.x: The centre of gravity of both Spanish and Portuguese has moved across the Atlantic, to the Americas.

cards.title: The Andes and the Amazon
cards.text: The Andes are the world's longest mountain range on land, about 7,000 km. To their east, the Amazon basin holds the largest rainforest on Earth.

deep.x: The Andes run about 7,000 km through seven countries, from Venezuela to southern Chile. They exist because the Pacific's **Nazca plate** slides beneath South America, crumpling the edge upwards and feeding volcanoes.
Life up high

Aconcagua, about 6,960 m, is the highest peak outside Asia. La Paz in Bolivia sits at about 3,600 m, and millions live on the high plateau, the Altiplano, where potatoes and quinoa were first farmed. The largest earthquake ever recorded struck Chile in 1960, at magnitude 9.5.
The great forest

The Amazon River carries more water than the next several largest rivers combined. Trees release huge amounts of water vapour, forming "flying rivers" that bring rain to farms in southern Brazil and Argentina.
Under pressure
Roughly a fifth of the original forest has been cleared, mainly for cattle and soy. Scientists warn that beyond a certain point, parts could dry out and turn to savanna.

deep.w: The Amazon produces 20% of the world's oxygen
deep.r: It uses almost as much as it makes; it matters for carbon and rain

deep.x: The Andes and the Amazon are linked: one makes the rain-catching wall, the other the world's greatest river system.

cards.title: The Panama Canal

items.l: saved on a New York–San Francisco voyage

cards.text: Opened in 1914, the canal lets ships cross between the Atlantic and Pacific without going around South America, saving about 13,000 km.

deep.x: The French, led by Ferdinand de Lesseps of Suez fame, tried first in the 1880s and failed. Tropical diseases like malaria and yellow fever killed over 20,000 workers. The USA took over in 1904, controlled the mosquitoes, and opened the canal on 15 August 1914.
How it works
Instead of cutting to sea level, engineers dammed a river to create Gatún Lake, about 26 m above the sea. Locks lift ships up to the lake and lower them on the other side.
Water is the limit

Each crossing uses about 200 million litres of fresh water, which flows out to sea. A drought in 2023–24 lowered Gatún Lake so much that daily crossings were cut, causing queues and higher shipping costs.

x: New York to San Francisco round Cape Horn ≈ 21,000 km
Through the canal ≈ 8,000 km
Saving ≈ 13,000 km

deep.x: The canal runs roughly north-west to south-east, so ships going from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually end up further east.
The Panama Canal turned a dangerous voyage round South America into a crossing of about ten hours.

cards.title: Food from the Americas
cards.text: The Americas gave the world maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cocoa, vanilla, peanuts and turkeys. Imagine Portuguese food without potatoes and tomatoes!

deep.x: After 1492, crops and animals moved between the hemispheres in the **Columbian Exchange**. Portuguese ships were key carriers, taking American crops to Africa and Asia within a few decades.
Changing the world's diet

Maize is now the most produced grain on Earth, used for food, animal feed and biofuel. Potatoes fed Europe's population boom, but dependence on them also led to the Irish famine of the 1840s, when blight destroyed the crop.
A Portuguese twist

x: Portuguese traders spread chillies to Africa and Asia; **piri-piri** and many Indian curries depend on them
Goan **vindaloo** comes from the Portuguese "carne de vinha d'alhos"
Portugal planted cocoa on São Tomé, which around 1900 was among the world's top producers
Tomatoes were first grown in Europe as ornamental plants, as many feared they were poisonous

deep.x: Before 1492 there were no tomatoes in Italy, no chillies in India or Thailand and no potatoes in Ireland.
Many "traditional" dishes worldwide, Portuguese ones included, are built on plants that came from the Americas.

quiz.q: Who reached Brazil in 1500?
quiz.explain: Cabral, on his way to India.

quiz.q: Which country is second largest by area?
Which foods came from the Americas?

lessons.title: Oceania and the poles
lessons.summary: Islands, Australia and the frozen ends of the Earth.

cards.title: Oceania
cards.text: Oceania includes Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and thousands of Pacific islands grouped as Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.

deep.x: Oceania is less a continent than an ocean with land scattered across it. It covers roughly a sixth of Earth's surface, yet holds only about 45 million people, more than half of them in Australia. There are 14 independent countries, from Australia (about 27 million people) to Tuvalu (about 11,000).
Three island regions
The names were coined by a French explorer, Jules Dumont d'Urville, in the 1830s, and they are still used today, although the boundaries are cultural rather than strict.

x: **Melanesia** ("black islands"): Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia
**Micronesia** ("small islands"): Palau, Guam, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, Nauru
**Polynesia** ("many islands"): a vast triangle with Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island at its corners

deep.x: Languages and peoples

Papua New Guinea alone has about 840 living languages, more than any other country on Earth. Its rugged mountains kept valleys isolated for thousands of years, so languages split and multiplied. Across the Pacific, many islands are still shared between their own nations and outside powers: Hawaii is a US state, French Polynesia and New Caledonia belong to France, and Easter Island to Chile.
Kiribati's islands are spread over about 3.5 million km² of ocean, more than India's area, but its land adds up to only about 800 km², similar to the Madeira archipelago.
Oceania is mostly water: its countries are defined as much by the sea between islands as by the land.

cards.title: Australia

items.l: live within 50 km of the coast

cards.text: Australia is both a country and a continent, mostly dry outback with most people living on the coast. It's home to unique animals like kangaroos, koalas and platypuses.

deep.x: Australia is about 7.7 million km², roughly 84 times the size of Portugal, but it has only about 27 million people. Around 70% of the land is arid or semi-arid, so people cluster on the wetter coasts, especially in the southeast. Sydney and Melbourne each have about 5 million inhabitants; the capital, Canberra, was purpose-built in between to settle their rivalry.
Why the animals are so different

Australia broke away from Antarctica about 35–45 million years ago and drifted north alone. Its mammals evolved in isolation, which is why it is dominated by **marsupials**, whose young finish developing in a pouch.

x: Kangaroos and wallabies: hop efficiently, using elastic tendons like springs
Koalas: eat eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most animals, and sleep up to 20 hours a day
Platypus and echidnas: **monotremes**, mammals that lay eggs

deep.x: A tough land

Australia is the driest inhabited continent and has some of the oldest, most weathered soils on Earth. Bushfires, droughts and floods are part of its normal rhythm; the 2019–20 "Black Summer" fires burned over 20 million hectares, about twice the size of Portugal.

deep.w: Australia is mostly desert sand
deep.r: Much of the outback is scrub, grassland and rocky plains; sandy dune deserts are only part of it

deep.x: Australia is huge but empty: geography, not size, decides where its people live.

cards.title: Aboriginal Australians
cards.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

deep.x: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples arrived by sea from Southeast Asia, crossing at least 90 km of open water even when sea levels were lower. Archaeological sites show people in Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and some researchers argue for about 65,000, though that date is debated.
Knowledge carried in songs

Before 1788 there were about 250 distinct languages and hundreds of nations, each with its own country (territory). Knowledge of water holes, seasons, food and law was passed down in stories, songs, dance and art. **Songlines** are routes across the land that are remembered as sung narratives, a kind of oral map.

x: Fire was used deliberately to manage land and encourage new growth
Rock art sites in places like Kakadu and the Kimberley are tens of thousands of years old
Torres Strait Islanders, from islands between Australia and New Guinea, are culturally distinct, with Melanesian links

deep.x: After colonisation

British settlement brought disease, violence and the loss of land. The legal idea of **terra nullius** ("nobody's land") was only overturned by the High Court's Mabo decision in 1992. Today Indigenous Australians are about 4% of the population, and gaps in health and life expectancy remain a national issue.
A 2023 referendum to give Indigenous Australians a formal advisory "Voice" to Parliament was rejected by about 60% of voters.
Aboriginal cultures kept knowledge alive for tens of thousands of years without writing, through land, song and story.

cards.title: The Great Barrier Reef
cards.text: Off northeast Australia, the Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 km, the largest structure built by living things. Warming seas cause coral bleaching.

deep.x: The Great Barrier Reef is not one reef but about 2,900 separate reefs and 900 islands, spread over about 344,000 km² of protected sea, an area larger than Italy. It is built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which lay down limestone skeletons layer upon layer over thousands of years.
How coral lives

Coral polyps host microscopic algae inside their tissues. The algae photosynthesise and pass sugars to the coral; the coral gives them shelter and nutrients. This partnership is why reefs thrive in clear, shallow, sunlit, nutrient-poor tropical water.
What bleaching is

When water stays about 1 °C above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down. The coral expels its algae and turns white. If the heat passes quickly, coral can recover; if it lasts, the coral starves and dies.

x: Mass bleaching hit the reef in 1998, 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025
Other pressures: crown-of-thorns starfish, cyclones, and farm run-off carrying sediment
Recovery between events takes about 10 years for fast-growing corals, longer for slow ones

deep.w: The reef is already dead
deep.r: Large parts still have live coral, but bleaching events now come too often for full recovery

deep.x: Coral reefs depend on a partnership with algae that breaks down when the sea gets too hot.

cards.title: New Zealand

events.l: first country to give women the vote

cards.text: New Zealand's two main islands have volcanoes, glaciers and fjords. The Māori arrived around 1300 CE, among the last large lands settled by humans.

deep.x: New Zealand, or **Aotearoa** in Māori, has about 5.3 million people on an area about three times that of Portugal. It sits right on the boundary between the Pacific and Australian plates, which is why it has so much dramatic scenery packed into a small space.
Shaped by plates and ice

x: The **Alpine Fault** runs along the South Island and pushes the Southern Alps upward; Aoraki/Mount Cook reaches 3,724 m
The Taupō volcano erupted massively around 230 CE; its crater is now Lake Taupō
Ice-age glaciers carved Fiordland's steep fjords, such as Milford Sound

deep.x: The last major land settled

Polynesian voyagers arrived around 1250–1300 CE, making New Zealand the last large landmass people reached. They became the Māori. Within about 150 years, the giant flightless **moa** birds, some over 3 m tall with neck stretched, had been hunted to extinction.

The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and Māori chiefs, is still the country's founding document, though its English and Māori versions differ in meaning, which has caused disputes ever since.

items.l: first nation to let women vote

deep.x: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all women the right to vote in national elections.
New Zealand is young land on a busy plate boundary, and one of the last places on Earth humans reached.

cards.title: Polynesian navigators
cards.text: Polynesians crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double canoes, navigating by stars, swells and birds, reaching Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand.

deep.x: Polynesian voyaging is one of humanity's great achievements. Starting from islands near New Guinea about 3,000 years ago, people sailed east into an ocean where the next island might be thousands of kilometres away, settling almost every habitable speck within the Polynesian triangle.
Reading the ocean

Navigators carried no instruments. They memorised where dozens of stars rose and set on the horizon, using them like a compass. They felt ocean swells through the hull, and could detect land beyond the horizon by its effect on the waves.

x: **Stars:** a mental "star compass" of rising and setting points
**Swells:** steady swells keep their direction for days
**Birds:** some species fly out to sea by day and return to land at dusk
**Clouds:** green-tinged or still clouds can sit above unseen islands

deep.x: Proving it again

In 1976 the double canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed about 4,000 km from Hawaii to Tahiti without instruments, guided by Mau Piailug, a navigator from Micronesia. It settled a long debate over whether Polynesians had sailed deliberately or simply drifted.
The sweet potato, a South American plant, was grown across Polynesia before Europeans arrived, strong evidence that Polynesians reached the Americas and came back.
Polynesians treated the ocean as a map that could be read, centuries before European ships crossed the Pacific.

cards.title: The Arctic
cards.text: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land, mostly covered by floating sea ice. It's warming about three to four times faster than the global average, shrinking summer ice.

deep.x: The Arctic is the opposite of Antarctica: an ocean almost surrounded by land, rather than land surrounded by ocean. Eight countries have territory there: Canada, the USA, Russia, Norway, Denmark (through Greenland), Iceland, Sweden and Finland. They cooperate through the Arctic Council, founded in 1996.
Why it warms so fast
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the planet as a whole. The main reason is a feedback loop: white ice reflects most sunlight, while dark open water absorbs it.
Shrinking summer ice

Sea ice reaches its smallest extent each September. Satellite records since 1979 show the September minimum has fallen by roughly 40%, with a record low in 2012. The ice is also thinner and younger than before.

x: Melting sea ice barely changes sea level, because it is already floating
Melting land ice on Greenland does raise seas: the whole sheet holds about 7 m of sea-level rise
Less ice opens new shipping routes and access to oil, gas and minerals, raising geopolitical tension

deep.w: Melting Arctic sea ice is raising sea levels
deep.r: Floating ice is already displacing water; it's melting land ice, like Greenland's, that raises seas

deep.x: The Arctic is warming fastest because losing ice makes it absorb even more of the Sun's heat.

cards.title: Polar day and night
cards.text: Above the Arctic Circle, the Sun never sets around the summer solstice and never rises around the winter solstice. At the poles themselves, there are six months of day and six of night.

deep.x: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°. As Earth orbits the Sun, each pole spends half the year leaning towards it and half leaning away. The Arctic and Antarctic Circles, at about 66.5° latitude, mark where this produces at least one full day without sunset and one without sunrise.
How it varies with latitude

The further you go towards the pole, the longer the midnight sun and the polar night last. On the Arctic Circle itself it is about one day each; in Tromsø, Norway (about 70° N), the Sun stays up from about late May to late July. At the North Pole, there is one sunrise in March and one sunset in September.
Living with it

x: Polar night is rarely pitch black: there is twilight at midday and often the aurora
People in the far north report sleep problems and winter low mood; light therapy lamps are common
In summer, sports matches and festivals run past midnight in full daylight

deep.x: Because the atmosphere bends sunlight, the Sun appears above the horizon a little before it really is, so polar "day" lasts slightly longer than polar "night".
Polar day and night are caused by Earth's tilt, not by changing distance from the Sun.

cards.title: Life in the cold
cards.text: Inuit, Sámi and other Arctic peoples have adapted to extreme cold for thousands of years. Animals use fat, fur and migration; Antarctic fish have antifreeze proteins in their blood.

deep.x: Humans have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. The ancestors of today's Inuit spread across Alaska, Canada and Greenland about 1,000 years ago. The Sámi have herded reindeer and fished across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia for much longer.
Human ingenuity

x: Layered clothing of caribou and seal skin trapped warm air; the word "anorak" comes from Greenlandic
Snow houses were temporary winter hunting shelters; snow is an excellent insulator
The **kayak** was invented in the Arctic for hunting seals
Diets rich in fat from seals, whales and fish provided energy where plants were scarce

deep.x: Animal tricks

items.b: fat up to 10 cm, dense fur

deep.x: Antarctic icefish live in water at about −1.9 °C, colder than the normal freezing point of blood. Special antifreeze proteins stick to tiny ice crystals and stop them growing. Many Arctic animals also follow a pattern: larger, rounder bodies lose heat more slowly than small, thin ones.
An Arctic tern can fly about 70,000 km a year between the Arctic and Antarctic, so it sees more daylight than any other animal.

deep.w: Polar bears have white skin
deep.r: Their skin is black; their hairs are clear and hollow and only look white

deep.x: Life in the cold succeeds by holding on to heat or escaping when it's too cold, and people learned both.

cards.title: Pacific islands and the sea
cards.text: Low-lying Pacific nations like Tuvalu and Kiribati are only a few metres above sea level and are among the most threatened by rising seas.

deep.x: Many Pacific nations are made of **atolls**: rings of coral islands around a lagoon, sitting on top of sunken volcanoes. Tuvalu's highest point is under 5 m above sea level, and most of Kiribati lies less than 3 m above the sea. For them, a few tens of centimetres of sea-level rise is a national emergency.
The threats are not just flooding

x: **King tides** and storm surges wash over land more often
Salt water seeps into the thin layer of fresh groundwater that islands depend on
Coastal erosion eats away at homes, roads and graves
Warmer seas bleach the reefs that protect the shore and feed people

deep.x: Responses

Islands are building sea walls and raising land, but they are also planning for the worst. Kiribati bought about 20 km² of land in Fiji in 2014 for food security. In 2023 Tuvalu signed a treaty with Australia allowing up to 280 citizens a year to migrate there. Vanuatu led the push for a 2025 International Court of Justice opinion, which said states have legal duties to tackle climate change.
Some studies show many atoll islands have kept or even grown their area over recent decades, as waves pile up new coral sand, but the fresh water and people on them are still at risk.
The Pacific islands have done least to cause climate change and are among the first to face its consequences.

quiz.q: How long have Aboriginal Australians lived in Australia?
quiz.explain: One of the oldest continuous cultures.

quiz.q: Which was the first country to give women the vote, in 1893?
The Arctic is mainly…
options: An ocean covered by sea ice

lessons.title: How the world earns a living
lessons.summary: GDP, trade and why some countries are richer.

cards.title: GDP
cards.text: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. It measures the size of an economy, not how well off people are.

deep.x: GDP can be measured three ways, and in theory they all give the same answer: add up everything produced, everything spent, or everything earned. The spending approach is the one most people learn.
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)

Portugal's GDP was about €285 billion in 2024. The modern measure was developed in the 1930s, partly by the economist Simon Kuznets, who himself warned that it shouldn't be read as a measure of welfare.
Nominal or real?

Nominal GDP uses current prices, so it rises with inflation. **Real GDP** removes price changes, showing whether the economy actually produced more. When news says "the economy grew 2%", it means real growth.

x: Nominal GDP up 6%
Prices up 4%
Real growth ≈ 6% − 4% = 2%

deep.x: What GDP misses
GDP also ignores how income is shared and whether growth is sustainable. That's why statisticians publish alternatives such as the UN's Human Development Index, which adds health and education.

deep.w: A higher GDP means people are better off
deep.r: GDP measures output; wellbeing also depends on health, inequality, free time and the environment

deep.x: GDP tells you how big an economy is, not how good life is inside it.

cards.title: The biggest economies
cards.text: The USA is the largest economy, followed by China, Germany, Japan and India. Measured by purchasing power, China is the largest.

deep.x: In 2025 the US economy was worth roughly $30 trillion and China's roughly $19 trillion, together about 40% of the world's output. Germany and Japan follow at about $4–5 trillion each, with India close behind Japan and expected to pass it. The world economy as a whole is around $115 trillion.
Purchasing power parity

Exchange rates don't capture what money buys locally. A haircut or a bus ride costs far less in Delhi than in Lisbon. **Purchasing power parity (PPP)** adjusts for these price differences. On that basis China has been the largest economy since the mid-2010s, and India is third.
Where Europe fits

x: The EU's 27 economies together are worth about $19–20 trillion, similar to China at market rates
Portugal's economy is about 0.3% of the world total
Big populations matter: India's GDP is large but spread over 1.4 billion people

deep.x: Measured at market exchange rates, the ranking can shift just because a currency rises or falls, even if nothing real has changed.
Which economy is "biggest" depends on whether you count in dollars or in what money actually buys.

cards.title: GDP per person
cards.text: Dividing GDP by population gives a better sense of average income. Luxembourg, Ireland and Switzerland rank high; Portugal is mid-table in the EU.

deep.x: Dividing GDP by population gives an average, and it changes the picture completely. China's economy is huge, but per person it is below Portugal's. Small, wealthy countries jump to the top.
GDP per person = GDP ÷ population
Why the leaders are odd

x: **Luxembourg:** nearly half its workers commute from France, Belgium and Germany; they add to GDP but aren't counted as residents
**Ireland:** many multinationals book profits there for tax reasons, inflating GDP; Ireland publishes an adjusted measure, "GNI*", to correct for it
**Switzerland:** genuinely high wages, plus finance and pharmaceuticals

deep.x: Portugal's position

Measured in purchasing power standards, a Eurostat unit that evens out price levels, Portugal sits at roughly 80% of the EU average. It has been overtaken in recent decades by several central and eastern European countries, such as Czechia, Slovenia, Lithuania and Estonia, which joined the EU in 2004.

x: Portugal GDP ≈ €285 billion
Population ≈ 10.7 million

items.r: A few very rich raise the average

deep.w: GDP per person is what an average person earns
deep.r: It includes company profits and taxes; median household income is usually much lower

deep.x: Per-person figures reveal living standards better than totals, but small countries with commuters or tax-driven profits can mislead.

cards.title: Sectors
cards.text: Economies have three broad sectors: primary (farming, mining), secondary (industry) and tertiary (services). Rich countries are mostly services; Portugal's tourism is a major service export.

deep.x: Economists divide work into sectors. As countries grow richer, workers move from fields to factories and then to offices, shops and hotels. This shift has happened in almost every wealthy country.
Portugal's shift

In 1960 more than 40% of Portuguese workers were in agriculture. Today it's only a few per cent, while services account for about three-quarters of economic output. Industry still matters: car parts, the Autoeuropa factory in Palmela, moulds, footwear and textiles in the north.
Tourism as an export

When a German visitor pays for a hotel in the Algarve, money flows into Portugal just as if a Portuguese product had been sold abroad. That's why tourism counts as a **service export**. Tourism revenue reached about €27 billion in 2024, and depending on how indirect effects are counted, tourism-related activity is roughly 12–16% of GDP.

x: Upside: jobs, foreign income, regional development
Downside: seasonal, low-wage jobs, vulnerable to shocks like the 2020 pandemic, pressure on housing

deep.x: Some economists add a quaternary sector for knowledge work like research, software and consulting.
Rich economies are mostly service economies, and for Portugal, tourists are one of the biggest export markets.

cards.title: Trade
cards.text: Countries specialise in what they do relatively well and trade. Portugal exports cars, machinery, fuels, clothing, cork, wine and tourism, mainly to Spain, France and Germany.

deep.x: The classic explanation of trade uses Portugal as its example. In 1817 the economist David Ricardo imagined England and Portugal making cloth and wine. Even if Portugal were better at both, both countries gain if each specialises in what it is *relatively* best at and trades. This is **comparative advantage**.

x: Portugal: 1 unit wine costs 80 hours, cloth 90
England: wine 120, cloth 100
Portugal's wine is relatively cheaper, so Portugal makes wine and England cloth

deep.x: Portugal today
Exports of goods and services are now close to half of Portugal's GDP, up from about a quarter in the 1990s. Spain is by far the largest market, taking roughly a quarter of goods exports.

x: Cars and car parts, machinery, refined fuels from Sines
Clothing and footwear, cork (Portugal produces about half the world's supply), wine
Services: tourism, transport, IT and business services

deep.x: Trade's costs

Opening up trade makes countries richer on average, but some workers and regions lose out when factories move abroad. Tariffs, like those the USA raised sharply in 2025, push up prices and invite retaliation.

deep.w: Trade is a contest with a winner and loser
deep.r: Both sides usually gain overall; the losses fall on particular industries within each country

deep.x: Countries get richer by doing what they are relatively best at and trading for the rest.

cards.title: Inflation
cards.text: Inflation is a general rise in prices. The European Central Bank aims for about 2% a year. In 2022 inflation spiked across Europe with energy prices.

deep.x: Inflation is measured by tracking the price of a "basket" of typical goods and services over time. The euro area uses the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), so countries can be compared. In Portugal, the INE publishes the figure every month.
Why 2%?

The European Central Bank (ECB) targets 2% inflation over the medium term. A little inflation gives a buffer against **deflation**, falling prices, which can freeze spending as people wait for things to get cheaper. It also lets real wages adjust without nominal pay cuts.

x: Prices rise 2% a year
Prices double in about 35 years

deep.x: What drives it
The 2022 spike

After the pandemic, demand bounced back faster than supply. Then Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent gas, electricity and food prices soaring. Euro-area inflation peaked at 10.6% in October 2022, the highest since the euro began. Higher interest rates and falling energy prices brought it back near 2% by 2025.

deep.w: When inflation falls, prices go back down
deep.r: Lower inflation only means prices rise more slowly; the earlier rises remain

deep.x: Inflation quietly shrinks what each euro buys, which is why central banks aim to keep it low and steady.

cards.title: Interest rates
cards.text: Central banks raise interest rates to cool inflation and lower them to encourage borrowing and growth. Mortgage payments in Portugal, mostly variable-rate, follow the Euribor.

deep.x: An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. The ECB sets the rates at which banks deposit and borrow from it. Those rates ripple out to the rates banks charge each other, then to mortgages, business loans and savings accounts.
Euribor and Portuguese mortgages

**Euribor** is the average rate at which big European banks lend to each other. Most Portuguese home loans have historically been variable: the rate is Euribor plus a fixed bank spread, reset every 3, 6 or 12 months. When the ECB raised rates from −0.5% in mid-2022 to 4% in 2023, family budgets felt it fast.

x: Loan €150,000 over 30 years
Total rate 1%: about €480 a month
Total rate 4%: about €715 a month

deep.x: The trade-off

x: Higher rates cool inflation, but slow growth and can raise unemployment
Lower rates help borrowers and investment, but can fuel inflation and house-price bubbles
Savers gain when rates rise; borrowers lose

deep.x: Since 2023 more Portuguese buyers have chosen fixed or mixed-rate mortgages, after the shock of variable payments jumping.
Interest rates are the central bank's main lever: up to cool prices, down to support growth.

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.text: Prices rise when demand outstrips supply, and fall when supply exceeds demand. Commodity markets, like wheat or soybeans, react quickly to harvests, weather and wars.

deep.x: In a market, buyers want to pay less and sellers want to receive more. The price settles where the quantity people want to buy equals the quantity offered: the **equilibrium**. If anything shifts either side, the price moves to a new balance.
Why food prices swing so much

People still need to eat when bread costs more, so demand for staple food is **inelastic**: it barely changes with price. That means even a small shortfall in supply must be cleared by a big price rise.
Real shocks

x: **2022:** Russia's invasion of Ukraine threatened about a quarter of world wheat exports; prices hit records within weeks
**2024:** disease and bad weather in West Africa sent cocoa above $10,000 a tonne, about four times its usual level
**2010:** a Russian drought and export ban pushed wheat prices up sharply

deep.x: High prices also send a signal: farmers plant more, which eventually brings prices back down. This cycle of booms and busts is common in commodity markets.

deep.w: High prices are always caused by greedy sellers
deep.r: Usually they reflect shortages or rising demand, though market power can add to them

deep.x: When supply and demand shift, price is how the market rations what's scarce.

cards.title: Why some countries are rich
cards.text: Economists point to institutions (rule of law, low corruption), education, infrastructure, technology, trade openness and stability. Natural resources alone don't guarantee wealth.

deep.x: In 1960 South Korea was about as poor as Ghana. Today it is one of the world's richest countries. North and South Korea share a language, history and climate, yet the South is many times richer. Differences like these point beyond geography to how societies are organised.
Institutions

The 2024 Nobel Prize in economics went to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson for showing how **institutions** shape prosperity. Where property is protected, contracts are enforced and power is checked, people invest and innovate. Where elites can seize wealth, they rarely do.
The resource curse

Oil, diamonds or gold can actually hold a country back. Big resource earnings can strengthen the exchange rate, crowd out other industries, and encourage corruption and conflict over who controls them.

x: **Norway** saved its oil money in a sovereign fund now worth about $2 trillion
**Venezuela** has the world's largest proven oil reserves, yet its economy collapsed in the 2010s
**Singapore** has almost no natural resources and is one of the richest places on Earth

deep.w: Countries are rich because they have natural resources
deep.r: Institutions, skills and stability matter far more; many resource-rich countries remain poor

deep.x: Wealth is built more by the rules people live under than by what lies beneath the ground.

cards.title: Inequality
cards.text: The Gini index measures inequality from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything). Nordic countries have low inequality; South Africa and Brazil high. Portugal is around the EU average.

deep.x: The Gini index is drawn from the **Lorenz curve**: line up everyone from poorest to richest and plot the share of income they hold. If income were shared equally, it would be a straight line. The Gini measures how far the real curve sags below it.
What brings it down

Market incomes before tax are unequal everywhere. The difference between countries comes largely from taxes and benefits: progressive income tax, pensions, child benefits and free public services narrow the gap. Education, wage bargaining and minimum wages matter too.
Income vs wealth

x: **Income** is what you earn each year
**Wealth** is what you own: houses, savings, shares
Wealth is always much more unequal than income; in most rich countries the top 10% own around half of it or more

deep.x: Global inequality between countries fell after about 1990, mainly because China and India grew fast, even as inequality within many countries rose.
Inequality depends less on what markets pay than on how a country taxes, spends and educates.

quiz.q: What does GDP measure?
options: The total value of goods and services produced

quiz.q: What does the ECB usually do to fight high inflation?
What share of Portugal's economy is services?

lessons.title: Feeding the world
lessons.summary: Crops, commodities and how food travels.

cards.title: The big crops
cards.text: Just a few crops supply most of humanity's calories: maize, rice, wheat and soybeans, plus sugar cane and palm oil.

deep.x: People have eaten thousands of plant species, yet today just three cereals, maize, rice and wheat, provide about half of all the calories humanity eats directly. Add soybeans, sugar cane and palm oil, and a handful of crops underpins the world's food system.
Different crops, different jobs

x: **Rice** is the staple for more than half the world, especially in Asia; most of it is eaten close to where it's grown
**Wheat** is the most traded grain, made into bread, pasta and noodles
**Maize** is the biggest by weight, but most of it feeds animals or becomes ethanol fuel, not food on a plate
**Soybeans** and **palm oil** supply protein meal and the world's most-used cooking oils

deep.x: Why so few?

Cereals store well for months, carry lots of energy per hectare and can be grown on a huge scale with machines. Centuries of breeding have made them far more productive than their wild ancestors. The cost is fragility: a disease or drought hitting one crop can ripple through prices everywhere.
Sugar cane is the world's largest crop by weight, at nearly 2 billion tonnes a year, but most of that weight is water and fibre.
A handful of crops feeds the world, which makes them efficient and vulnerable at the same time.

cards.title: Where they grow
cards.text: The USA, China and Brazil lead maize; China and India rice; China, India and Russia wheat; Brazil and the USA soybeans. Weather in a few regions can move world prices.

deep.x: Production is concentrated in a few breadbaskets with good soil, reliable rain or irrigation, and flat land for machines. That concentration is what makes world prices sensitive to weather in places like Iowa, Mato Grosso or the Black Sea steppe.
Producers vs exporters
The biggest producers aren't always the biggest sellers. China and India grow huge amounts of wheat and rice but eat almost all of it. What matters for world prices is the **exportable surplus**.

x: Russia is the largest wheat exporter, at about a fifth of world trade
India supplies roughly 40% of world rice exports, so its export bans in 2022–23 shook Asian markets
Brazil now produces about 40% of the world's soybeans; China buys roughly 60% of all soybeans traded

deep.x: Two hemispheres, two harvests
Northern farms harvest maize and soybeans around September–November; Brazil and Argentina harvest theirs around February–June. Traders watch both seasons, so a dry spell in either can move prices.
Brazil often grows two crops a year on the same field: soybeans first, then a "safrinha" (little harvest) of maize straight afterwards.
Prices are set by the few countries with grain to spare, so their weather becomes everyone's problem.

cards.title: Most soy feeds animals
cards.text: About three-quarters of soybeans are crushed into meal for animal feed (chickens, pigs, fish), with the oil used for cooking and biodiesel.

deep.x: A soybean is about 20% oil and 80% protein-rich solids. Crushing plants press out the oil and grind the rest into **soybean meal**, which is about 45% protein. That meal is the world's most important protein feed for farm animals.

x: Crush 1 tonne of soybeans
About 0.79 t meal for feed
About 0.19 t oil for food and fuel

deep.x: Who eats it

x: Chickens are the largest users, followed by pigs, farmed fish and dairy cattle
Only about 7% of soy is eaten directly by people, as tofu, soy milk, edamame or tempeh
Soy oil is used for frying, margarine and in Europe and the Americas as biodiesel

deep.x: The forest link

Soy expansion has driven deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon and especially the Cerrado savanna. Since 2006 the **Amazon Soy Moratorium** has stopped big traders buying soy from newly cleared Amazon land, but the Cerrado was left out. The EU has adopted a law to block imports linked to deforestation, though its start has been delayed repeatedly.

items.r: Meat, eggs and milk drive soy demand

deep.w: Vegetarians are the main reason for soy farming
deep.r: Most soy ends up feeding livestock for meat, eggs and dairy

deep.x: When you eat chicken or pork, you are indirectly eating soybeans, often grown in South America.

cards.title: Commodity trading
cards.text: Global traders buy grain and oilseeds from farmers, store them, ship them and sell them to millers, crushers and food companies worldwide, managing price, quality and logistics risks.

deep.x: Between a farm in Mato Grosso and a bakery in Lisbon there are silos, trucks, trains, ports, ships and mills. Global traders link them. A small group of firms, often called **ABCD** after ADM, Bunge, Cargill and Louis Dreyfus, has handled a large share of world grain trade for decades, now joined by others such as COFCO International.
How traders make money
Margins on each tonne are thin, so profit comes from volume and from three kinds of **arbitrage**:

x: **Space:** buy where grain is cheap, sell where it's scarce
**Time:** store grain after harvest and sell later when prices are higher
**Form:** process it, for example crushing soybeans into meal and oil

deep.x: Managing risk

Traders also face currency risk (buying in reais, selling in dollars) and counterparty risk (a buyer who can't pay). Much of the business is about managing these risks carefully, hedging the price while keeping the physical flow running.
Grain is graded on details like moisture, protein and broken kernels; a shipment a fraction off-spec can be discounted or rejected.
Commodity traders turn scattered harvests into a steady global supply, and earn their living by managing risk.

cards.title: Futures and hedging

items: exposed if prices fall or rise

cards.text: Futures contracts fix a price today for delivery later. Farmers and traders use them to hedge price risk. The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) sets benchmark prices for corn, soybeans and wheat.

deep.x: A **futures contract** is a standardised promise to buy or sell a set amount of a commodity at an agreed price on a future date. It's traded on an exchange, which guarantees both sides. Most futures are closed out with an opposite trade before delivery; they're used to manage price, not to move grain.
How a hedge works
A farmer who will harvest soybeans in autumn worries prices may fall. By selling futures now, she locks in today's price: if the market falls, her loss on the crop is offset by a gain on the futures.

x: Spring: sell futures at $400/t
Autumn: price falls to $350/t
Crop sells $50 lower, futures gain $50
Net: about $400/t

deep.x: The benchmarks
The **Chicago Board of Trade**, founded in 1848 and now part of CME Group, sets world reference prices for corn, soybeans and wheat. Other key exchanges:

x: Euronext in Paris for European milling wheat
ICE in New York and London for coffee, cocoa and sugar
Dalian in China for soybean meal and other products

deep.x: Basis
The local cash price rarely equals the futures price. The difference is called **basis** and reflects transport costs, local supply and quality.
Basis = local cash price − futures price

deep.w: Futures are just gambling
deep.r: They exist mainly so producers and buyers can lock in prices; speculators take the other side and add liquidity

deep.x: Futures let farmers and traders swap an uncertain future price for a known one.

cards.title: Shipping routes
cards.text: Grain moves on bulk carriers through key chokepoints: the Panama Canal, the Black Sea, the Suez Canal and the Strait of Malacca. Disruptions raise freight costs and prices.

deep.x: Grain crosses oceans on **dry bulk carriers**, ships whose holds are loaded like giant buckets. A typical "Panamax" carries about 60,000–80,000 tonnes, enough wheat for roughly 100 million loaves. Freight can be a large share of the final cost of cheap commodities.

items: Panama Canal: US Gulf to Asia
Strait of Malacca: into East Asia

deep.x: When chokepoints fail

x: **2022:** war closed Ukraine's ports; a UN-brokered Black Sea deal shipped about 33 million tonnes before it ended in 2023
**2023–24:** drought lowered the lakes that feed the Panama Canal, cutting daily transits by about a third
**Late 2023 onward:** attacks on ships in the Red Sea pushed many vessels around Africa's Cape of Good Hope

deep.x: Rivers matter too

Most US grain reaches the coast by barge on the Mississippi. In dry autumns like 2022 and 2023, low water forced barges to carry lighter loads, raising costs. Brazil moves much of its soy by truck over long distances to ports like Santos and Paranaguá, which adds cost.
Portugal's grain imports arrive mostly by sea at ports such as Lisbon, Leixões and Aveiro, where large silos store them for millers and feed makers.
Food prices depend not only on harvests but on a few narrow waterways staying open.

cards.title: Coffee and cocoa
cards.text: Coffee grows mostly in Brazil, Vietnam and Colombia; cocoa mainly in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Both are traded worldwide and sensitive to weather and plant disease.

deep.x: Both are tropical tree crops grown mostly by smallholders and consumed mostly in rich countries. Coffee grows in a "bean belt" between the tropics; cocoa needs hot, humid lowlands within about 20° of the equator.
Two kinds of coffee
Why prices jump

Trees take three to five years to produce, so supply can't respond quickly. Brazil's frosts in 2021 and droughts since lifted arabica to record highs above $4 per pound in 2025. In West Africa, swollen shoot virus, ageing trees, heavy rain then drought cut cocoa harvests, and prices roughly tripled during 2024.

x: Most cocoa farmers earn very little; child labour remains a documented problem
Climate change is pushing suitable land uphill or out of production

deep.x: Around 1908 the Portuguese colony of São Tomé and Príncipe was the world's largest cocoa producer; coffee itself reached Brazil in 1727 with a Portuguese officer.
Coffee and cocoa prices swing hard because trees take years to replace what one bad season destroys.

cards.title: Food waste

items.l: of food lost or wasted (FAO estimate)

cards.text: Roughly a third of food produced is lost or wasted, from field to fridge. Reducing waste is one of the easiest ways to feed more people with less land and emissions.

deep.x: The "one third" figure comes from a 2011 UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimate. Newer UN data split it into two parts: about 13% of food is **lost** between harvest and shops, and about 19% is **wasted** in shops, restaurants and homes.
Where it happens

Households are the biggest single source of waste, responsible for about 60% of what's thrown away at the retail and consumer end. In the EU, about 130 kg of food per person is wasted each year across the whole chain.
The hidden costs

Wasted food carries all the land, water, fertiliser and fuel used to make it. Food loss and waste produce about 8–10% of global greenhouse gas emissions, partly as methane from food rotting in landfill.

x: Plan meals and check the fridge before shopping
Understand dates: "use by" is about safety, "best before" is about quality
Freeze leftovers and bread; use apps that sell surplus food cheaply

items.r: Often fine after; use your senses

deep.x: If food waste were a country, it would be the third-largest greenhouse gas emitter after China and the USA.
Wasting less food is one of the cheapest ways to cut emissions and feed more people.

cards.title: Fertilisers
cards.text: Modern yields depend on fertilisers. Nitrogen fertiliser made with the Haber–Bosch process feeds roughly half the world's population, but uses natural gas and causes pollution if overused.

deep.x: Plants need three main nutrients in large amounts: **nitrogen (N)**, **phosphorus (P)** and **potassium (K)**. Nitrogen gas makes up 78% of the air, but plants can't use it directly; it has to be "fixed" into compounds like ammonia.
The Haber–Bosch process

In 1909 the German chemist Fritz Haber made ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Carl Bosch scaled it up at BASF by 1913. It runs at about 400–500 °C and 150–300 times atmospheric pressure, and it still produces almost all synthetic nitrogen today.
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
The downside

x: Making ammonia uses about 1–2% of the world's energy and emits a similar share of CO₂
Crops typically take up only about half the nitrogen applied; the rest washes into water or escapes to air
Runoff feeds algal blooms that create oxygen-starved "dead zones", as in the Gulf of Mexico
Soil microbes turn some into nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas about 270 times stronger than CO₂ over a century

deep.x: When gas prices spiked in 2022, several European fertiliser plants shut down, showing how closely food and energy are linked.
Nitrogen fertiliser made from air and gas is one of the inventions that most shaped the modern world.

cards.title: Portugal's food
cards.text: Portugal imports most of its cereals but exports wine, olive oil, tomatoes, fruit and cork. Olive groves in the Alentejo have expanded hugely thanks to Alqueva irrigation.

deep.x: Portugal produces only about a fifth of the cereals it consumes, and much less of its wheat, so it imports wheat, maize and soybeans, largely by sea. It is strong in Mediterranean crops suited to its hot, dry summers.
Alqueva and the olive boom

The Alqueva dam on the Guadiana river, completed in 2002, created the largest artificial lake in Western Europe, about 250 km². Its irrigation network now covers well over 100,000 hectares. With reliable water, the Alentejo has planted vast intensive olive groves in hedgerow rows harvested by machine, plus almonds and vines.

x: Olive oil output has risen several-fold since the early 2000s, turning Portugal from importer into major exporter
Concerns include water use in dry years, soil health, pesticides and loss of traditional landscapes

deep.x: Other strengths
The Portuguese eat about 55–60 kg of fish and seafood per person a year, the most in the EU, and much of their beloved bacalhau comes from Norway.
Portugal imports the grains it lacks and pays for them partly with the Mediterranean crops its climate grows best.

quiz.q: Most soybean meal is used for…
What does a futures contract do?
options: Fixes a price today for later delivery

quiz.q: Roughly how much food is lost or wasted?

lessons.title: Energy around the world
lessons.summary: How the world powers itself, and how that's changing.

cards.title: Primary energy mix
cards.text: Fossil fuels (oil, coal, gas) still supply about 80% of the world's primary energy. Renewables and nuclear make up the rest, growing quickly in electricity.

deep.x: **Primary energy** is energy in its raw form: crude oil, coal, gas, uranium, wind, sunlight and flowing water, before it's converted into petrol or electricity. The world uses about 600 exajoules a year, roughly the energy in 14 billion tonnes of oil.

v.unit: share of world primary energy, % (2024, approx.)

deep.x: Why fossil fuels still dominate

They are dense, storable and easy to transport, and the whole world is built around them: engines, boilers, furnaces and pipelines. Even as clean energy grows quickly, total energy demand keeps growing too, so the fossil share falls only slowly.
A measuring trap

Burning fuel in a power station wastes about 60% as heat. Wind and solar have no such loss. So comparing them in primary energy can either overstate fossil fuels or require an adjustment that inflates renewables. Different statistics use different methods, which is why published shares vary.

items.w: 1 kWh of coal = 1 kWh of power
items.r: About 2.5 kWh of coal per kWh

deep.x: Hydropower is still the largest renewable source worldwide, though wind and solar together now produce more electricity than it.
The energy transition is happening fastest in electricity; the overall mix still runs mostly on fossil fuels.

cards.title: Electricity vs energy
cards.text: Electricity is only about 20% of final energy use. Transport, heating and industry still burn fuels directly, which is why electrifying them matters.

deep.x: **Final energy** is what users actually receive: petrol in a tank, gas in a boiler, electricity at a socket. Electricity is only about a fifth of that worldwide. Most energy is still burned directly in vehicles, furnaces and heating systems.
Why electrifying saves energy

Electric machines waste far less energy than engines and burners. Switching a car or a boiler to electricity often cuts the energy needed by a factor of three or more, even before the electricity gets cleaner.

x: Petrol car: about 6 L/100 km ≈ 55 kWh
Electric car: about 16 kWh/100 km
Roughly 3 times less energy

deep.x: Portugal's grid

Portugal produces most of its electricity from renewables, around 70% in recent years, mainly wind, hydro and fast-growing solar. Dry years cut hydro output, so the share varies. Yet oil products still supply a large part of the country's final energy, mostly for transport.

x: Electric cars, heat pumps and electric industrial heat are the main ways to bring clean power into the rest of the economy
More electricity demand means grids, storage and connections must grow

deep.w: Clean electricity means a clean energy system
deep.r: Electricity is only about a fifth of final energy; transport, heat and industry must switch too

deep.x: Making electricity clean is half the job; the other half is using it for things that now burn fuel.

cards.title: Solar's rise

events.l: cheapest new power in many places

cards.text: Solar power has become the cheapest electricity in history in many places. Global solar capacity grew more than tenfold in a decade.

deep.x: Solar panels turn light directly into electricity using silicon cells. In 2010 they were an expensive niche; by the 2020s, new solar farms were the cheapest source of electricity ever built in sunny places. Panel prices fell about 90% in a decade.
Why it got so cheap

Solar follows a **learning curve**: each time cumulative production doubles, the price falls by roughly 20%. Mass manufacturing, mostly in China, which makes about 80% of the world's panels, drove costs down year after year.
Portugal's sunshine

Portugal gets some of the strongest sunshine in Europe. A 2020 Portuguese auction set a then world-record low price of about €11 per megawatt-hour for solar power. Large solar farms are spreading across the Alentejo, and rooftop panels on homes and businesses have boomed.
The catch

x: Solar only works in daylight, so output peaks at midday and stops at night
Too much midday solar can push wholesale prices to zero or below
Batteries, flexible demand and grids are needed to shift energy into the evening

deep.x: Solar now makes up about three-quarters of all the new renewable power capacity the world adds each year.
Solar became cheap because making more of it kept making it cheaper.

cards.title: Oil
cards.text: Oil fuels most transport. The biggest producers are the USA, Saudi Arabia and Russia. OPEC+ coordinates production to influence prices.

deep.x: The world uses about 103 million barrels of oil a day; a barrel is 159 litres. Oil is so useful because liquid fuels pack a lot of energy into a small, easily moved volume. Cars, trucks, ships and planes run on it, and it's also the raw material for plastics and chemicals.

x: 103 million barrels × 159 L
≈ 16 billion litres a day
about 2 litres per person on Earth daily

deep.x: OPEC and OPEC+

OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960 by five producers. In 2016 it formed **OPEC+** with Russia and other exporters. By agreeing to pump less or more, they influence world prices, though high prices also encourage US shale drillers to produce more.
Portugal's oil

Portugal has no oil production of its own, so all crude is imported. Galp refines it at Sines; its Matosinhos refinery closed in 2021. Fuel prices at the pump follow the world price of Brent crude, plus taxes, which make up a large part of the price.

x: Electric vehicles are starting to cut oil demand for cars, especially in China and Europe
Trucks, ships, planes and petrochemicals are harder to switch

deep.w: The world is about to run out of oil
deep.r: Reserves keep being found; the bigger question is how much we can afford to burn

deep.x: Oil runs the world's transport, which is why its price and its producers have so much power.

cards.title: Gas and Europe
cards.text: Europe imported much of its gas from Russia until 2022. After the invasion of Ukraine, it switched to LNG from the USA, Qatar and others. Portugal's Sines terminal receives LNG.

deep.x: Natural gas is mostly methane. It heats homes, fuels industry and generates electricity. Until 2021 Russia supplied around 40% of the EU's imported gas, mainly by pipeline. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, flows were cut, the Nord Stream pipelines were blown up, and prices spiked to about ten times normal levels.

v.unit: Russian share of EU gas imports, % (approx.)

deep.x: LNG to the rescue

**Liquefied natural gas (LNG)** is gas cooled to −162 °C, which shrinks it about 600 times so it can travel by ship. Europe built floating import terminals in months and bought LNG from the USA, Qatar, Norway and others. The USA is now the world's largest LNG exporter.
Portugal and Sines

Portugal took little Russian gas, getting most of its supply as LNG through the Sines terminal, mainly from Nigeria and the USA. Spain and Portugal also won a temporary EU exception in 2022–23 to cap the gas price used in power plants, the "Iberian exception".
Gas transit through Ukraine to Europe ended on 1 January 2025, and the EU has agreed to phase out Russian gas imports entirely by the end of 2027.
Europe learned in 2022 that cheap energy from one supplier can become a weapon.

cards.title: Coal

items.l: of world coal burned in China

cards.text: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fuel. China burns over half the world's coal. Portugal closed its last coal power plants in 2021.

deep.x: Coal is ancient plant matter, compressed and heated underground for hundreds of millions of years. It powered the Industrial Revolution and still produces about a third of the world's electricity, more than any other single source. Global use hit a record of nearly 9 billion tonnes in 2024.

v.unit: CO₂ per kWh of electricity, grams (approx.)

deep.x: Who burns it

China and India rely on coal because they have large domestic reserves and fast-growing demand. Yet China is also building more solar and wind than the rest of the world combined, and its coal use may be near its peak.
Portugal goes coal-free

Portugal had two coal plants, Sines and Pego. Sines closed in January 2021 and Pego in November 2021, years ahead of the original plan. Portugal was one of the first EU countries to stop burning coal for power, after Belgium, Austria and Sweden.
Besides CO₂, coal smoke releases fine particles, sulphur dioxide and mercury; air pollution from coal causes hundreds of thousands of early deaths every year.
Coal is the dirtiest major fuel, and phasing it out is the single biggest step in cleaning up power.

cards.title: Energy per person

viz.unit: kWh per person per year (primary, approx.)
