cards.text: Energy use per person varies hugely: an average American uses several times more than an average Portuguese and dozens of times more than someone in many African countries.

deep.x: Energy use per person is one of the clearest signs of how people live: heated and cooled homes, cars, flights, factories and goods. The differences are enormous. An average American uses roughly three times as much energy as an average Portuguese, and several dozen times as much as an average Ethiopian.
Why the gaps?

x: **Climate:** cold or very hot countries spend more on heating or cooling
**Distances:** large, car-based countries like the USA and Canada use more for transport
**Industry:** places with heavy industry, like Iceland's aluminium smelters, rank very high
**Wealth:** richer people buy more goods, travel more and live in bigger homes

deep.x: Energy poverty

About 730 million people, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, have no electricity at home. Around 2 billion still cook on wood, charcoal or dung, and the indoor smoke kills millions each year. For them, more energy means better health, education and income.
Portugal uses less energy per person than most EU countries, partly thanks to its mild climate, but many Portuguese homes are poorly insulated and cold in winter.
The energy challenge is two-sided: rich countries must use less fossil energy, while billions still need more energy.

cards.title: Hydrogen
cards.text: Green hydrogen, made by splitting water with renewable electricity, could fuel steelmaking, fertiliser and shipping. Portugal is planning projects, notably around Sines.

deep.x: Hydrogen burns or reacts with oxygen to give energy, leaving only water. But hydrogen doesn't exist freely on Earth; it must be made. Today about 100 million tonnes a year are produced, almost all from natural gas or coal, mainly for oil refining and fertiliser.
How green hydrogen is made

An **electrolyser** passes electricity through water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen. It takes about 50–55 kWh of electricity to make one kilogram of hydrogen, losing roughly a third of the energy on the way.
2H₂O + electricity → 2H₂ + O₂
Where it makes sense
Because making hydrogen wastes energy, it's best kept for jobs that electricity can't do directly. Using it in cars or home boilers usually loses out to batteries and heat pumps.
Portugal's plans

Portugal published a national hydrogen strategy in 2020, betting on cheap solar and wind. Sines, with its port, refinery and grid links, is the hub: Galp is building a 100 MW electrolyser at its refinery. A planned H2Med corridor would link Iberia's hydrogen to France and beyond. Many projects worldwide have been delayed, however, because green hydrogen still costs much more than grey.

deep.w: Hydrogen will power most of our cars
deep.r: Battery cars are far more efficient; hydrogen fits heavy industry and shipping better

deep.x: Green hydrogen is a precious fuel for the hardest jobs, not a replacement for electricity everywhere.

cards.title: Energy security
cards.text: Countries want energy that's affordable, reliable and not dependent on a single supplier. Renewables, storage, interconnections and efficiency improve security.

deep.x: The International Energy Agency was created in 1974 after the Arab oil embargo showed how vulnerable importers were. Its members must hold emergency oil stocks equal to at least 90 days of net imports. The 2022 gas crisis taught Europe the same lesson again.
Ways to improve it

x: **Domestic renewables:** sunshine and wind can't be embargoed
**Storage:** batteries, pumped hydro and gas storage bridge gaps
**Interconnections:** cables and pipes to neighbours share supply
**Efficiency:** energy you don't need can't be cut off

deep.x: Iberia: an energy island

Spain and Portugal have weak electricity links to France: interconnection capacity is only around 3% of their generating capacity, far below the EU target of 15% by 2030. A new cable under the Bay of Biscay is being built. On 28 April 2025 a blackout shut down almost the entire Iberian grid for many hours; investigations pointed to problems controlling voltage, and the event sparked a debate about grid stability and storage.
China refines most of the world's lithium, graphite and rare earths, so clean energy brings a new kind of supply risk.
Energy security means never depending too heavily on one fuel, one supplier or one wire.

cards.title: Energy transition
cards.text: The world is shifting from fossil fuels to clean electricity, but the transition requires huge investment in grids, storage, minerals and new industries.

deep.x: Past energy transitions were slow: coal took about a century to overtake wood worldwide, and oil took decades to overtake coal. Today's shift is deliberate and faster, but it means rebuilding the system that powers almost everything.
What it takes

Global investment in clean energy reached about $2 trillion in 2024, about twice the amount invested in fossil fuels. Electric cars made up more than a fifth of new car sales worldwide, and about a fifth of new cars in Portugal are fully electric.
The bottlenecks

x: **Grids:** connections to new solar and wind farms often take years to approve and build
**Minerals:** an electric car needs several times more minerals than a petrol car, mostly in its battery
**Fairness:** coal and refinery workers, like those at Sines and Pego, need new jobs; the EU funds a "just transition"

deep.w: The transition means less energy and lower living standards
deep.r: Electrified systems waste less, so the same comfort needs much less primary energy

deep.x: The energy transition is less about inventing new technology than about building and connecting it at enormous scale.

quiz.q: About how much of world primary energy still comes from fossil fuels?
quiz.explain: Oil, coal and gas still dominate.

quiz.q: When did Portugal stop burning coal for power?
What is green hydrogen made with?

lessons.title: Water
lessons.summary: A precious and unevenly shared resource.

cards.title: Fresh water is scarce
cards.text: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or deep underground. Rivers and lakes hold a tiny fraction.

deep.x: Earth holds about 1.4 billion km³ of water, but about 97.5% of it is salty seawater. Of the small fresh share, roughly two-thirds is locked in ice sheets and glaciers, mainly in Antarctica and Greenland, and almost a third lies underground. Lakes, rivers, soil moisture and the air hold only around 1%.
Shrink it to a bucket

x: All Earth's water = a 10-litre bucket
Fresh water ≈ 250 mL, one glass
Lakes and rivers ≈ less than 1 mL, a few drops

items: Lakes and rivers: a few drops

deep.x: Unevenly shared

The water that matters for people is the renewable flow, the rain that refills rivers and aquifers each year. That is shared very unequally. Canada, Brazil and Russia have vast amounts per person; much of the Middle East and North Africa has almost none.

x: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water
In Portugal, rainfall falls sharply from north to south: parts of the Minho and Gerês get over 2,000 mm a year, while parts of the Alentejo and Algarve get under 500 mm

deep.w: There's plenty of water because Earth is a blue planet
deep.r: Almost all of it is salty or frozen; usable fresh water is tiny

deep.x: Earth is wet, but the fresh water we can easily reach is only a few drops in the bucket.

cards.title: The water cycle
cards.text: The Sun evaporates water from oceans and land; it condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back via rivers and groundwater. The cycle never stops.

deep.x: The water cycle is powered by the Sun and pulled along by gravity. About 500,000 km³ of water evaporates every year, around 86% of it from the oceans. Plants add more by **transpiration**, releasing water vapour through their leaves.
How long water stays put
A water molecule spends very different times in each part of the cycle. That's why polluted rivers can recover quickly, but contaminated groundwater can take centuries.
Energy in the cycle

Evaporating water absorbs heat; when vapour condenses into clouds it releases that heat again. This moves huge amounts of energy from the tropics towards the poles and powers storms. Warmer air can hold about 7% more water vapour for every 1 °C of warming, which is one reason heavy downpours are getting heavier.

x: Atlantic weather fronts bring most of Portugal's rain between October and April
Mountains force moist air to rise and cool, so the north and west get far more rain than the interior and south

deep.x: Water molecules you drink today have been around the cycle countless times; some may once have fallen as rain on dinosaurs.
The water cycle is a solar-powered machine that keeps recycling the same water, moving heat and life around the planet.

cards.title: Farming uses most
cards.text: Agriculture accounts for about 70% of fresh water withdrawals worldwide. Drip irrigation, used widely in the Alentejo, can cut water use dramatically.

deep.x: Worldwide, about 70% of fresh water withdrawn from rivers, lakes and aquifers goes to agriculture, about 20% to industry and about 12% to homes and cities. Irrigated land is only about a fifth of cropland, yet it grows around 40% of the world's food.
Irrigation methods

Drip irrigation delivers water through pipes with small emitters right at each plant's roots, often with fertiliser mixed in. Little evaporates or runs off. Sensors in the soil and weather forecasts can schedule watering precisely. In the Alentejo, olive groves, almonds and vineyards irrigated from Alqueva use drip systems almost everywhere.
The rebound trap

Efficiency doesn't always save water overall. When farmers can grow more with each litre, they often expand the irrigated area or switch to thirstier, more profitable crops. Total water use can stay the same or even rise. Real savings need limits on total extraction as well as better technology.
It takes roughly 1,000 tonnes of water to grow one tonne of wheat.
Farming is the world's biggest water user, so the biggest savings must come from the fields.

cards.title: Virtual water
cards.text: Producing goods uses water. A cup of coffee takes about 140 litres along the supply chain; a kilo of beef around 15,000 litres.

deep.x: **Virtual water** is the water used to produce something, all along its supply chain. The idea was proposed by the British geographer Tony Allan in the 1990s, and the related **water footprint** was developed by the Dutch researcher Arjen Hoekstra.
Three colours of water

Most of beef's footprint is green water, rain falling on pasture and feed crops, which would fall anyway. Blue water, pumped from rivers and aquifers, is the scarcer kind. A tomato irrigated in a dry region may put more pressure on local water than its small number suggests.
Trading water without pipes

When a dry country imports wheat, it's effectively importing the water used to grow it. Much of the Middle East relies on this. Portugal is a net importer of virtual water, mainly through cereals and soy for animal feed.

x: 1 cup of coffee ≈ 7 g of roasted beans
Growing and processing those beans ≈ 140 L
About 1,000 cups' worth per day for a busy café

deep.w: A product's water footprint tells you how much harm it does
deep.r: Rain-fed water on pasture differs from irrigation pumped from a stressed river

deep.x: Every product carries hidden water, and where that water comes from matters as much as how much.

cards.title: Access to safe water
cards.text: About 2 billion people still lack safely managed drinking water, and many more lack safe sanitation, mostly in rural areas of Africa and Asia.

deep.x: **Safely managed** drinking water means water at home, available when needed and free from contamination. By that standard, about 2 billion people still go without, and about 3.4 billion lack safely managed sanitation such as a toilet connected to safe treatment.
Why it matters

x: Unsafe water and sanitation cause around a million deaths a year, mostly from diarrhoeal disease, mostly young children
Women and girls do most of the water-carrying, often for hours a day, time lost from school and work
Clean water and toilets were among the biggest causes of rising life expectancy in Europe after the 1850s

deep.x: Progress and gaps

Since 2000, billions of people have gained access to better water. But progress is slowest in rural sub-Saharan Africa and in fragile, conflict-hit countries. The UN's goal of safe water for all by 2030 is far off track.
Portugal's turnaround

In the early 1990s many Portuguese homes still lacked reliable treated water and sewage connections. With heavy investment, much of it EU-funded, about 99% of tap water now meets quality standards, according to the water regulator ERSAR.
Clean water and sewers did more to extend human lives in the 19th and early 20th centuries than almost any medicine.
Safe water and sanitation are among the cheapest, most powerful public health tools ever invented.

cards.title: Drought in Iberia
cards.text: Southern Portugal and Spain face more frequent droughts. Reservoirs like Alqueva, desalination plans in the Algarve and water reuse help, along with careful farming.

deep.x: Southern Iberia has a Mediterranean climate: wet winters, long dry summers, and big swings from year to year. Climate change is making hot, dry years more common. 2022 was one of the driest years on record in Portugal, and the Algarve faced a severe drought in 2023–24.
The Algarve crunch

By early 2024, Algarve reservoirs were around a quarter full. The government ordered cuts of about 15% for urban use and 25% for farms. The region's water demand is pushed up by tourism in summer, golf courses and expanding avocado and citrus orchards.
The toolkit

x: **Storage:** Alqueva holds over 4,000 hm³, the largest reservoir in Western Europe
**Desalination:** a plant near Albufeira is planned to supply part of the Algarve's needs
**Reuse:** treated wastewater can irrigate golf courses, parks and some crops
**Leaks:** some Portuguese water networks lose a quarter or more of their water before it reaches taps
**Connections:** pipelines can move water between basins, for example from the Guadiana

deep.x: Spain's Tagus–Segura transfer has piped water from central Spain to Murcia's farms since 1979, a long-running source of conflict between regions.
In southern Iberia, drought is no longer a rare event but a condition to plan around.

cards.title: Desalination
cards.text: Desalination removes salt from seawater, mostly by reverse osmosis. It's reliable but energy-intensive. Countries like Israel and Saudi Arabia rely heavily on it.

deep.x: Seawater contains about 35 grams of salt per litre. Modern plants mostly use **reverse osmosis**: seawater is pushed at high pressure through membranes with pores so fine that water molecules pass but salt doesn't. Older plants, still common in the Gulf, boil seawater and condense the steam.
The costs

x: **Energy:** about 3–4 kWh per cubic metre with reverse osmosis, more than other sources but far less than in the past
**Brine:** for each litre of fresh water, about 1.5 litres of extra-salty brine go back to the sea and must be spread out to protect marine life
**Money:** usually around €0.5–1 per m³, which is affordable for cities but too much for most farming

deep.x: Who relies on it

Saudi Arabia is the biggest producer of desalinated water. Israel gets most of its drinking water from big coastal plants such as Sorek, and has turned from shortage to surplus. Spain has more desalination capacity than any other European country.
Porto Santo, in the Madeira archipelago, has drawn its drinking water from a desalination plant since 1980.
Desalination turns the ocean into a reliable tap, but at an energy and environmental price.

cards.title: Shared rivers
cards.text: Many rivers cross borders. Portugal and Spain manage their shared rivers under the 1998 Albufeira Convention, which sets minimum flows Spain must let through.

deep.x: There are more than 300 river and lake basins shared by two or more countries, holding about 60% of the world's river flow. Upstream countries can build dams or take water; downstream countries depend on what's left. This can cause tension, but shared rivers more often lead to treaties than to wars.
Portugal downstream

Five major rivers flow from Spain into or along Portugal: the Minho, Lima, Douro, Tagus and Guadiana. Their basins cover about two-thirds of mainland Portugal, and much of their water originates in Spain. That makes Portugal heavily dependent on Spanish decisions about dams, irrigation and transfers.
The Albufeira Convention

Signed in Albufeira in 1998, the convention commits both countries to share information, protect water quality and guarantee flows. A 2008 protocol added more detailed seasonal and weekly minimum flows. In drought years, Spain can invoke exceptions, which has led to disputes over the Tagus in particular.
In 2025 India suspended its 1960 Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, a treaty that had survived several wars.
Rivers ignore borders, so the countries that share them have to share rules too.

cards.title: Groundwater
cards.text: Aquifers store water underground. Pumping faster than rain refills them lowers water tables and can let seawater in near coasts.

deep.x: An **aquifer** is a layer of rock, sand or gravel whose pores and cracks hold water, like a sponge. Rain soaks down and slowly recharges it, sometimes over years or centuries. Groundwater supplies about half the world's drinking water and about 40% of irrigation.
Overpumping
When water is pumped out faster than rain replaces it, the water table drops. Wells must go deeper, pumping costs rise and shallow wells dry up.

x: **India** is the world's largest user of groundwater, and tables are falling in Punjab and elsewhere
The **Ogallala aquifer** under the US Great Plains is being drained far faster than it refills
**Mexico City** is sinking by up to tens of centimetres a year in places as its aquifer is emptied

deep.x: Seawater intrusion
Near coasts, fresh groundwater floats on denser seawater. Pump too hard and salt water moves inland underground. The Algarve's Querença–Silves aquifer, its largest, is closely watched for this risk.

deep.w: Groundwater is an underground river or lake
deep.r: Mostly it's water held in the tiny pores and cracks of rock and sand

deep.x: Aquifers are savings accounts of water: easy to withdraw from, slow to refill.

cards.title: Saving water at home
cards.text: Fixing leaks, efficient taps and showers, full loads in the dishwasher and washing machine, and collecting rainwater for the garden all cut use.

deep.x: Household water is only about a tenth of total use, but it's the part we control directly, and treating, pumping and heating it uses a lot of energy. Hot water for showers is one of the biggest energy uses in many homes.
Quick wins

x: **Leaks:** a dripping tap can waste several thousand litres a year; a running toilet even more
**Showers:** low-flow heads use about 6–8 litres a minute instead of 12–15
**Toilets:** dual-flush cisterns use 3 or 6 litres instead of 9–12
**Machines:** run the dishwasher and washing machine only when full; a modern dishwasher uses about 10 litres, often less than washing by hand

deep.x: Outdoors

Water the garden early in the morning or evening, when less evaporates. Mulch keeps soil moist. Native and Mediterranean plants such as lavender, rosemary and cistus need little water once established. A rain barrel catches water from the roof for plants.

x: Tap drips once a second
≈ 20 L a day
≈ 7,000 L a year, about 50 baths

deep.x: In Portugal tap water is safe to drink almost everywhere, and costs far less per litre than bottled water.
The cheapest water is the water you don't waste, and saving hot water saves energy too.

quiz.q: Which sector uses most fresh water?
Which agreement manages rivers shared by Portugal and Spain?
How is most seawater desalinated?

lessons.title: International organisations
lessons.summary: How countries cooperate.

cards.title: The United Nations
cards.text: Founded in 1945, the UN has 193 member states. The General Assembly gives each one vote; the Security Council handles peace and security.

deep.x: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 by 50 countries, and the UN formally came into being on 24 October 1945, now celebrated as UN Day. Its aims: keep peace, develop friendly relations, solve shared problems and promote human rights. Portugal joined in 1955.
The main organs

The General Assembly meets in New York each September, when world leaders give speeches. Its resolutions are mostly recommendations, not law. The Economic and Social Council coordinates work on development, and the UN also has offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi.
Money

The UN's core budget is about $3.5 billion a year, less than many big cities spend. Peacekeeping has its own budget of around $5 billion. Each country's share depends on its wealth; the USA pays the most. Late and unpaid contributions, and US funding cuts in 2025, forced the UN into deep budget and staff reductions.
Two states sit as non-member observers in the General Assembly: the Holy See and Palestine.
The UN gives every country a seat and a voice, even if real power stays concentrated.

cards.title: The Security Council
cards.text: It has 15 members: five permanent ones with veto power (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and ten elected for two years. Portugal last served in 2011–12.

deep.x: The Security Council is the only UN body whose decisions are legally binding on all members. It can impose sanctions, authorise peacekeeping missions and, as a last resort, approve the use of force.
Resolution passes = at least 9 of 15 votes + no veto from the five
The veto

The five permanent members were the main victors of the Second World War. Any one can block a resolution. The Soviet Union and Russia have used the veto most, followed by the USA. Vetoes have blocked action on wars in Syria, Ukraine and Gaza, frustrating many smaller countries.
Calls for reform

The Council's shape still reflects 1945. Africa and Latin America have no permanent member, while Europe has two. Brazil, Germany, India and Japan seek permanent seats; the African Union wants two. But changing the Charter needs approval from the permanent five, so reform has stalled for decades.

x: Elected members are chosen by regional groups and need two-thirds of the General Assembly's votes
Portugal has served three terms and has sought a fourth, for 2027–28

items.w: The UN can stop any war
items.r: Only if all five permanent members agree

deep.x: Since 2022 a General Assembly rule requires a debate whenever a permanent member uses its veto, so the vetoing country must explain itself.
The Security Council has real power, but any one of five countries can switch it off.

cards.title: António Guterres
cards.text: Former Portuguese prime minister António Guterres became UN Secretary-General in 2017, after leading the UN Refugee Agency. His second term runs to the end of 2026.

deep.x: António Guterres was born in Lisbon in 1949 and trained as an engineer at the Instituto Superior Técnico. He led the Socialist Party and was prime minister of Portugal from 1995 to 2002. From 2005 to 2015 he headed the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), during the Syrian refugee crisis.
The job

The Secretary-General is chosen by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation. The role is part diplomat, part chief administrator. He can't order countries to act, but can use his voice, mediate and bring issues to the Council.
His priorities

x: Climate: he has warned repeatedly that the world is heading for dangerous warming, calling it an "era of global boiling" in 2023
In 2023 he invoked Article 99 of the Charter on Gaza, a rarely used power to warn the Council of a threat to peace
He has pushed reforms to cut costs as funding fell

deep.x: What comes next
He is the ninth Secretary-General and the first former head of government to hold the post. His successor is chosen during 2026 and takes office on 1 January 2027.
The 2016 selection was the first in which candidates presented their plans in public hearings; Guterres won the Council's straw polls throughout.
A Portuguese engineer and former prime minister has led the world's main forum for a decade.

cards.title: UN agencies
cards.text: Specialised agencies work on health (WHO), food (FAO, WFP), children (UNICEF), refugees (UNHCR), culture (UNESCO) and more.

deep.x: The UN family includes specialised agencies, funds and programmes, many older or as large as the UN itself. They have their own members, budgets and heads, and much of their money comes from voluntary donations rather than fixed dues.
What they achieve

x: **WHO** led the campaign that eradicated smallpox, declared in 1980
**WFP** delivers food to around 100 million people a year in a normal year and won the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize
**UNESCO**, in Paris, runs the World Heritage list
**UNHCR** has won the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981

deep.x: Funding pressure

Because agencies depend on voluntary funding, their work rises and falls with donors' priorities. In 2025 the USA, the largest donor, announced its withdrawal from WHO and sharply cut foreign aid, forcing several agencies to cut staff and programmes.
The oldest bodies now in the UN system predate it: the International Telecommunication Union (1865) and the Universal Postal Union (1874).
UN agencies do much of the world's practical cooperation, from vaccines to food aid, often with uncertain funding.

cards.title: The EU institutions
cards.text: The European Commission proposes laws, the Parliament (elected) and Council (national governments) adopt them, and the Court of Justice interprets them.

deep.x: The EU isn't a state, but it isn't just an alliance either. Member countries pool some powers, such as trade and the single market, and share decision-making through a set of institutions. Portugal joined, as the EEC, on 1 January 1986.
Who's who

x: The **Commission** has one commissioner per country; Ursula von der Leyen began her second term as president in December 2024
The **Parliament** is elected every five years; Portugal has 21 of the 720 seats
The **Council of the EU** often votes by qualified majority: 55% of member states representing 65% of the EU's population
The **European Council** of presidents and prime ministers sets overall direction; its president since December 2024 is the former Portuguese prime minister António Costa

deep.x: The courts and the bank
The Court of Justice in Luxembourg makes sure EU law is applied the same way everywhere. The European Central Bank in Frankfurt runs the euro.

deep.w: Brussels imposes laws on countries
deep.r: National governments in the Council and elected MEPs must both approve most EU laws

deep.x: EU law needs both the voters' Parliament and the governments' Council to agree.

cards.title: NATO
cards.text: NATO is a military alliance founded in 1949. An attack on one member is treated as an attack on all (Article 5). It has 32 members after Finland and Sweden joined in 2023–24.

deep.x: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949 by 12 countries, including Portugal, which was a founding member despite being a dictatorship at the time. Its core is Article 5: an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
How it works

NATO has headquarters in Brussels and an integrated military command. Members keep their own armies but plan, train and exercise together. Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the 11 September 2001 attacks on the USA.
Spending

In 2014 members agreed to aim for 2% of GDP on defence. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, most reached it, and at the 2025 summit in The Hague they agreed a new target of 5% by 2035, including 3.5% on core defence.
Portugal's role

x: Lajes air base in the Azores has been a key Atlantic stopover for allied aircraft since the Second World War
NATO's naval strike command (STRIKFORNATO) is based in Oeiras
A NATO lessons-learned centre is based in Lisbon

deep.x: Not every EU member is in NATO: Austria, Ireland, Malta and Cyprus remain outside.
NATO's promise is simple: an attack on one is an attack on all.

cards.title: Economic organisations
cards.text: The IMF lends to countries in crisis (including Portugal in 2011), the World Bank funds development, the WTO sets trade rules and the OECD compares policies among richer countries.

deep.x: In 1944, at Bretton Woods in the USA, the Allies designed institutions to avoid a repeat of the 1930s, when trade wars and currency crises deepened the Great Depression. The result was the IMF and the World Bank; trade rules followed.
Portugal and the IMF

Portugal has borrowed from the IMF three times: in 1977, 1983 and 2011. In 2011, facing a debt crisis, it received a €78 billion bailout from the "troika" of the European Commission, the ECB and the IMF, in return for spending cuts, tax rises and reforms. Portugal exited the programme in 2014 and repaid the IMF early.
Trade rules under strain

The **WTO**, created in 1995, has 166 members and a rule that countries can't discriminate between trading partners. Its appeals body has been unable to work since 2019, after the USA blocked new judges, and rising tariffs since 2025 have tested its rules further.
Comparing countries
The **OECD** in Paris, which Portugal helped found in 1961, has 38 mostly rich members. It publishes the PISA tests of 15-year-olds and policy comparisons.

deep.w: The IMF just imposes austerity
deep.r: Its loans come with conditions, but it lends when no one else will; the conditions themselves are much debated

deep.x: These organisations are the rulebook and the safety net of the world economy.

cards.title: The CPLP

items: Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé, Timor-Leste, Equatorial Guinea

cards.text: The Community of Portuguese Language Countries, founded in 1996, links nine countries where Portuguese is official, promoting the language and cooperation.

deep.x: The **Comunidade dos Países de Língua Portuguesa** was founded in Lisbon on 17 July 1996, and its headquarters is in Lisbon. It brings together about 300 million people on four continents.
Who joined when

Seven countries founded it. East Timor joined in 2002 after independence, and Equatorial Guinea in 2014, a controversial choice since Portuguese is little spoken there and the country is criticised over human rights.
What it does

x: Promotes the Portuguese language, including 5 May as World Portuguese Language Day, recognised by UNESCO
Political cooperation, for example in election observation
A 2021 **mobility agreement** makes it easier for citizens to live and work in other member states
Many countries, from Japan to the UK, have joined as associate observers

deep.x: Brazil has about 70% of the CPLP's population, so most Portuguese speakers in the world are Brazilian.
The CPLP turns a shared language into a diplomatic network across four continents.

cards.title: International courts
cards.text: The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states; the International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Both sit in The Hague.

deep.x: The two courts in The Hague are often confused, but they judge different things. One settles arguments between countries; the other puts individuals on trial.
The International Court of Justice

The ICJ has 15 judges elected for nine years. It sits in the Peace Palace and hears cases only when states accept its jurisdiction. It also gives advisory opinions; in 2025 it said that countries have legal obligations to protect the climate. Major cases include genocide claims brought by The Gambia against Myanmar and by South Africa against Israel.
The International Criminal Court

The ICC was created by the 1998 Rome Statute and began work in 2002. It's a court of last resort, acting only when national courts are unable or unwilling. About 125 countries are members, but the USA, China, Russia and India are not.

x: The ICC has no police force and relies on states to arrest suspects
Arrest warrants for leaders like Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu have strained relations with several countries

deep.x: The Peace Palace, which houses the ICJ, was paid for by the Scottish-American industrialist Andrew Carnegie and opened in 1913.
The ICJ judges countries, the ICC judges people, and both depend on governments to enforce their rulings.

cards.title: Limits of cooperation
cards.text: International organisations depend on members' willingness. Vetoes, unpaid budgets and rivalries limit what they can do, but they remain the main forums for global problems.

deep.x: International organisations are only as strong as their members let them be. There's no world government to enforce decisions; countries cooperate when they see benefit, and can walk away when they don't.
Why it's hard

x: **Free riders:** every country benefits from a stable climate or safe seas, even if it doesn't pay its share
**Sovereignty:** governments resist rules that limit their freedom
**Power:** strong countries can ignore rulings or withdraw, as the USA did from WHO and the Paris Agreement in 2025

deep.x: Why it still works

Much quiet cooperation goes unnoticed: shared aviation and shipping rules, postal agreements, radio frequencies, disease surveillance and weather data. The 1982 Law of the Sea gives Portugal a huge exclusive economic zone of about 1.7 million km², one of the largest in Europe.
The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phased out ozone-destroying chemicals, is the first UN treaty ratified by every country in the world.
International organisations can't force countries to cooperate, but they make cooperation far easier when countries choose it.

Which Portuguese politician became UN Secretary-General in 2017?
quiz.explain: He'd led the UN Refugee Agency.

quiz.q: What does NATO's Article 5 say?
options: An attack on one is an attack on all

lessons.title: World religions and cultures
lessons.summary: Beliefs, festivals and customs, in brief.

cards.title: Major religions
cards.text: Christianity and Islam are the largest religions, followed by Hinduism and Buddhism. About 15% of people are unaffiliated with any religion.

deep.x: Counting believers is harder than it looks. Surveys ask different questions, and many people belong to a tradition by culture or family without practising it. Figures below come from large studies and are rounded.
The "nones"

Older estimates put the religiously unaffiliated at about 15%. A 2025 Pew Research study, counting more carefully, put them nearer a quarter, which would make them the third-largest group. Most live in China, and many still pray, visit temples or hold spiritual beliefs.
Who is growing?

x: **Islam** is the fastest-growing major religion, mainly because Muslim populations are young and have more children
**Christianity** is shrinking in Europe but growing in sub-Saharan Africa, now home to the largest number of Christians
**Buddhism** is roughly stable or declining as East Asian populations age

deep.w: The unaffiliated are all atheists
deep.r: Most do not call themselves atheist; many hold some beliefs without a religion

deep.x: Most people on Earth still identify with a religion, but the map is shifting south to Africa and away from Europe.

cards.title: Abrahamic religions
cards.text: Judaism, Christianity and Islam share roots in the figure of Abraham and belief in one God. Jerusalem is sacred to all three.

deep.x: All three religions trace their story back to Abraham, who in tradition left the city of Ur in Mesopotamia and was promised descendants "as many as the stars". They share a belief in one God who speaks through prophets and scripture.
How they relate

**Judaism** is the oldest, centred on the covenant between God and the people of Israel. **Christianity** grew out of Judaism in the 1st century, around Jesus, whom Christians see as the Son of God. **Islam** began in Arabia in 610 CE, when Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad began receiving the Quran.
Shared figures

x: Abraham, Moses and David appear in all three
Islam honours Jesus as a great prophet, though not as divine
All three have holy days of rest: Saturday, Sunday, and Friday prayers

deep.x: Sizes today
Christianity has about 2.3 billion followers, Islam about 2 billion, and Judaism around 15 million, most of them in Israel and the USA.
Arabic Christians and Jews also say "Allah" for God: it is simply the Arabic word for God.
Judaism, Christianity and Islam are branches of one family tree, which is why they share prophets, stories and Jerusalem.

cards.title: Religions of India and East Asia
cards.text: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism began in South Asia. Confucianism, Taoism and Shinto shaped China and Japan, often blended with Buddhism.

deep.x: The religions born in India share key ideas: **karma** (actions have consequences), **rebirth** in a cycle of lives, and the hope of release from that cycle.

items.b: end suffering by the Middle Way

deep.x: Buddhism's journey
The Buddha taught in north India around the 5th century BCE. His teaching later almost vanished from India but spread across Asia, changing as it went.
The East Asian mix

x: **Confucianism**, from Confucius (551–479 BCE), is more an ethic than a religion: respect for parents, elders, learning and good government
**Taoism** seeks harmony with the Tao, the "way" of nature, and balance of yin and yang
**Shinto**, Japan's native tradition, honours **kami**, spirits in nature, ancestors and places, at shrines marked by red torii gates

deep.x: In China, Korea and Japan people often combine these freely. A Japanese family may celebrate a birth at a Shinto shrine and hold a funeral at a Buddhist temple.
Sikhism is one of the youngest world religions: Guru Nanak was born in 1469, and the Golden Temple in Amritsar serves free meals to tens of thousands of people every day.
In much of Asia, religions are mixed and combined rather than chosen one at a time.

cards.title: Religion in Portugal
cards.text: Most Portuguese identify as Catholic, though regular practice has declined. Fátima, where Marian apparitions were reported in 1917, is one of the world's major pilgrimage sites.

deep.x: In the 2021 census, about 80% of people aged 15 and over who answered said they were Catholic, and about 14% said they had no religion. The share of non-believers has grown fast among young people and in cities.
Belonging without attending

Many Portuguese baptise children, marry in church and join local festas, but only a minority go to Mass every week. Catholic traditions still shape the calendar: holidays like 15 August, 1 November and 8 December, and popular saints' days such as Santo António in Lisbon and São João in Porto.
Fátima

In 1917 three shepherd children, Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta, reported apparitions of the Virgin Mary on the 13th of each month from May to October. On 13 October a crowd of tens of thousands reported the "miracle of the sun".
Today Fátima receives several million visitors a year, with the largest crowds on 12–13 May and October.
A secular state
Since the 1976 Constitution, church and state are separate and freedom of religion is guaranteed. Immigration has brought growing evangelical, Orthodox, Muslim and Hindu communities.
Portugal expelled or forcibly converted its Jews in 1496–97; in 2015 it offered citizenship to descendants of those Sephardic Jews.
Portugal remains culturally Catholic, even as fewer people practise regularly.

cards.title: Calendars
cards.text: Most of the world uses the Gregorian calendar (1582). The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each year. Chinese New Year follows a lunisolar calendar.

deep.x: A calendar is a way of fitting human counting to the sky. The trouble is that the Sun, the Moon and the day don't divide into each other neatly.
Why Pope Gregory changed it

The old Julian calendar was 11 minutes a year too long, so by the 1500s Easter was drifting. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII dropped 10 days: in Portugal, Spain and Italy, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October. Britain only switched in 1752 and Russia in 1918.
Leap year: divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400

x: 2024 ÷ 4 → leap year
1900 ÷ 400 not exact → not leap
2000 ÷ 400 exact → leap

deep.x: The Islamic calendar

It counts 12 lunar months of 29 or 30 days, about 354 days in all. With no correction, Ramadan comes about 11 days earlier each year and travels through all the seasons in about 33 years. Year 1 begins with the Hijra in 622 CE.
Lunisolar calendars

Chinese and Jewish calendars use lunar months but add an extra month about 7 times every 19 years to stay in step with the seasons. That's why Chinese New Year always falls between late January and late February.
Ethiopia uses its own calendar, about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one, with 13 months.
Every calendar is a compromise between the Sun, the Moon and tradition.

cards.title: Festivals of light
cards.text: Many cultures celebrate light in the dark season: Diwali (Hindu), Hanukkah (Jewish), Christmas (Christian) and Lunar New Year lanterns.

deep.x: In the northern hemisphere, the darkest weeks come around the winter solstice, about 21 December, when Lisbon gets only about 9.5 hours of daylight. Lighting lamps against the darkness is one of humanity's oldest instincts.
The stories behind them

x: **Diwali** celebrates the victory of light over darkness, often the god Rama's return home; families clean houses, light small clay lamps called diyas and honour Lakshmi, goddess of wealth
**Hanukkah** remembers the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the 2nd century BCE, when a little oil is said to have burned for eight days
**Christmas** marks the birth of Jesus, with candles, lights and the idea of Christ as "light of the world"
The **Lantern Festival** closes Lunar New Year celebrations on the first full moon

deep.x: Borrowed customs
Festivals mix over time. The Christmas tree came from Germany, Father Christmas from several European folk figures, and Diwali is now celebrated by Sikhs and Jains too, each with their own story.

deep.w: Jesus was born on 25 December
deep.r: The date is unknown; the Church chose it in the 4th century, near the solstice

deep.x: Across faiths, people answer the darkest time of year in the same way: by lighting lamps together.

cards.title: Greetings around the world
cards.text: Customs differ: handshakes, bows in Japan, cheek kisses in Portugal and France (two kisses in Portugal), the wai in Thailand, namaste in India.

deep.x: Greetings signal respect, closeness and status in a second or two. Getting them wrong rarely causes offence for a visitor, but getting them right builds trust fast.
The rules inside the gesture

x: In **Japan**, a light bow of about 15° is casual; about 45° shows deep respect or apology. Business cards are offered with both hands.
In **Thailand**, the higher the hands in the wai, the more respect shown; younger people wai first.
In **Portugal**, two kisses are normal between women, and between men and women, in social settings; men usually shake hands or hug.
In **France** the number of kisses varies by region, from one to four. The Netherlands and Belgium often use three.
In some Muslim countries, people may avoid touching someone of the opposite sex and place a hand on the heart instead.

deep.x: Changing habits
The COVID-19 pandemic made many people briefly drop handshakes and kisses for elbow bumps and nods, though most habits came back.
In New Zealand, the Māori **hongi** greeting involves gently pressing noses and foreheads together, sharing the breath of life.
A greeting is a small ritual of respect, and watching what locals do is the safest guide.

cards.title: Time and punctuality
cards.text: Attitudes to time vary: Swiss and German meetings start exactly on time; in many Mediterranean and Latin American cultures, schedules are more flexible. Knowing the norms avoids misunderstandings.

deep.x: The anthropologist Edward T. Hall described two broad attitudes to time. In **monochronic** cultures, time is a line of slots: one thing at a time, on schedule. In **polychronic** cultures, time is flexible: several things at once, with relationships taking priority over the clock.
Examples

x: Switzerland, Germany and Japan prize punctuality; Japanese bullet trains are on average late by under a minute
Spain, Portugal, Italy, Brazil and much of the Arab world tend to treat social times more loosely
In Brazil, arriving exactly on time for a party at a friend's home may find the hosts still getting ready

deep.x: It depends on the setting
Most cultures mix both. A Portuguese dinner invitation for 20:00 may start at 20:30, but a job interview, a flight or a doctor's appointment still expects you on time.

deep.w: People in flexible cultures don't care about time
deep.r: They value different things, like relationships and adapting to events

deep.x: Being "on time" is a cultural agreement, not a universal rule, so ask what it means where you are.

cards.title: High and low context
cards.text: In low-context cultures (Germany, Netherlands, USA), people say things explicitly. In high-context cultures (Japan, China, Arab countries), much is implied by relationship and situation.

deep.x: Edward T. Hall also introduced this idea, in his 1976 book Beyond Culture. **Context** means everything around the words: shared history, tone, status, silence and setting.
How it sounds

In a low-context culture, "This plan won't work" means exactly that. In a high-context culture, the same message might be "That's an interesting idea; it could be difficult", and listeners understand it as a polite no.

items.r: In high context, 'maybe' often means no
In low context, blunt means clear

deep.x: Why it matters at work

x: Low-context teams write detailed contracts, agendas and emails
High-context teams rely on trust built over meals and long relationships
Mixed teams misread each other: one side feels insulted, the other feels confused

deep.x: Where Portugal sits

Portugal is somewhere in the middle, more indirect than Germany or the Netherlands, more direct than Japan. Portuguese people often soften criticism and value personal relationships before doing business.
The writer Erin Meyer found that people from high-context cultures often read more into a message than was meant, while low-context listeners miss the hints entirely.
Low-context cultures put the meaning in the words; high-context cultures put it in the situation.

cards.title: UNESCO heritage
cards.text: UNESCO lists over 1,200 World Heritage sites. Portugal has 17, including the Jerónimos Monastery, Sintra, the historic centres of Porto, Évora and Guimarães, and the Douro wine region.

deep.x: The World Heritage Convention, signed in 1972, protects places of "outstanding universal value". There are now about 1,250 sites, cultural, natural or both. Italy and China have the most, around 60 each.
Portugal's 17 sites
Others include Angra do Heroísmo, Évora, Alcobaça, Porto, the Côa Valley rock art, Madeira's laurel forest, Pico's vineyards and Elvas. Only the Laurisilva of Madeira is listed as natural heritage.
What listing means

x: The country must protect the site and report on its condition
Sites can be put on a "danger" list, and a few have been removed
Listing often brings a surge in tourists, which can strain small places

deep.x: Living heritage too
Since 2003 UNESCO also lists **intangible heritage**: traditions rather than places. Fado (2011), cante alentejano (2014) and the Mediterranean diet, shared with other countries, are on it.
The Côa Valley engravings were discovered during work on a dam; protests in the 1990s stopped the dam and saved thousands of Stone Age carvings.
World Heritage status recognises a place as belonging to all humanity, and obliges its country to look after it.

quiz.q: How many cheek kisses are usual in Portugal?
quiz.explain: Two, starting with the right cheek.

quiz.q: Why does Ramadan move earlier each year?
options: The Islamic calendar is lunar, about 11 days shorter

quiz.q: Which three religions consider Jerusalem sacred?

lessons.title: Cities
lessons.summary: Urbanisation, megacities and liveable places.

cards.title: An urban planet
cards.text: Since about 2007, more people live in cities than in the countryside. By 2050 about two-thirds of humanity is expected to be urban.

deep.x: For almost all of history, most people lived on farms. In 1800 perhaps 1 in 10 people lived in towns. By 1950 it was about 30%, and around 2007 the world became majority urban for the first time.

v.unit: % of people living in cities (UN est.)

deep.x: Where the growth is

Europe and the Americas are already about three-quarters urban. Nearly all new urban growth to 2050 will be in Asia and Africa. India, China and Nigeria alone are expected to add hundreds of millions of city dwellers.
What counts as "urban"?

Every country uses its own definition, from 2,000 people in a settlement to 50,000. In 2025 the UN adopted a common method based on population density, which counts cities, towns and rural areas separately. Numbers shift with the method, but the direction is the same.
Portugal
About two-thirds of Portuguese live in urban areas, mostly along the coast between Braga and Setúbal and in the Algarve. Many inland villages have lost half their population since 1960.
The UN estimates that the urban population grows by roughly 200,000 people a day, the size of a city like Braga.
Humanity became an urban species only in the 21st century, and the shift is still accelerating in Africa and Asia.

cards.title: Megacities
cards.text: Cities with over 10 million people are megacities. There are over 30 today, most in Asia: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo, Mexico City, Cairo, Mumbai.

deep.x: The UN calls a city with more than 10 million inhabitants a **megacity**. In 1950 there were only two, New York and Tokyo. By 2018 there were 33, and over 40 are expected by 2030.
Beyond Asia

x: **São Paulo** and **Mexico City** each have over 20 million people in their urban areas
**Cairo** is the largest city in the Middle East and North Africa
**Lagos** and **Kinshasa** are among the fastest growing, adding hundreds of thousands each year
Europe's largest are **Istanbul**, **Moscow** and **Paris**

deep.x: Size brings problems

Megacities struggle with traffic, air pollution, water supply and housing. Many in poorer countries grow faster than governments can build pipes, roads and schools. Some, like Lagos and Jakarta, also face flooding as land sinks and seas rise.

deep.w: Megacities are mostly in rich countries
deep.r: Most are in middle-income countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America

deep.x: The world's biggest cities have moved from the rich West to the growing South.

cards.title: Why cities grow
cards.text: Cities offer jobs, education, healthcare and opportunity. Clustering people and firms boosts productivity and innovation.

deep.x: People move to cities for higher wages, more kinds of work, better schools and hospitals, and simply more choice. On average, urban workers are more productive than rural ones, even in the same country.
Agglomeration
Economists call the benefits of clustering **agglomeration economies**. They come from three things:
Bigger is more productive

Studies of many cities found that output and patents grow slightly faster than population, while roads and cables grow slower. That's why big cities are both richer per person and more efficient in infrastructure.

x: City doubles in size
Output per person rises about 15%
Road length per person falls about 15%

deep.x: Costs of growth
The same density raises rents, congestion and pollution, which can push people back out to the suburbs.
Silicon Valley, Hollywood and the City of London show the same effect: once a cluster forms, talent keeps arriving because the others are already there.
Cities grow because putting people close together makes them more productive and gives them more choice.

cards.title: Lisbon and Porto
cards.text: Lisbon's metropolitan area has about 2.9 million people, Porto's about 1.8 million. Together they hold nearly half of Portugal's population.

deep.x: The **Lisbon Metropolitan Area** has 18 municipalities and about 2.9 million people; the **Porto Metropolitan Area** has 17 municipalities and about 1.8 million. The cities themselves are much smaller: about 550,000 in Lisbon and 230,000 in Porto.
A coastal country

Since the 1960s, people have moved from the interior to the coast and abroad. Most growth went to the suburbs: Sintra, Amadora, Vila Nova de Gaia and Matosinhos are now among the most populous municipalities.
Different histories

Lisbon's centre, the **Baixa**, was rebuilt on a grid after the 1755 earthquake, using an early anti-earthquake wooden frame, the gaiola. Porto's medieval Ribeira grew around its river trade and has been a World Heritage site since 1996.
Strengths and strains

x: Both now attract foreign students, remote workers and tech firms
Both suffer from high rents and long commutes for those priced out
Inland regions keep losing people, ageing and closing services

deep.x: The Lisbon metro area produces over a third of Portugal's GDP, more than its share of the population.
Portugal is increasingly a country of two metropolitan regions, with the interior emptying around them.

cards.title: Informal settlements

items.l: people in slums or informal settlements (UN estimate)

cards.text: About a billion people live in slums or informal settlements without secure housing, clean water or sanitation, mostly in fast-growing cities of Africa and Asia.

deep.x: UN-Habitat estimates that about 1.1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements. A household counts as a slum household if it lacks at least one of: clean water, decent sanitation, durable housing, enough living space or secure tenure.
Why they form

When cities grow faster than formal housing, newcomers build their own homes on vacant or risky land: hillsides, riverbanks, rail edges. Without legal title, they can be evicted, and authorities often don't provide water, sewers or rubbish collection.
Famous examples

x: **Dharavi** in Mumbai: about a million people on roughly 2 km², with thriving workshops and recycling
**Kibera** in Nairobi: one of Africa's largest informal settlements
Brazil's 2022 census counted about 16 million people in favelas, about 8% of the population

deep.x: What works

Upgrading settlements in place usually works better than demolishing them and moving people far from their jobs. Medellín in Colombia linked hillside barrios to the centre with cable cars and libraries.
Portugal had its own "bairros de lata": in the early 1990s tens of thousands still lived in shacks around Lisbon and Porto until a large rehousing programme, the PER, began in 1993.
Informal settlements are the housing of last resort for growing cities, and they improve fastest when residents are secure.

cards.title: Transport
cards.text: Good public transport, cycling and walking make cities more liveable. Lisbon's trams and metro, Porto's metro (opened 2002) and new bus rapid transit lines aim to reduce car dependence.

deep.x: A street lane can carry very different numbers of people depending on how they travel. Cars use space inefficiently, because most carry one person and sit parked over 90% of the time.
Lisbon and Porto

Porto's metro is mostly a light rail running on the surface, which made it cheaper to build and gave it about 70 km of lines. In 2019 metropolitan passes were cut to about €40 a month, and ridership jumped. Porto has added a **Metrobus** line along Avenida da Boavista, a bus rapid transit route with its own lane.
What makes transport work

x: Frequent services, so you don't need a timetable
Fast, dedicated lanes or tracks, so buses aren't stuck in traffic
One ticket across all operators
Safe paths for walking and cycling to and from stations

deep.x: Lisbon's famous tram 28 still uses small 1930s-style cars, because modern trams don't fit its steep, narrow streets.
The most liveable cities make the train, bus, bike and footpath the easiest way to get around.

cards.title: The 15-minute city
cards.text: The idea: everyday needs like shops, schools, health and parks should be reachable within 15 minutes on foot or by bike. Paris has promoted it since 2020.

deep.x: The term was popularised by the Franco-Colombian researcher Carlos Moreno around 2016. Anne Hidalgo made it the centre of her 2020 campaign for mayor of Paris.
Old idea, new name

In the 1920s, planners designed "neighbourhood units" around a school. In the 1960s, Jane Jacobs praised lively mixed streets. Car-centred planning after the Second World War separated homes, offices and shops, and the 15-minute city tries to mix them again.
In practice

x: **Paris** added hundreds of km of bike lanes, closed some riverbanks to cars and opened schoolyards as neighbourhood parks
**Barcelona** created "superblocks", groups of nine city blocks where through traffic is diverted and streets become squares
**Melbourne** plans "20-minute neighbourhoods"

deep.x: Limits
It needs enough density to support local shops and services. Rising house prices in popular neighbourhoods can push out the people it was meant to help.

deep.w: 15-minute cities stop people leaving their area
deep.r: No one is restricted; the aim is to make travel optional, not forbidden

deep.x: The 15-minute city aims to bring daily life back within walking distance, rather than banning travel.

cards.title: Heat in cities
cards.text: Concrete and asphalt absorb heat, making cities several degrees warmer than surrounding countryside. Trees, parks, light-coloured roofs and water features cool them.

deep.x: The **urban heat island** effect makes cities warmer than the countryside around them, especially at night, when the difference in big cities can reach 5–10 °C.
Why concrete heats up

x: Asphalt and dark roofs reflect little sunlight, so they absorb most of it
Stone and concrete store heat by day and release it slowly
There are few plants and little soil, so less water evaporates to cool the air
Cars, air conditioners and factories add waste heat

deep.x: Why it matters
Hot nights stop bodies recovering, so heatwaves are most dangerous in cities, especially for older people. A study estimated that Europe's summer heat in 2022 caused over 60,000 deaths.
Old wisdom

Southern cities long used whitewashed walls, narrow shaded streets, courtyards and fabric shades. Seville and Córdoba still stretch awnings over streets in summer, and many Alentejo towns are painted white.
On a sunny summer day, dark asphalt can exceed 60 °C on its surface, while grass nearby stays close to air temperature.
Cities make their own heat, but trees, water and lighter surfaces can take several degrees off.

cards.title: Housing pressure
cards.text: Many popular cities, including Lisbon and Porto, face rising rents and house prices driven by demand, tourism and limited supply. Governments try new construction, rent rules and limits on short-term rentals.

deep.x: Housing prices follow supply and demand, and in Portugal demand has grown much faster than supply. House prices more than doubled between 2015 and the mid-2020s, while wages rose far more slowly.
Why demand rose

x: Tourism: short-term rentals (alojamento local) took many central homes off the long-term market
Foreign buyers, digital nomads and, until 2023, "golden visas" for property investment
Low interest rates in the 2010s and more people living alone

deep.x: Why supply lagged

After the 2008 crisis construction collapsed, many builders closed, and licensing remained slow. Portugal also has a small public housing stock, about 2% of homes, compared with over 15% in the Netherlands and Austria.
What other cities try

**Vienna** owns or funds a large share of its housing, keeping rents moderate. **Barcelona** plans to end tourist flat licences. Each tool has trade-offs: strict rent caps can discourage new building, while building takes years.
In Lisbon, the average asking rent for a typical flat has been well above the national minimum wage.
Housing gets expensive when demand outruns supply; lasting fixes need more homes, not only rules.

cards.title: Smart cities
cards.text: Sensors and data help cities manage traffic lights, parking, waste collection, water leaks and air quality more efficiently.

deep.x: A smart city uses sensors, networks and data to run services better. The idea is simple: measure what is happening, analyse it, then act, often automatically.
Everyday examples
Why it matters

Water networks often lose a fifth or more of their water through leaks, so finding them early saves money and energy. Bins that report when they are full can cut collection routes. Lisbon runs an urban management platform that brings together data from transport, weather and emergency services.
The risks

x: **Privacy**: cameras and phone data can track people's movements
**Lock-in**: cities can become dependent on one tech supplier
**Hype**: some projects cost a lot and change little

deep.x: Toronto's plan for a high-tech neighbourhood run by a Google sister company was dropped in 2020 after public concern about data and control.

items.r: Smart = solving real problems with data

deep.x: Singapore models the whole island in 3D as a "digital twin", so planners can test how new buildings affect wind, shade and traffic.
A city is smart when data helps it serve people better, not simply when it has more gadgets.

quiz.q: Since about when have more people lived in cities than in the countryside?
What is a megacity?
options: A city of over 10 million people

lessons.title: Climate change
lessons.summary: What's happening, why, and what can be done.

cards.title: The greenhouse effect
cards.text: Greenhouse gases like CO₂ and methane let sunlight in but trap some of the heat Earth radiates. Without them Earth would be about −18 °C on average; with more of them, it warms.

deep.x: Sunlight arrives mostly as visible light, which passes easily through the air and warms the ground and oceans. The warm surface then gives off energy as invisible **infrared** radiation. Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour absorb some of that infrared and send part of it back down, so the surface ends up warmer than it would otherwise be.
A natural blanket, thickened

Without any greenhouse gases, Earth's average temperature would be about −18 °C. With them it is about 15 °C, a difference of roughly 33 °C that makes liquid oceans and life possible. The problem is not the effect itself but adding more gas, which thickens the blanket.
Not all gases are equal

x: Water vapour is the biggest greenhouse gas, but it acts as a feedback: warmer air holds more of it, which amplifies warming caused by other gases
Methane traps about 80 times more heat than CO₂ over 20 years, but breaks down in about a decade
CO₂ is weaker per molecule, but a large share of it stays in the air for centuries

deep.w: A real greenhouse works the same way
deep.r: Glasshouses stay warm mainly by stopping warm air escaping; the atmosphere traps infrared radiation

deep.x: Greenhouse gases don't create heat; they slow its escape, so the surface warms until balance returns.

cards.title: CO₂ is rising
cards.text: CO₂ in the air was about 280 parts per million before industry. It passed 420 ppm in 2023, the highest in at least 800,000 years.

deep.x: Since 1958, CO₂ has been measured continuously at Mauna Loa in Hawaii, a project started by Charles David Keeling. The **Keeling Curve** shows a steady climb with a yearly zigzag: CO₂ falls each northern summer as plants grow, and rises in winter as leaves decay.
How we know about the past

Bubbles of ancient air are trapped in Antarctic ice. Drilling cores up to about 3 km deep gives a record going back about 800,000 years. Through all the ice-age cycles, CO₂ swung between about 180 and 300 ppm. Today's level is far outside that range, and it is rising about 2–3 ppm a year.
Where the CO₂ goes
Humans emit roughly 40 billion tonnes of CO₂ a year. Only about half stays in the air. Roughly a quarter dissolves in the oceans and a quarter is taken up by plants and soils.

x: We know the extra CO₂ comes from fossil fuels: it carries a chemical fingerprint of old plant carbon, with almost no carbon-14 left
The ocean's share makes seawater more acidic; surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 since 1850, which harms shellfish and corals
1 ppm of CO₂ ≈ 7.8 billion tonnes of CO₂ in the air
Yearly rise of about 2.5 ppm
≈ 20 billion tonnes added to the air each year

deep.x: The last time CO₂ was this high, probably around 3 million years ago, sea levels were many metres higher than today.
CO₂ has risen by half since industry began, and the rise is still speeding up rather than slowing.

cards.title: How much warmer?
cards.text: The world is about 1.2–1.3 °C warmer than pre-industrial times on average. 2024 was the warmest year on record, around 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial average.

deep.x: Global temperature is calculated by averaging thousands of measurements from weather stations, ships and buoys, compared with the 1850–1900 average. Several independent teams, in Europe, the US and Japan, get almost the same answer.
Small number, big change

A degree sounds tiny next to daily swings of 10 °C or more. But this is an average over the whole planet, all day and all year. During the last ice age, about 20,000 years ago, the world was only about 5–6 °C colder, and ice sheets covered northern Europe.

x: Land has warmed faster than the oceans, about 1.6 °C on average
The Arctic has warmed about three to four times faster than the global average
Each of the last ten years has been among the ten warmest on record

deep.x: Why 2024 doesn't break Paris yet

The Paris limits refer to the average over about 20 years, not single years. Natural swings, such as El Niño warming the Pacific, add or subtract a tenth of a degree or two. At current rates, the long-term average is expected to pass 1.5 °C around 2030.

deep.w: One cold winter disproves warming
deep.r: Weather varies day to day; climate is the long-term average, and that keeps rising

deep.x: About 1.3 °C of global warming is already a large shift; the ice-age difference was only about five degrees.

cards.title: Where emissions come from
cards.text: Most emissions come from burning fossil fuels for electricity and heat, transport, industry and buildings. Agriculture and land use (deforestation, livestock) add a large share.

deep.x: About three-quarters of greenhouse gas emissions come from burning energy: coal, oil and gas. The rest comes mostly from farming and land, chemical reactions in industry such as making cement, and rotting waste in landfills.
Inside the energy slice

x: Industry, such as steel, chemicals and cement kilns: about a quarter of all emissions
Buildings, mainly heating and electricity used in homes and offices: about a sixth
Transport: about a sixth, three-quarters of it from road vehicles
Leaks of methane from oil, gas and coal production add several per cent more

deep.x: Who emits

China emits about 30% of the world's CO₂, the US about 13%, India and the EU about 7% each. Per person the picture changes: an average American emits about 14 tonnes of CO₂ a year, a Portuguese person about 4 tonnes. Over history, the US and Europe have emitted the most in total.

v.unit: tonnes CO₂ per person per year (approx.)

deep.x: Cement alone causes about 8% of world CO₂, half from the chemical reaction that turns limestone into lime, not from the fuel.
Most emissions come from how we make energy, so changing the energy system is the heart of the solution.

cards.title: Impacts
cards.text: Warming brings more heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and heavy rain; rising seas; shrinking glaciers and sea ice; and stress on crops and ecosystems.

deep.x: Extra heat in the climate system shows up in many ways. More than 90% of it goes into the oceans, which expand as they warm. Together with melting glaciers and ice sheets, this has raised global sea level by about 20–25 cm since 1900, and the rate has roughly doubled since the 1990s to about 4 mm a year.
Heavier rain and fiercer heat

Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour for each degree, so when it rains hard, it rains harder. At the same time, higher temperatures dry soils and vegetation faster, making droughts and wildfires worse. A heatwave that would have happened about once in 50 years before industry now happens almost five times as often.
Ice and ecosystems

x: Arctic sea ice in late summer covers about 40% less area than in 1979
Swiss glaciers lost about half their volume between the 1930s and 2016
Warmer seas cause coral bleaching; mass bleaching events now hit most of the world's reefs
Species are shifting towards the poles and up mountains, and spring arrives earlier

deep.w: Climate change is a problem for the future
deep.r: Its effects, such as record heat deaths and sea-level rise, are already measured today

deep.x: Each fraction of a degree makes the extremes more frequent and more severe, which is why every tenth matters.

cards.title: Portugal's risks

items: Droughts in the Alentejo and Algarve

cards.text: Portugal is among Europe's most exposed countries: hotter summers, longer droughts in the south, more severe wildfires, and coastal erosion along the Atlantic.

deep.x: The Iberian Peninsula sits on the boundary between temperate Europe and the dry subtropics. As the climate warms, the dry subtropical belt is expanding northwards. For Portugal this means hotter, longer summers and less rain, especially in the south and interior.
Water and heat

The Alentejo and Algarve are most exposed. In 2022 almost the whole country was in severe or extreme drought, and in 2023–24 the Algarve imposed water restrictions as reservoirs fell very low. Portugal's highest recorded temperature, over 47 °C at Amareleja in 2003, was nearly matched by 47 °C in Pinhão in July 2022.
The coast and the forests

Much of Portugal's sandy coast is retreating. Rising seas combine with fewer sediments, because dams trap sand that rivers once carried to the sea. Places like Costa da Caparica, Espinho and Ofir need repeated sand replenishment and sea walls. Inland, hotter and drier summers lengthen the fire season; in 2017 over 500,000 hectares burned.

x: The 2017 fires killed over 100 people
Wine regions are already harvesting earlier

deep.x: Some winemakers in the Douro are planting at higher altitudes and on north-facing slopes to escape rising heat.
Portugal faces climate change from both sides: heat and drought inland, and a rising, eroding sea on the coast.

cards.title: The Paris Agreement
cards.text: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, almost every country agreed to limit warming to well below 2 °C, aiming for 1.5 °C, with national plans updated every five years.

deep.x: The Paris Agreement was adopted at the COP21 climate conference in December 2015 and came into force in November 2016. Almost every country joined. Unlike the earlier Kyoto Protocol, which set targets only for rich countries, Paris asks every country to set its own goals.
How it works

Each country submits a **nationally determined contribution** (NDC): its own plan for cutting emissions. Every five years, plans must be updated and should become more ambitious, a process called the ratchet. A global stocktake checks collective progress.
Strengths and weaknesses

x: Targets are not legally binding, but reporting is; it relies on transparency and peer pressure
Rich countries pledged climate finance to help poorer ones; at COP29 in 2024 the goal was raised to at least $300 billion a year by 2035
The EU submits one shared plan for all its members, including Portugal
The United States has left the agreement twice, most recently with a withdrawal announced in 2025

deep.x: Before Paris, the world was heading for about 3.5–4 °C of warming by 2100. Current policies point to roughly 2.5–3 °C: better, but still far above the goal.

deep.w: Paris failed because warming continues
deep.r: It bent the curve down, but current plans still fall well short of 1.5 °C

deep.x: Paris is a framework that relies on countries raising their ambition every five years.

cards.title: Net zero
cards.text: Net zero means cutting emissions as close to zero as possible and balancing the rest with removals (forests, carbon capture). Portugal aims for climate neutrality by 2045.

deep.x: Warming stops roughly when CO₂ emissions reach **net zero**: no more is added to the air than is removed. That's because CO₂ accumulates; temperature tracks the total amount ever emitted. Cutting emissions by half slows warming, but only net zero stops it.
net emissions = emissions − removals
Removals are limited

Forests and soils can absorb carbon, but fires, droughts and logging can release it again. Machines that capture CO₂ directly from air exist but are small and costly, often several hundred euros per tonne. So removals should balance only the hardest-to-cut emissions, such as some from farming, aviation and cement.
The targets

x: The EU aims for climate neutrality by 2050, with a cut of at least 55% by 2030 compared with 1990
Portugal's Climate Law of 2021 set neutrality by 2050, with the government aiming to bring it forward to 2045
Portugal closed its last coal power station, Pego, in 2021
Think of a bath
Emissions = the tap, removals = the plug hole
The level stops rising only when inflow = outflow

deep.x: To keep a 50% chance of staying under 1.5 °C, the world has only a few years of current emissions left.
Net zero means the CO₂ level stops rising: whatever we still emit, we must also take back.

cards.title: Solutions
cards.text: The biggest levers: clean electricity, electrified transport and heating, efficient buildings and industry, protecting forests, less food waste and changes in diet.

deep.x: Most of the technology needed already exists, and much of it is cheap. Solar power costs fell by about 90% between 2010 and 2020, and wind by about 70%. In most countries new solar or wind is now the cheapest electricity to build.
Electricity first, then electrify
Once electricity is clean, switching other uses to it cuts emissions twice over. Electric motors and heat pumps are also far more efficient than burning fuel.

x: An electric car turns about 80–90% of its battery energy into motion; a petrol car about 25–30% of its fuel
A heat pump delivers about 3–4 units of heat for each unit of electricity
Portugal got about 70% of its electricity from renewables in 2024, mainly wind, hydro and solar

deep.x: Food and land

About a third of food produced is lost or wasted, and food waste causes about 8–10% of global emissions. Beef and lamb produce many times more emissions per gram of protein than beans, poultry or tofu. Stopping deforestation, especially in the tropics, protects one of the largest carbon stores.

deep.w: Individual choices don't matter
deep.r: Policies matter most, but choices like heating, travel and diet shape demand and markets

deep.x: No single fix exists: the big wins come from clean electricity, then using it for almost everything.

cards.title: Adaptation
cards.text: Even with cuts, some change is locked in. Adaptation means preparing: heat plans, fire-resistant landscapes, water storage, flood defences and resilient crops.

deep.x: Even if emissions stopped tomorrow, some change is locked in. Oceans react slowly, and sea level will keep rising for centuries. **Adaptation** means reducing harm from changes we can no longer avoid, while **mitigation** means cutting emissions to limit how bad they get. Both are needed.
What adaptation looks like

x: Heat-health warning systems, cooled public spaces and shade trees; Portugal has run a heat-warning system for over two decades
Fire-resistant landscapes: clearing fuel around houses, grazing, and a mosaic of farmland and mixed native forest
Water: fixing leaky pipes, reusing treated wastewater, storing winter rain, and desalination planned for the Algarve
Flood defences, drainage tunnels in Lisbon, and not building on flood plains
Crops and varieties that need less water or tolerate heat

deep.x: Limits to adaptation

Adaptation gets harder and costlier as warming rises. Some coral reefs and glaciers cannot be saved, and some coastal places may eventually need to be abandoned. That's why adaptation cannot replace cutting emissions.
The Netherlands, with about a quarter of its land below sea level, already plans its dykes and storm barriers for sea levels expected around 2100.
Adaptation buys safety against the change already coming; only cutting emissions limits how much more arrives.

quiz.q: What was the CO₂ concentration before industry?
