lessons.title: Natural hazards
lessons.summary: Earthquakes, volcanoes, storms and how to prepare.

cards.title: Earthquakes
cards.text: Earthquakes happen when stress along a fault is suddenly released. Most occur at plate boundaries. Portugal sits near the boundary between the Eurasian and African plates.

deep.x: Earth's outer shell is broken into tectonic plates that creep a few centimetres a year. Where plates meet, rocks grind and lock together. Stress builds for decades or centuries until the rock suddenly slips along a **fault**, releasing energy as seismic waves. Geologists call this elastic rebound.
Waves through the ground

The point where slip starts underground is the focus; the spot directly above it is the epicentre. Fast **P-waves** (pressure waves) arrive first as a jolt. Slower **S-waves** and surface waves follow with stronger side-to-side and rolling motion, which does most damage.

x: Instruments record about 20,000 earthquakes a year worldwide
About 15 are magnitude 7 or more
The Pacific "Ring of Fire" has most of the biggest ones

deep.x: Portugal's earthquakes

South of Portugal, the African plate pushes slowly against the Eurasian plate along the Azores–Gibraltar zone. The great Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755, estimated around magnitude 8.5, was followed by a tsunami and fires; tens of thousands died. Marquês de Pombal rebuilt the Baixa with an early anti-seismic wooden frame, the **gaiola pombalina**.

deep.w: Big earthquakes only happen in faraway places
deep.r: Portugal has had several large ones and will have more; only the date is unknown

deep.x: Earthquakes are stored-up strain released in seconds, and Portugal sits close to a plate boundary that does it.

cards.title: Magnitude
cards.text: Magnitude scales are logarithmic: each whole step releases about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 8 releases about 1,000 times more energy than a magnitude 6.

deep.x: **Magnitude** measures the energy released at the source. Charles Richter created the first scale in 1935. Seismologists now use the moment magnitude scale, based on the area of fault that slipped and how far it moved, but it gives similar numbers.

x: Magnitude 6 to 7 = 32 × the energy
7 to 8 = 32 × again
32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 × the energy of a magnitude 6

deep.x: Magnitude versus intensity

Magnitude is one number for the whole earthquake. **Intensity** describes how strong the shaking felt at a particular place, using the Mercalli scale from I (not felt) to XII (total destruction). A moderate quake under a city can be deadlier than a huge one offshore.
The biggest

x: Chile, 1960: magnitude 9.5, the largest ever recorded
Alaska, 1964: 9.2
Sumatra, 2004: about 9.1
Japan, 2011: about 9.1

deep.x: A magnitude 9 releases about as much energy as a million magnitude 5 earthquakes.
Each step up the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy, so the top of the scale is vastly more powerful.

cards.title: What to do in an earthquake

steps: After shaking: coast? Go to high ground

cards.text: Drop, cover and hold on: get under a sturdy table, protect your head and hold on until shaking stops. Stay away from windows. Near the coast, move to high ground if shaking is strong or long.

deep.x: Most injuries in earthquakes come from falling objects and collapsing furniture or walls, and from people trying to move while the ground shakes. The aim is to protect your head and neck and avoid being thrown about.
Indoors, outdoors, driving

x: Indoors: stay inside; don't run for the exit, as glass and masonry fall outside walls
No table: crouch by an inside wall, away from windows, and cover your head with your arms
In bed: stay there and protect your head with a pillow
Outdoors: move away from buildings, trees and power lines
Driving: stop away from bridges and overpasses and stay in the car

deep.x: After the shaking
Expect aftershocks. Check for injuries and gas leaks; if you smell gas, open windows and leave. Don't use lifts. Use the phone only for emergencies, so lines stay free.
Near the coast

If shaking is strong or lasts more than about 20 seconds, or the sea suddenly draws back, move quickly to high ground or inland. Don't wait for an official warning: in 1755 the tsunami reached Lisbon within about half an hour.

deep.w: The safest place is a doorway
deep.r: Modern doorways are no stronger than other walls, and doors can swing and injure you

deep.x: Portugal's civil protection holds an annual "A Terra Treme" exercise: one minute when schools, offices and families practise drop, cover and hold on.
When the ground shakes, drop, cover and hold on; on the coast, then head for high ground.

cards.title: Tsunamis
cards.text: Undersea earthquakes can lift the sea floor and launch tsunamis that cross oceans at jet speed. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people.

deep.x: A **tsunami** is a series of waves made when a large volume of water is suddenly displaced, usually by an undersea earthquake lifting or dropping the sea floor. Landslides and volcanic eruptions can also cause them. The name is Japanese for "harbour wave".

steps: Slow and grow at the coast

deep.x: Fast and hidden

In deep water a tsunami can be less than a metre high, but its wavelength is hundreds of kilometres. Its speed depends on depth. As it reaches shallow water it slows down, and the water piles up into a wall or a fast-rising flood several metres high.
speed ≈ √(g × depth)

x: Ocean depth 4,000 m
≈ 700 km/h, as fast as a jet

deep.x: Deadly examples

x: 26 December 2004: a magnitude 9.1 quake off Sumatra sent waves across the Indian Ocean, killing about 230,000 people in 14 countries
2011, Japan: waves over 10 m high killed about 18,000 people and flooded the Fukushima nuclear plant
1755: the Lisbon tsunami struck the Tagus, the Algarve and Morocco

deep.x: Warning signs

A strong quake near the coast, a roar from the sea, or the sea suddenly withdrawing all mean: go to high ground now. There were no warning systems in the Indian Ocean in 2004; one has operated since 2006. IPMA monitors Portugal's coast.

deep.w: A tsunami is one giant wave
deep.r: It's a series of waves, often over hours, and the first is not always the largest

deep.x: A tsunami can cross an ocean in hours; the natural warning signs are often your best alarm.

cards.title: Volcanoes
cards.text: Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, at plate boundaries or hotspots. The Azores have active volcanoes; Capelinhos on Faial erupted in 1957–58, adding new land.

deep.x: A **volcano** forms where molten rock, called magma, rises from deep underground and erupts at the surface. Once it erupts it is called lava. About 1,350 volcanoes on land are considered potentially active, and around 50 to 70 erupt each year.
Gentle or explosive

The style of eruption depends on the magma. Runny, low-silica basalt lets gas escape easily, producing lava fountains and flows, as in Hawaii and Iceland. Sticky, silica-rich magma traps gas until it blasts out in ash clouds, as at Mount St Helens in 1980.
The Azores

The Azores lie where three plates meet, with a hotspot underneath. São Miguel, Terceira, Faial, Pico and São Jorge all have active volcanic systems. Pico's summit, at 2,351 m, is the highest point in Portugal.

x: Capelinhos on Faial erupted from September 1957 to October 1958, adding about 2.5 km² of new land
Thousands of Azoreans emigrated to the US afterwards under a special law
Hot springs at Furnas are used to cook "cozido" in the ground

deep.x: The 1815 eruption of Tambora in Indonesia threw so much ash and gas into the sky that 1816 became "the year without a summer" in Europe.
Volcanoes are where Earth's interior reaches the surface; in the Azores they built the islands themselves.

cards.title: Hurricanes and typhoons
cards.text: Tropical cyclones form over warm oceans (above about 26.5 °C). They're called hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the northwest Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

deep.x: A **tropical cyclone** is a giant heat engine. Warm sea water evaporates, the moist air rises, and as the vapour condenses into clouds it releases heat, which makes the air rise faster and pulls in more moist air. Earth's rotation makes the whole system spin.
What it needs

x: Sea surface above about 26.5 °C, warm to a depth of about 50 m
Light winds high up, so the storm isn't torn apart
Distance from the equator, at least about 500 km, so the spin from Earth's rotation can start the swirl

deep.x: Wind, rain and surge

Storms are rated 1 to 5 on the Saffir–Simpson scale; category 5 means sustained winds above about 252 km/h. But the biggest killer is often the **storm surge**, sea water pushed onto land by wind and low pressure. In 2005 Hurricane Katrina's surge flooded about 80% of New Orleans.
Portugal's encounters

The Azores are sometimes hit: Hurricane Lorenzo in 2019 destroyed the port of Lajes das Flores. On the mainland, storms usually arrive weakened. Leslie struck near Figueira da Foz in October 2018 with gusts around 175 km/h. As seas warm, such storms may reach Iberia more often.

deep.w: A hurricane's category tells you how dangerous it is
deep.r: Rain and storm surge often kill more than wind, even in low categories

deep.x: Tropical cyclones are fuelled by warm oceans, so their power rises as the seas heat up.

cards.title: Wildfires
cards.text: Hot, dry, windy weather plus fuel (dense undergrowth, eucalyptus and pine plantations) makes fires spread fast. In 2017, wildfires in Portugal killed over 100 people.

deep.x: A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. How fast it spreads depends on weather, fuel and terrain. Firefighters in Portugal talk of the **30-30-30 rule**: when it's above 30 °C, humidity is below 30% and wind is over 30 km/h, fires can quickly become uncontrollable.
Why Portugal burns

x: About a quarter of Portugal's forest is eucalyptus, grown for paper pulp; along with maritime pine, it burns readily
Rural depopulation has left fields and woods unmanaged and full of scrub
The vast majority of fires are started by people, through carelessness or arson
Hotter, drier summers make the fuel more flammable

deep.x: On 17 June, a fire at Pedrógão Grande killed 66 people, many trapped in cars on a road. On 15 October, winds from storm Ophelia fanned hundreds of fires across the centre and north, killing about 50 more. That year over 500,000 hectares burned, the worst in Portugal's history.
Reducing the risk

Owners must clear vegetation within 50 m of houses and 100 m around villages. Grazing goats, controlled burning in winter and replacing plantations with a mosaic of farmland and native oaks and chestnuts all slow fires.
Large fires can create their own weather, building towering pyrocumulus clouds and winds that spread flames even faster.
Fire risk comes from weather, fuel and people; we can't control the weather, but we can manage fuel and behaviour.

cards.title: Floods
cards.text: Floods come from heavy rain, rivers overflowing, storm surges and flash floods in steep valleys. Building on flood plains increases the damage.

deep.x: Floods happen when water arrives faster than the ground, rivers and drains can carry it away. There are several kinds, each with different warning times.
Flash floods are deadliest

In steep valleys and dry riverbeds, water can rise metres in minutes. In Madeira on 20 February 2010, torrential rain sent floods and debris down ravines into Funchal, killing about 45 people. In October 2024, extreme rain near Valencia in Spain killed over 220 people.
Concrete makes it worse

In a forest most rain soaks in. Roads, roofs and car parks are impermeable, so water rushes straight into drains and streams. Building on flood plains puts homes exactly where rivers naturally spread.
Staying safe

x: Never walk or drive through floodwater: about 15 cm of fast water can knock you over, and about 30 cm can float a car
Move to higher floors, not cellars or underground car parks
Lisbon is building large drainage tunnels to protect its low-lying Baixa

deep.x: In November 1967, a night of torrential rain caused floods around Lisbon that killed about 500–700 people, Portugal's deadliest flood.
Floods are water with nowhere to go, made worse when we pave the ground and build where rivers spread.

cards.title: Heatwaves

items: Never leave anyone in a parked car

cards.text: Heatwaves are the deadliest weather hazard in Europe, especially for older people. Drink water, stay cool, check on vulnerable neighbours and avoid the midday sun.

deep.x: Heatwaves kill more people in Europe than any other weather hazard, yet the deaths are often unseen: they happen quietly at home and show up later as excess deaths in statistics. The summer of 2003 caused about 70,000 extra deaths across Europe, and 2022 about 60,000.
How heat harms the body

The body cools itself by sweating; evaporation carries heat away. When air is very hot or humid, this works less well and core temperature rises. The heart must pump harder to send blood to the skin, which strains people with heart or lung disease.
Who is most at risk

x: Older people, who feel thirst less and sweat less
Babies and young children
People with chronic illness or on some medicines
Outdoor workers and people living alone or in hot top-floor flats

deep.x: Keeping cool

Keep shutters and curtains closed by day and open windows at night when it's cooler. Drink water regularly before feeling thirsty, avoid the sun between about 11:00 and 17:00, and check daily on neighbours who live alone. Never leave a child or pet in a parked car, which can exceed 50 °C inside.

deep.w: Only very hot days are dangerous
deep.r: Warm nights matter too: without cooler nights the body can't recover

deep.x: Heat is a silent killer; the most important protection is keeping vulnerable people cool and checked on.

cards.title: Preparedness
cards.text: Know your local risks, have an emergency kit (water, torch, radio, medicines, documents), agree a family meeting point and follow official alerts from Proteção Civil.

deep.x: Emergency services can't reach everyone at once in a big disaster. Being ready to look after yourself for the first few days makes a real difference. The EU advises households to be able to manage on their own for at least 72 hours.
An emergency kit

x: Water: a few litres per person per day, for three days
Food that keeps and needs no cooking
Torch, battery or wind-up radio, spare batteries, power bank
Medicines, first aid kit, copies of documents, some cash

deep.x: A family plan

Agree where to meet if you are separated and phone lines are down. Choose a contact person outside the area. Know how to turn off gas, water and electricity. Learn your local risks: coastal tsunami zone, flood plain or forest edge.
Official alerts

In Portugal, the national civil protection authority (ANEPC, known as Proteção Civil) sends SMS alerts during fires and storms. IPMA issues weather warnings in yellow, orange and red. In an emergency, call 112.
The Iberian blackout of 28 April 2025 left mainland Portugal and Spain without power for many hours; a battery radio was one of the few ways to get news.
Preparing takes an hour; in a disaster it can save the hours that matter most.
